entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Twenty-Eighth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 83 days until the first spring-training game.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 143 · Saturday, the Twenty-Eighth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

83 days until the first spring-training game (Friday, the 19th of February, 2027).

News Around the League

THE PACIFIC DESK, SWEPT BARE: THE LAST GREAT LOT OF THE EASTERN SHELF GOES TO WRIGLEY — ITOH JOINS THE CUBS THE SAME DAY SATO AND ROGERS TURN OFFICIAL, AND TAKAHASHI, WHO NEEDED NO POSTING BELL AT ALL, TAKES HIS GROUND BALLS TO THE DESERT FOR THREE MILLIONS

The republic calls the day after its feast a shopping holiday, and the Cubs kept it like a sacrament. On Friday morning the club made official its two $120 million purchases — the left-hander Trevor Rogers for five years, the slugger Teruaki Sato for six — and by Friday night the wires carried a third stroke: the Wrigley establishment has reached agreement with the right-hander Hiromi Itoh, the finest arm left on the eastern shelf, on terms not yet known, pending a physical, the club not confirming. These columns left the man Wednesday as the shelf's last great lot, "lately seen calling in Chicago, his window shorter than ever" — the window has now closed, and it closed exactly where the paper last saw him standing.3

He is 29, six seasons a Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighter, and comes recommended less by the radar gun than by the finer instruments: a deep arsenal, a praised feel for spin and the shaping of pitches — the wire reaches, carefully, for comparisons to Yu Darvish — and command of the first order. This past season he pitched to a 3.18 earned-run average across 172 and two-thirds innings, 159 strikeouts against 34 walks and a walk rate of 4.7 percent; the year before, he took the Sawamura Award, the eastern game's answer to the Cy Young, at 2.52 with 195 strikeouts. The fit is the plainest thing about the purchase. The Cubs' pitching shop prizes exactly this blend of command, spin and durability, the defense behind him is stocked with Gold Glove-caliber men, and the rotation wants bodies: all five men who finished the season in Chicago's rotation walked to the market, and of the arms that remain only Assad returns from a season unmarred, with Steele and Garrett mending from elbow surgery, Cabrera from blisters and a leg, and Brown and Horton not expected until the new season is well grown. Rogers and Itoh would front the room; the club plans its introductions early in the week, and the newest man may share the dais.3

The desert, meanwhile, shopped an aisle nobody was watching. The Sonoran nine agreed with the right-hander Kona Takahashi on one year and $3 million, by the account of multiple reports — a man who needed no posting bell, having been posted a winter ago alongside his Seibu stablemate Tatsuya Imai and, when Imai took $54 million from Houston and no offer suited him, gone home on a contract whose opt-outs now deliver him to the open market unrestricted.5 He turns 30 in February and has thrown 1,337 and a third innings for the Lions since debuting at 18, all in the one uniform, at a career 3.30. The fastball sits in the low 90s and the trade is the ground ball — better than half his outs by that route for years, and nearer 60 percent this past season, when he pitched to a 2.54 with a career-best strikeout rate besides. Arizona pencils him into the contest for the back of a rotation fronted by Burnes, Rodríguez, Kelly and Pfaadt, the club hunting its first October since 2023.4 And the reader keeping the eastern ledger may now close it: Sato, Taira, Itoh and Takahashi — the winter's whole Pacific freight, landed inside of four days.

THE INK DESK: TORONTO BUYS A YEAR OF JAZZ — CHISHOLM, EIGHT-AND-TWENTY, TAKES TWENTY MILLIONS WRAPPED IN A LABYRINTH OF OPTIONS, THE MAPLE LEAF NINE DREAM OF SEMIEN'S PRECEDENT, AND THE QUEUE THE HERALD HAS KEPT ALL WEEK RESOLVES IN CANADA

The queue these columns have kept behind Jazz Chisholm Jr. since the GM Meetings — eleven clubs for conversation; the Jays, the Mets and the Nationals for intent — resolves in Canada. The Blue Jays agreed Friday with the second baseman on a contract of one year and $20 million, by a source's account, the club not confirming — this only hours after making official the five-year, $80 million purchase of the right-hander Kaima Taira, whose formal introduction comes Monday at the Rogers Centre.6

The paper is short but the clockwork inside it is not. The $20 million assembles from a 2027 wage of $12.5 million, a $6 million bonus, and a $1.5 million buyout of a player option for 2028 set at $16 million — and should the man decline that option, it transforms into a club option at $40 million, so that the two years together could pay him $58.5 million. Which is to say: Toronto has bought a year of upside and priced every outcome of it. The upside is real. He is 28, coming off a down Bronx year — .231 with 19 home runs and a .711 on-base-plus-slugging — that still carried 41 stolen bases, a strong glove and his customary voltage; he plays second chiefly, third and the outfield at need. The Toronto desk reaches at once for the house precedent: Marcus Semien, who came north on one year off a down season and struck 45 home runs with an .873 on-base-plus-slugging in 2021. That is a high bar, but motivation should want for nothing, with the open market waiting again as early as next winter.6

The addition firms an infield without unseating anyone so much as redeploying him: Ernie Clement, whose 2026 began hot and faded, is read not as demoted but as loosed upon all four infield posts and perhaps a corner of grass besides, with the platoon arithmetic — Chisholm long the better hitter against right-handers — writing the daily lineups. The want that remains is the one the whole league knows. No club in the majors scored fewer runs last season, the outfield is still open for business, and Suzuki remains the clean fit these columns have carried for days, with Arozarena likewise at liberty. A year of swagger is a fine start; the batting order wants a broadside yet.6

THE YOUTH DESK: QUEENS PAPERS ITS MORNING STAR THROUGH 2035 — EWING, TWO-AND-TWENTY, TAKES EIGHT YEARS AND FIVE-AND-NINETY MILLIONS, HIS FIVE-AND-TWENTY STOLEN BASES THE GRANDEST ROOKIE HAUL IN METROPOLITAN ANNALS

The Metropolitans, whose winter has run to the grandest purchases — Skubal's record $450 million among them, as these columns have chronicled — spent Friday securing the smallest wage on their books. The center fielder A.J. Ewing, 22 years old and seven months a big-leaguer, finalized an extension of eight years and $95 million, and with it the club holds him through 2035 — four seasons past the free agency the current rules would have granted him after 2032, with arbitration due after 2028. The Herald notes the timing without comment, save to observe that "the current rules" is a phrase with 3 mornings left on its own contract.7

The season that earned the paper was the bright spot of a dim year at Flushing: a May debut, then a .252 average with 11 home runs, 43 driven in and a .700 on-base-plus-slugging across 120 games, a sharp eye at the plate, a strong finish after a summer slump — and 25 bases stolen in 33 tries, a franchise record for a rookie. He made 96 starts in center field, took the corners and even second base at need, and with Benge in right and Soto in left he completes an outfield the club means to grow old slowly. The team around its three prize rookies — Ewing, Benge and the pitcher McLean — finished 74-88 and last in its division for the first time in 23 years, a record $358 million Opening Day payroll notwithstanding: perhaps the plainest argument yet printed that pennants are bought by the year but built by the decade. Ewing was a fourth-round selection in 2023, out of a high school in Springboro, Ohio.7

THE EXCHANGE DESK: THE WEEK THE WIRE GAVE KING RUNS TO ITS LAST GRAINS — SAN DIEGO IS CALLED 'MOST FOCUSED' ON ITS OLD ACE'S RETURN, THE MOUND CITY HUNTS THE MIDDLE SHELF, HALF A DOZEN CLUBS RING FOR VESIA, AND WOODRUFF, RISING FOUR-AND-THIRTY, DECLARES HE IS NOT DONE

Michael King remains at liberty, and the week the wire allotted him — these columns have carried Morosi's prophecy of a signature "before the week is out" since Wednesday — is down to its last grains with the pen still dry. The likeliest desk only grows likelier: the Mission nine, whose entire rotation save Vásquez walked to the market at once, are reported by the wire's AJ Cassavell to want their old right-hander home, and the Post's Jon Heyman calls them "most focused on" King — a man who has himself spoken warmly of a return — with the All-Star Nick Martinez, 3.10 for the Rays this past season, under consideration besides. The same club is tied to both Arozarena and Suzuki — ESPN's Passan has San Diego as perhaps "the favorites" on the latter, having lately hosted him — and its surplus of catchers draws the Pinstripes, who are thought to want Fermin or Campusano as right-handed company for Wells.8

The Mound City nine, quiet while the market roared, are reported shopping the middle shelf in earnest: the Post-Dispatch's Goold has them checked in on Imanaga, Bieber and Mize, and Morosi — whose King prophecy stands above, at hazard — adds a fourth name, saying he would believe "Nick Pivetta or a comparable starting pitcher" signs in St. Louis in the days to come. The left-handed relief market stirs behind Morejon meanwhile: some half a dozen clubs, by The Athletic's Kuty, are ringing for Alex Vesia — a 2.64 across 72 games for the Angelenos last season, 74 strikeouts in 58 innings on a fastball that rises out of an over-the-top slot, and since 2021 a 2.67 that stands tied for fourth-lowest among the game's qualified left-handed relievers.8

In Chicago the morning's shopping does not end the list: the Bruins are still expected to add starting pitching beyond Itoh, and The Athletic's Sharma and Mooney observe that Sato's six-year paper makes the club's deep shelf of position prospects — six of its top eight — into trade capital, with the wire naming the familiar sellers: Webb available by the Bay, the Pinstripes long on arms and short on bats, Texas listening on deGrom, Eovaldi and Gore, the Gulf Coast club on McClanahan and Jax — the same window this paper dressed only yesterday.8 And from Milwaukee, word that the oldest storyline on the shelf intends another chapter: Brandon Woodruff, 34 next season and healthy entering a winter for the first time since 2022, declares "I'm going to keep playing" — talks open with clubs, "the Brewers being one of them." The man took a single week's rest after pitching the final inning of the World Series' Game 3 rout and standing a champion two games later; he throws now off a mound built at his Mississippi home, his newborn son nearby, and the Herald — which carried his small, gleaming ledger in yesterday's inventory, 110 innings at 3.11 across two mended years — wishes the shoulder a quiet winter.9

THE INK DESK, SMALLER TYPE: THE DESERT TRADES FOR A FIRST-OVERALL GLOVE, SENDING TAWA TO PITTSBURGH FOR DAVIS — AND THE CUBS HAND COUNSELL ANOTHER 'OUT-GETTER' IN THE SOFT-CONTACT ARTIST YARBROUGH

Arizona's Friday ran to volume. Besides the Takahashi signing above, the desert establishment traded for its backup catcher, sending the utilityman Tim Tawa to Pittsburgh for Henry Davis — first overall in the whole draft of 2021, out of Louisville, and still only 27. The bat has never answered the billing: a .172 average and a .585 on-base-plus-slugging this past season, a third consecutive year below .200, though with career highs in home runs (10) and runs driven in (38). The glove is another matter entirely — across the past two seasons no regular catcher in the majors has thrown out base-stealers at a better rate, 35.6 percent, ahead of Contreras and Bailey, and only Contreras betters his 3.54 catcher's earned-run figure — and it is the glove Arizona bought, to stand behind Gabriel Moreno, the league's reigning batting champion. Tawa, an 11th-round man of the same draft, gave Arizona 178 games at every post but shortstop, catcher and the mound, batting .240 this past season; he crosses to the Smoky City men in exchange.10

And late Friday the Cubs added to the bullpen a man built to Counsell's specification: Ryan Yarbrough, 34 and left-handed, agreed on one year, terms undisclosed, the club not confirming. The manager famously keeps no titles in his relief room — "out-getters," he calls them all — and Yarbrough's whole career is the job description: 57 relief appearances and ten starts for the Pinstripes across the past two seasons at better than two innings an outing, a 3.69 this past year across 63 and a third innings, and contact so soft the instruments nearly refuse to grade it, the 100th percentile of the whole league in both average exit velocity and hard-hit rate and the 96th in barrels, off a five-pitch spread. Nine seasons, five clubs, a 4.18 in 253 games: the role has never had a name, and he has never needed one.11

THE WINTER CIRCUIT: THE FIRST SWING BACK — CASAS, A YEAR AND A HALF IN THE SURGEONS' LEDGER, RETURNS IN DOMINICAN FLANNELS AND CLEARS THE BASES AT SANTO DOMINGO

The winter circuits these columns commended to the armchair only yesterday wasted no time repaying the endorsement. At Estadio Quisqueya Juan Marichal in Santo Domingo on Friday night, Triston Casas of the Red Sox — who ruptured the patellar tendon of his left knee on the 2nd of May, 2025, and then lost the whole of 2026 besides to abdominal and wrist complaints in the mending — stepped in for his first plate appearance with the Tigres del Licey, his first in that league since the winter after his big-league debut in 2022, and with the count 0-2 put a changeup from the Gigantes' Bryan Rodriguez over the right-field barrier with the bases full: a grand slam, and a 5-0 lead before the first inning was done.12

The sentiment writes itself; the ledger is colder. Casas is 26, owns a career .241 average with a .348 on-base figure, a .452 slugging mark and 45 home runs across 952 plate appearances, and returns to a Fenway establishment that has meanwhile installed Contreras at first base and signed Jake Bauers this very month — which is why the wire ranks him as likely trade matter even as he rounds the bases. The Herald, for one morning, declines that arithmetic and simply marks the scene: a year and a half and better of surgeons' schedules, one pitch out of the hand, and the full tour of the bases at the end of it.12

No rest in Saturday's ledger: the nation made a shopping holiday of the feast's morrow and the ballclubs kept it faithfully — the eastern shelf sold out to its walls, Toronto wagered a year on Jazz, Queens papered its morning star through 2035, and a first baseman a year and a half in the mending announced himself with one swing at Santo Domingo — the whole of it set down above. The forward ledger was read before any word was set, by the house custom, and stands unmoved: the camps' reporting dates remain unposted, so the count runs to the first rung bearing a date — the spring exhibition openers of Friday, the 19th of February, 83 mornings from this one, with Opening Night to follow on Wednesday, the 24th of March, 116 mornings off.2 The nearer columns: the collective agreement has 3 mornings left to live; Cooperstown's committee of sixteen reports in 8; the Winter Meetings convene at San Diego with the Rule 5 drafting on December 9, 11 mornings from this one; and the writers' envelope waits for the 19th of January, 52 mornings off. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~

entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Twenty-Seventh of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 84 days until the first spring-training game.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 142 · Friday, the Twenty-Seventh of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

84 days until the first spring-training game (Friday, the 19th of February, 2027).

News Around the League

THE EXCHANGE DESK: THE MARKET KEEPS THE FEAST WITH ITS SHELVES HALF-CLEARED — SIX STARTERS SOLD AT FIFTY MILLIONS OR BETTER, KING STANDS ALONE AT THE HEAD OF WHAT REMAINS, SEVEN SOUND MID-ROTATION ARMS WAIT BEHIND HIM, AND THE TRADE WINDOW DRESSES WEBB, THE TEXAS DISCONTENTS AND TWO RESTLESS RAYS

The wires carried no new signature on the feast day itself, which makes this the morning for an inventory, and the wire's Thomas Harrigan has drawn one up. The month's bill of sale now runs to six starting pitchers at $50 million guaranteed or better: Skubal's record nine years and $450 million in Queens, Peralta's five and $125 million in Baltimore, Rogers' five and $120 million on the North Side, Taira's five and $80 million in Toronto, Sonny Gray's two and $55 million in the Twin Cities, and Dustin May's three and $52.5 million with the Pale Hose. Foster Griffin's three years and $48 million in Cleveland miss the threshold by a whisker, and the week's remaining purchases — Gausman to Detroit, Bubic to Cleveland, the Rockies' pair of ground-ball left-handers — stand recorded in these columns already.4

At the head of what remains stands Michael King, whom these columns have carried all week as tipped to sign before the week is out. The case for him is the ledger: a 3.15 earned-run average with 436 strikeouts across 432 innings for the Padres over the past three seasons, and 32 starts at a 3.21 this past year — whereupon he declined the last two years of his $75 million paper and walked back onto the market. Behind him waits a deep bench of mid-rotation soundness: seven unsigned men threw at least 200 innings over the past two seasons with both their adjusted earned-run and fielding-independent figures better than the league's common run — Nick Martinez, Matthew Boyd, Casey Mize, Clay Holmes, Tyler Mahle, Nick Pivetta and Michael Soroka — with Pivetta easily the best of them by the inning, though a flexor-tendon complaint swallowed much of his 2026. Ray, Bassitt, Flaherty and Imanaga cleared one bar of the two, and Brandon Woodruff's sample is small but gleaming: 110 innings in two years at a 3.11.4

The demand outruns the supply. The Cubs, the Orioles, the Jays, the White Sox and the Mets are all reckoned still shopping even after their purchases; the Astros, the Athletics, the Braves, the Snakes, the Cardinals, the Capital nine and the Giants could each use an arm; and no want is so pressing as the Padres', whose entire rotation — King, Pivetta, Ray, Mize, Buehler, Giolito and Canning — walked to the market at once. For the clubs that find the shelves too dear, the trade window dresses itself: the Orange and Black are now willing to listen on Logan Webb — a softening of the summer stance, and of a piece with the grander designs these columns noted Tuesday — while in Texas the names of deGrom, Eovaldi, Gore and the shortstop Seager all circulate as the Rangers hunt payroll relief — deGrom, Eovaldi and Seager each hold a no-trade clause, which leaves Gore, a free agent after 2027, the simplest to move. The Tampa men, for their part, insist Rasmussen stays after his $20 million option — the highest one-year wage in the franchise's history — but might yet part with McClanahan or Jax.4

THE LABOR QUESTION: FOUR MORNINGS REMAIN — THE OLD PEACE'S ONE UNDISPUTED INSTRUMENT PAYS ITS YOUNG MEN ON SCHEDULE, CROW-ARMSTRONG DRAWS A RECORD THREE MILLIONS AND A HALF FROM THE PRE-ARBITRATION POOL, AND THE POOL ITSELF SITS ON THE BARGAINING TABLE AT FIGURES MORE THAN A HUNDRED MILLIONS APART

While the principals kept the holiday, the machinery of the old agreement made its last scheduled payment. The figures of the pre-arbitration bonus pool — the $50 million instrument built into the March 2022 labor settlement to carry money to the game's best young men before arbitration can — were finalized by the league and the union midweek, and Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Cubs draws the largest sum ever paid from it: $3,548,994, past the record Paul Skenes set a year ago. The season so rewarded wants no argument — the center fielder was the unanimous Most Valuable Player of the National League at .280 with 45 home runs, 107 driven in and 41 bases stolen across all 162 games3 — and the arithmetic of the program tells its whole purpose in one line: the pool has now paid him $5,097,329 over three years, better than double the $2,282,186 his actual wages came to across the same seasons. His six-year, $115 million extension, signed in March, only begins with the new year.5

The rest of the roll reads like the autumn's honors list, which is the design working. The Milwaukee right-hander Jacob Misiorowski, the National League's Cy Young man, stands second at $3,164,848; the Bronx's Cam Schlittler, his American League counterpart, third at $3,124,038; Tampa Bay's Junior Caminero fourth and Cleveland's Parker Messick fifth. De La Cruz, Chourio, Varland and the Rookie of the Year McGonigle also cleared a million apiece. A hundred players shared the pool in all — the White Sox placed the most men with eight, while the champion Brewers' five split the largest club sum, $5,443,421 — and the cautionary entry is Skenes himself, fallen from first place to 35th and $316,248 on the strength of a down year: the pool pays the season, not the name.5

The Herald prints the ledger with its usual lean, and this week the lean is nearly a straight line: here is the one instrument of the last peace that both parties call a success, and the parties stand more than a hundred millions apart on it. The league's cap-and-floor proposal would raise the pool to $65 million next year and $75 million by 2033; the union asks $180 million next year, climbing by $15 million annually thereafter. That distance — on the mechanism everyone likes — measures the whole quarrel better than any statement either side has issued. The agreement that created the pool has 4 mornings left to live, expiring at one minute before midnight on the first of December, and the league's courthouse maneuver of Wednesday, asking a judge to bless its lockout in advance, stands as yesterday's columns recorded it.5

THE INFIRMARY WARD: THE SURGEON CLAIMS A SEASON ENTIRE — CASPARIUS, SEVEN-AND-TWENTY, LOSES HIS ELBOW LIGAMENT TO THE KNIFE AND ALL OF 2027 WITH IT, AND THE BULLPEN OF THE BOYS IN BLUE GROWS THINNER STILL

A grim bulletin from Los Angeles: the right-hander Ben Casparius underwent reconstruction of the ligament in his pitching elbow on Wednesday — Dr. Neal ElAttrache at the knife — and will miss the whole of the 2027 season. He is 27, and his 2026 was already a lost year in miniature: an 0-1 mark and a 9.64 earned-run average across five appearances with the big club, a 7.84 across 12 games at Triple-A Oklahoma City. The club will remember instead the 2025 edition — 7-5 with a 4.64 and two saves across 46 games of long, flexible relief for a championship staff.6

The loss lands on a bullpen already inventoried in these columns Tuesday: Phillips gone to Atlanta, Vesia to the open market, and the thrice-mended Robert Stephenson signed to minor-league terms as a lottery ticket behind Díaz and Scott. The arithmetic of that room now wants one arm more than it did a week ago.6

THE APPOINTMENTS COLUMN: THE BRONX HIRES AN OLD TORMENTOR FOR THE CHAIR BESIDE BOONE — HYDE, SIX SEASONS THE ORIOLES' MANAGER AND LATELY A TAMPA ADVISER, COMES TO THE YANKEES AS BENCH COACH, CHOSEN OVER HIS OWN BROTHER-IN-LAW

The Yankees have filled the chair at Aaron Boone's right hand with a man who spent six years trying to beat him from the opposite dugout. Brandon Hyde, 53, comes to the Bronx as bench coach, by sources' account to ESPN's Jorge Castillo, succeeding Brad Ausmus, who left this month to manage the Astros. The resume is a full one: six seasons and part of a seventh managing the Orioles, including the 101-win division champions of 2023 and the wild-card club of 2024, before the axe fell 41 games into 2025; a year since as an adviser in the Rays' baseball operations; and, earlier, the bench coach's post with the Cubs under Renteria and Maddon. The footnote is the stuff of a family novel: the Yankees chose Hyde over Joe Espada — his brother-in-law, the Astros' deposed manager and once the Yankees' own third-base coach — and the club still wants a hitting coach besides, James Rowson having departed to run the Giants' offense.7

THE WINTER CIRCUIT: LIVE BASEBALL NIGHTLY WHILE THE STOVE SMOLDERS — THE AUSTRALIAN LEAGUE'S WHOLE SEASON COMES TO THE LEAGUE'S OWN SCREEN FOR THIRTY DOLLARS, FOUR CLUBS AT NINE-AND-THIRTY GAMES APIECE, AND THE TALLEST MAN EVER TO PITCH FOR PAY

For the reader taking stock of a winter that may yet grow quieter still, the league's own screen offers an antipodean remedy: the Australian Baseball League's entire season — regular campaign and postseason alike — now streams on MLB.TV's MLB+ tier for $29.99, the Dominican and Mexican winter circuits riding in the same subscription. The season down under has been running since the 19th of November; its four clubs play 39 games apiece over ten weeks through the 23rd of January, with a best-of-three championship series set for the 29th through the 31st.8

The circuit's alumni book argues for the ticket: Acuña, Cristopher Sánchez, Imanaga and Caminero all passed through it on their way up, as did the Guardians' All-Star second baseman Travis Bazzana, the Australian taken first overall in the 2024 draft. And for the connoisseur of curiosities, the Sydney Blue Sox offer James Boeree, 7-foot-2 and the tallest man ever to play the professional game — summer baseball in December, visible from the armchair.8

THE SANDLOT DESK: EIGHT SURGERIES, ONE HERO, AND A TEXT THAT READS 'WELCOME TO THE NO-HIT CLUB' — A LONG ISLAND BOY OF THIRTEEN, BORN WITH A FUSED RIGHT HAND, HITS A GRAND SLAM AT COOPERSTOWN, THROWS A NO-HITTER ON HIS MOTHER'S BIRTHDAY, AND HEARS FROM JIM ABBOTT HIMSELF

A story for the morning after the feast, told at length by the wire's Anthony Castrovince. Carmine Pagano of Lindenhurst, New York, is 13, and was born with the fingers of his right hand fused — a condition it took eight surgeries, begun before he was two, to shape into three working fingers. His hero, from the time he knew anything of the game, was Jim Abbott, who pitched in the majors with one hand and threw a no-hitter for the Yankees against Cleveland in September of 1993; father and son studied the old films of the famous glove switch and practiced it together in the yard, the father buying himself a wrong-handed glove to make a fair contest of it.9

The bat was the stubborn problem — the right hand could not hold it through a swing — until a strapping accessory called the 9 Strap, built to bind a hitter's hands together through contact, solved in one winter what years of therapy could not. In August, at a youth tournament in Cooperstown, the boy worked a full count with the bases loaded and put the ball off the top of the fence and over: a grand slam, teammates pounding his helmet, the stands by his father's account become one large family. The company behind the strap heard the story and arranged a video call in September between the boy and his hero, who talked with him for half an hour about struggle and what follows it.9

Then, in October, on his mother's birthday, Carmine took the mound in a fall-league semifinal and carried a no-hitter through all five innings of a game ended early by the mercy rule — one walk, three strikeouts, not a hit. He texted the news to Abbott, who had kept in touch since the call, and the answer came back in five words the Herald prints as received: "Welcome to the no-hit club!" The paper's own sentiment desk, consulted on the holiday weekend, rules the item fully verified and entirely restorative.9

The republic fed yesterday, and the market rested with it: no new signature crossed the wires overnight, and the paper's columns turn instead to inventories — the state of the pitching shelves, the young men's pool paying out its record, and a boy on Long Island who joined the no-hit club. The forward ledger was read before any word was set, by the house custom, and stands unmoved: the camps' reporting dates remain unposted, so the count runs to the first rung bearing a date — the spring exhibition openers of Friday, the 19th of February, 84 mornings from this one, with Opening Night to follow on Wednesday, the 24th of March, 117 mornings off.2 The nearer columns: the collective agreement has 4 mornings left to live; Cooperstown's committee of sixteen reports in 9; the Winter Meetings convene at San Diego with the Rule 5 drafting on December 9, 12 mornings from this one; and the writers' envelope waits for the 19th of January, 53 mornings off. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Twenty-Sixth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 85 days until the first spring-training game.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 141 · Thursday, the Twenty-Sixth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

85 days until the first spring-training game (Friday, the 19th of February, 2027).

News Around the League

THE LABOR QUESTION: FIVE MORNINGS REMAIN — THE OWNERS SPEND THE EVE OF THE FEAST IN A FEDERAL COURTHOUSE, ASKING A JUDGE TO PRONOUNCE THEIR LOCKOUT LAWFUL BEFORE IT EXISTS, AND THE UNION CALLS THE SUIT COMPLETELY FRIVOLOUS

The owners went to law on the eve of the feast. On Wednesday — the last day the courthouse sits before the holiday weekend — Major League Baseball filed a class-action complaint in the federal court for the Southern District of New York, asking a judge to declare in advance that the lockout the whole game expects on the first of December would be lawful under the antitrust statutes, and would remain lawful even should the players' association renounce its standing as the men's bargaining agent. The league styles the filing purely defensive. "Today's filing is a defensive measure simply intended to keep the parties at the bargaining table to work towards a new collective bargaining agreement and a full 2027 season," said the spokesman Glen Caplin, who accused the union of "pretending to 'disclaim'" its status in order to sue under the antitrust laws — a maneuver the league calls the union's "nuclear option," and which it asked the court to "proactively disarm."3

The mechanics, for the reader who keeps the docket beside the box scores: the complaint seeks three declarations — that a lockout is protected by the labor exemption to the antitrust laws and would remain so after any disclaimer; that even unexempted it would be a reasonable restraint, temporary and designed to drive the parties to terms; and that the federal courts lack jurisdiction to enjoin it at all, Congress having long ago taken them "out of the labor injunction business." The playbook the league says it fears is a real one with a long pedigree: the disclaimer of interest — quicker and less formal than decertification, wanting no election of the men, only a letter from the leadership — has been run by the union's interim executive director Bruce Meyer and its outside counsel Jeffrey Kessler against the other leagues for three decades, football in 1989 and 2011, basketball in 1987, 1995 and 2011, hockey in 2012. By the league's own account the union could disclaim as early as Monday or Tuesday next — on the agreement's very deathbed — and the suit, which seeks no damages and does not interrupt the bargaining, was filed where the league means the fight to stay, in Manhattan, and not in "some unrelated location cherry-picked by the Union."3

The union required one paragraph. "The lawsuit filed today by MLB is completely frivolous," its statement read. "We will respond appropriately, but MLB's decision to run to court in the middle of negotiations rather than bargain in good faith is incredibly disappointing." The league answers that it is the union that has refused to so much as consider the cap-and-floor design, holding its antitrust threat as coercion; the Herald, whose sympathies on matters of the purse are of long record, notes only the novelty of the posture — the employer asking a judge to certify the padlock before the door is shut, and suing the workmen, in effect, for a thing they have not yet done. Both parties, it should be said plainly, remain at the table. The agreement expires at one minute before midnight on the first of December, 5 mornings from this one, and the week's furious ledger, set down below, says what the market thinks of the deadline.3

THE INK DESK: THE ROTATION SHELVES CLEAR BY THE ARMFUL — GAUSMAN, SIX-AND-THIRTY COME JANUARY, TAKES FIVE-AND-TWENTY MILLIONS TO DETROIT, CLEVELAND KEEPS ITS RESTORED WANDERER GRIFFIN FOR THREE YEARS AND EIGHT-AND-FORTY, AND DENVER SIGNS TWO GROUND-BALL LEFT-HANDERS BEFORE SUPPER

"We're going to continue to add arms," the Detroit president of baseball operations Scott Harris said this week, and these columns barely finish recording one purchase before the next wants ink. On Wednesday the Detroits agreed with Kevin Gausman on one year and $25 million, pending a physical and unconfirmed by the club. The right-hander turns 36 on the 6th of January, and what Detroit is buying is the rarest commodity in the modern game — innings on schedule: 175 or better in eight of his last ten full seasons (and one out shy in 2022), five consecutive seasons without a visit to the injured list, six seasons of 3.0 wins above replacement or more. The 2026 ledger between Toronto and the Cubs reads 9-12 with a 4.51, but the underwriting is sounder than the surface — a 3.74 fielding-independent figure against a career 3.61, with 9.3 strikeouts per nine and nearly four strikeouts for every walk, his best such marks since 2023, and 14 quality starts besides. The reunion is personal: his 14-win, 5.2-WAR season for the 2021 Giants came under a general manager named Scott Harris, and his history on the Detroit grounds runs seven quality starts in seven visits at a 1.93. He joins Valdez atop a young company of Melton, Jobe, Ryan, Olson and the newly arrived Gil — and the connoisseur of the wire's mortality will note that Toronto's "mutual interest" in a Gausman reunion was reported the very day Detroit signed him.414

Cleveland, whose purchase of a year of Bubic's mended arm these columns recorded only yesterday, spent Wednesday keeping its own: the Forest City nine are re-signing Foster Griffin for three years and $48 million, by a source's account, the club not confirming. The file is the season's best serial. A first-round choice of Kansas City in 2014, Griffin made his big-league debut on the 27th of July, 2020, and his elbow gave out in that very outing; seven appearances were his whole account through 2022, and he spent 2023 through 2025 pitching in Japan. He returned on a one-year wager with Washington and, at 31, made the All-Star team — a 3.06 across 129 and a third innings and 22 starts — was sold to Cleveland at the August deadline, posted an ugly 5.19 there that one eight-run wreck against Baltimore largely explains (3.73 across his other seven starts), and pitched October creditably, a 3.48 in three appearances with the Game 1 win of the league championship series against the Rays among them. The president of baseball operations Chris Antonetti called him, at the deadline, "one of the best starters in baseball"; the seven-pitch left-hander now joins Bubic, the strikeout king Williams and young Messick — and here too the wire's shelf-life is instructive, for Wednesday's rumor columns had Toronto eyeing him, and by nightfall he was off every list.514

And in Denver the winter that these columns observed Monday at least produces transactions now produces them in pairs. The Mountain men agreed with David Peterson on two years and $32 million and with Patrick Sandoval on three and $42 million, by multiple sources, neither announced — this on the heels of last week's Castillo-and-Martin freight from the White Sox, so that a staff which ran the game's worst starting figure, a 6.28, through a fourth consecutive season of 100 losses, has conjured some four-fifths of a rotation inside a fortnight. Peterson is the hometown entry — raised at Aurora, a first-rounder out of Oregon by the Mets in 2017, an All-Star in 2025, and lately the owner of a redemptive half-season: demoted to the Queens bullpen in May at a 6.09, traded to the Cubs at June's end, and thereafter 3.70 across 16 appearances with three earned runs or fewer in 12 of his final 13 starts. The trade of both men is the same trade — Peterson's career ground-ball rate stands at 50.7 percent and his fastball at a modest 92.3, Sandoval at his best living likewise on weak contact, his 2025 lost entire to elbow surgery — which is to say the Rockies have stopped shopping for strikeouts the altitude will not sell them, and started buying the ball on the ground.6

THE INK DESK, SMALLER TYPE: ROBERT COMES BACK TO BALTIMORE AT TWELVE MILLIONS ON A WAGER OF HEALTH, BOHM TAKES THE THIRD-BASE HOLE IN KANSAS CITY, SÁNCHEZ CARRIES HIS WALKS AND HIS NEW RING TO MIAMI, AND THREE BULLPENS DO THEIR MARKETING BEFORE THE HOLIDAY

The Baltimores, who declined Luis Robert Jr.'s $20 million option at October's end, re-signed the man Wednesday evening for one year and $12 million, by a source's account, the club not confirming. He is 29, and he wore Baltimore flannels for precisely three games — a lumbar herniation having cost him nearly three months of a season begun with the Mets after January's trade from the White Sox, a .223 average and 10 home runs his whole Queens account, before waivers carried him to the Chesapeake in August and a hamstring ended his year at 2-for-11. What $12 million buys is the memory of 2023 — .264 with 38 home runs, 36 doubles and an .857 on-base-plus-slugging, an All-Star and Silver Slugger season, in a career that opened with a Gold Glove and the runner-up's share of the Rookie of the Year vote — and another right-handed bat for an outfield where the left-swinging Beavers and Cowser had only O'Neill for balance. The club that crowned Peralta on Tuesday, as yesterday's columns recorded, is assembling its winter at speed.7

In Kansas City the hole the club dug itself a week ago is filled: Alec Bohm, late of Philadelphia, takes two years and $20 million to play the third base the Garcia freight to Seattle emptied — the six-player exchange that brought Miller to town, as these columns have recorded. Bohm is 30, an All-Star of 2024, and a run-producer by trade: 88 driven in this past season though he started but twice in the order's top third, against a career best of 97. The slash line sagged to .249/.315/.383, his faintest since 2021, but the contact instruments call him unlucky — an expected average of .265 against the printed .249 — and he closed at .298 after the All-Star break. He hits right-handed, which suits a club whose first baseman Pasquantino swings left; the platoon suggests itself.8

Miami's purchase is a connoisseur's: Gary Sánchez, one year and $6.5 million. The catcher is 33 until Wednesday next, twelve seasons deep, and arrives wearing a World Series ring from Milwaukee, where he hit .209 but walked at a 16.7 percent rate — third in the game among men with 250 trips to the plate, behind only Kurtz and Trout — and slugged 12 home runs behind Contreras, a 112 OPS+ in the sum. The power remains the resume: 201 career home runs, one for every 15.68 at-bats, tenth among active men of 3,000 plate appearances, wedged between Olson and Soto on that roll. He backs the sophomore Mack on a club that ranked 23rd in home runs, and he will take his swings as the designated hitter when a left-hander is up.9

The bullpens, too, did their marketing before the feast. The San Diego nine made their first notable stroke of the whole winter, three years and a reported $21 million for the left-hander JoJo Romero — seven seasons at a 3.51, a 2.07 for the 2025 Cardinals, a ring with Milwaukee this autumn and eight postseason innings of one run with 11 strikeouts, the lone run being Cronenworth's go-ahead blow in Game 3 of the division series — struck, the reader may relish, by a man of the very club that now signs him; whether the purchase portends Morejon's departure the wire cannot say. The Twin Cities nine agreed to two years with Kevin Ginkel, a career Diamondback of 341 appearances at 3.91, whose 2026 ran 72 strikeouts against 17 walks in 67 and two-thirds innings. And the Washingtons spent one year and $5 million on the tallest lottery ticket at liberty: A.J. Puk, 6-foot-7, who has not thrown a big-league pitch since April of 2025 — an elbow mended by internal brace, then a shoulder that swallowed 2026 whole — but whose 2022-24, a 3.38 with 242 strikeouts across 194 and a third innings, was the work of one of the game's best left-handed relievers.101112

THE PACIFIC DESK: THE LAUREL CATCHES UP TO THE FORTUNE — SATO IS NAMED THE CENTRAL LEAGUE'S MOST VALUABLE FOR A SECOND YEAR RUNNING, BY 213 FIRST-PLACE VOTES, SOME EIGHTEEN HOURS AFTER SIGNING HIS CHICAGO PAPER

The laurel has caught up to the fortune. At the Japanese game's awards ceremony Wednesday evening in Japan, Teruaki Sato was formally named the Central League's Most Valuable Player for the second consecutive season — 213 first-place votes, his Hanshin teammate Haruto Takahashi, the newly minted Sawamura laureate, a distant second at 34 — roughly eighteen hours after agreeing to the six-year, $120 million Chicago contract that led yesterday's edition of these columns. The season so honored is the one Chicago bought: the Central League's Triple Crown at .306 with 39 home runs and 106 driven in, 40 doubles and 68 walks beside a 1.017 on-base-plus-slugging across 143 games, following the 40-homer campaign of 2025 that won him the laurel the first time. The Herald admires the tidy order of operations — the fortune Tuesday, the crown Wednesday — and records the plain sum of it: the North Side establishment has purchased the reigning everything of the Japanese game.13

THE EXCHANGE DESK: WHAT THE FEAST FINDS STILL ON THE TABLE — ONE 'BIG THREE' OF TORONTO, PHILADELPHIA AND SAN DIEGO CIRCLES BOTH SUZUKI AND AROZARENA, MOREJON'S PRICE MAY SET A LEFT-HANDED RECORD, AND KING IS STILL TIPPED TO SIGN INSIDE THE WEEK

With Sato sold, the grandest bats at liberty are Seiya Suzuki and Randy Arozarena, and the wire's Jon Paul Morosi finds the same three establishments circling both sluggers: the Torontos, the Philadelphias and the San Diego nine. The fits are not mysterious. Toronto hit the fewest home runs in the majors this past season and Suzuki has struck 58 across the last two — Sportsnet's Ben Nicholson-Smith reckons an offer is probably coming if not already made, and the man would stand a third Japanese star beside Okamoto and the newly signed Taira — while Arozarena's 53 over the same span answers the identical want. Philadelphia seeks a right-handed bat to flank Harper and Schwarber, the need sharpened Wednesday when Bohm signed in Kansas City, as the smaller type above records; and San Diego could set either man in left beside Merrill and Tatis.14

The arms column is shorter and dearer. Adrian Morejon remains the best reliever at liberty, the Yankees and the Torontos both engaged by Morosi's account, a San Diego return not expected — the Romero purchase above reading naturally as cover — and the eventual contract could approach a record for a left-handed reliever in both length and yearly wage; the Bronx men weigh one large commitment against spreading the money across their other wants, a deliberation these columns recorded Tuesday. Michael King stands where yesterday's edition left him, the best starter unsigned and tipped by Morosi to find a home before the week is out, with Toronto — "busy and motivated" for pitching even after Taira, a six-man rotation contemplated to keep the newcomer's once-a-week habits — holding a radar of King, Mahle, Holmes and Martinez. The reader may take the measure of a Wednesday rumor's life expectancy from the fate of the list's other two names: Griffin re-signed in Cleveland and Gausman signed in Detroit before the report's ink was dry. And in Baltimore, by The Athletic's account, the next starter may arrive by trade, the club's glut of infielders and shelf of pitching prospects reckoned capital enough for a significant strike.14

THE ANGELENO DESK: OHTANI, ASKED WHY HE STILL INSISTS ON DOING TWO MEN'S WORK, ANSWERS THAT IT IS THE POST FROM WHICH HE HELPS MOST — AND VOWS TO REPAY THE YEAR'S FRUSTRATION WITH INTEREST

Speaking with the Japanese press by video on Wednesday, Shohei Ohtani settled the question the autumn's odder interviews had tried to raise: he remains a two-way man. "That's the position where I can help the team the most and make the best use of my strengths," he said, a man who once found the hitter-only life lonely answering as if the question puzzled him — and of the winter ahead: "I want to make this a good period to make up for this year's frustration next year." The frustration has a precise shape. The Angelenos' bid for a third consecutive championship died in a four-game sweep by Milwaukee in the league championship series, Ohtani's three-run clout in Game 4 arriving in a 6-4 loss, the bat having come good only at the end — "a little too late," by his own audit. "Of course I feel frustrated," he allowed.15

The season the infirmary interrupted had opened like his finest: 8-2 with a 1.79 earned-run average across 14 starts before a left knee and a right biceps, among other complaints, ended the pitching after the 3rd of July, while the bat ran to .275 with 30 home runs and 81 driven in across 135 games around a September spell on the shelf. He is 32, and he has not strung together a full two-way season since 2023 — the shoulder of the 2024 World Series, then the Classic-shortened winter, having each taken their toll on the ramp. The next ramp is itself unsettled: he and the club weigh several plans for Opening Day readiness, and the labor agreement's expiration on the first of December adds its own variable, a pitcher who throws too much in a stoppage buying nothing but fatigue. The aim he named is the only one that establishment recognizes: "The real battle is in October, so whether I can get there in the right spot is the battle ahead."15

A Thanksgiving paper, and the fullest eve-of-feast ledger of the winter: the owners went to law to have their padlock blessed in advance, nine clubs signed ten men between them, and the eastern league pinned its laurel on the man Chicago bought — the whole of it set down above. The forward ledger was read before any word was set, by the house custom, and stands as it has all week: the camps' reporting dates remain unposted, so the count runs to the first rung bearing a date — the spring exhibition openers of Friday, the 19th of February, 85 mornings from this one, with Opening Night to follow on Wednesday, the 24th of March, 118 mornings off.2 The nearer columns: the republic sits to its feast this very morning, and the market, as the reader has seen, did its shopping before the bird went in; the collective agreement has 5 mornings left to live; Cooperstown's committee of sixteen reports in 10; the Winter Meetings convene at San Diego with the Rule 5 drafting on December 9, 13 mornings from this one; and the writers' envelope waits for the 19th of January, 54 mornings off. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~

entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Twenty-Fifth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 86 days until the first spring-training game.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 140 · Wednesday, the Twenty-Fifth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

86 days until the first spring-training game (Friday, the 19th of February, 2027).

News Around the League

THE PACIFIC DESK, EMPTIED: THE EASTERN SHELF SELLS ITS TWO GRANDEST LOTS IN A SINGLE DAY — SATO CARRIES HIS TRIPLE CROWN TO WRIGLEY FOR SIX YEARS AND ONE HUNDRED TWENTY MILLIONS, TAIRA TAKES HIS IMPOSSIBLE FASTBALL TO TORONTO FOR FIVE YEARS AND FOURSCORE, AND THE FIRST OF DECEMBER COLLECTS ITS ACCOUNTS EARLY

The first of December has stood over the eastern market all week like a bailiff at the door, and on Tuesday the house sold its two grandest lots rather than test him. The slugger Teruaki Sato, the finest bat the posting season carried, agreed with the Cubs on a contract of six years and $120 million, by the account of sources — pending a physical, the club not confirming.4 Within hours the right-hander Kaima Taira, whose unlikely fastball these columns put under the instruments only yesterday, agreed with the Blue Jays on five years and $80 million, an opt-out standing after the third season, likewise unannounced.5 The reader will recall the clock beneath both courtships, set down in yesterday's Pacific column: should the labor agreement die on the first of December with no successor, the posting windows die with it — and the date has concentrated minds, as the prospect of hanging is said to do.

The man Chicago bought is 27, swings left-handed, and arrives wearing the Central League's Triple Crown: a .306 average, 39 home runs and 106 runs driven in for the Hanshin Tigers this past season, with 40 doubles, a .383 on-base figure and a .609 slugging mark besides. He is a five-time All-Star of the Japanese game, twice the Central League's Most Valuable Player, and took a Gold Glove at third base in 2025; the strikeouts that once shadowed the profile thinned a shade this past year, the rate easing to 26.7 percent while the walks climbed to 11.1. Third base in Chicago belongs to Alex Bregman for four seasons yet, so the newcomer projects to a corner of the outfield and the designated hitter's post — which is to say, into the twin vacancies left by Seiya Suzuki and Ian Happ, both at liberty. The wire reaches naturally for the Murakami comparison — the last man before Sato to wear an NPB Triple Crown, likewise a left-handed power bat, who struck 35 home runs as a rookie sensation for the White Sox — while noting the differences in kind: Sato the more aggressive swinger, with rather more contact in the zone; Murakami the more selective, with more walks and more missing.4

The purchase wants two annotations from the Herald's own files. First, the arithmetic: between Monday night and Tuesday the Cubs committed $240 million — five years and $120 million to the left-hander Trevor Rogers, as yesterday's columns recorded, and now six and $120 million to Sato — answering inside a single day both the emptied rotation and the emptied outfield these columns have inventoried all week. Second, the standing of the handicappers: industry sources had the Sato field narrowed only yesterday to the Yankees, the Phillies and the Jays, the Cubs expressly shorn from it — and the Cubs signed him all the same, though the wire's other prophecy, The Athletic's word that the signature would land before Thanksgiving, is hereby proven with room to spare. The club's long Japanese groundwork — the Suzuki purchase of 2022, Imanaga's after it, the scouting network the president Jed Hoyer has tended for years — did not wait upon the odds-makers' permission.48

Toronto's purchase is the bolder wager and the neater fit. Taira is likewise 27, stands 5-foot-8, and comes from the Seibu Lions, for whom he pitched this past season to a 1.36 earned-run average across 146 innings — the best figure in all Nippon Professional Baseball — with a fastball that touches 99 and departs, as yesterday's anatomy had it, from a slot only Joe Ryan undercuts among regular big-league starters, released further down the mound than most men a half-foot taller manage. The Toronto desk reaches for Marcus Stroman, the 5-foot-7 Jay of 2014 through 2019, then withdraws the comparison as quickly: Stroman lived on the ground ball, where Taira's trade is the swing and the miss. The rotation now reads Cease, Taira, Yesavage and Soriano, with Ponce fifth and Miles behind — respectable company for a club that finished 79-83 and last in its division — and the shopping is understood to turn next to the batting, where the need is absolute, no club in the majors having scored fewer runs. Suzuki remains the obvious fit, which would dress three Japanese stars in Toronto flannels beside Okamoto; and the Herald notes the wider arc, for this is the establishment whose losing Skubal bid of $420 million came to light only yesterday, now spending its consolation deliberately.5 What remains of the eastern shelf is chiefly one man: the Sawamura laureate Hiromi Itoh, lately seen calling in Chicago, his window shorter than ever.8

THE INK DESK: BALTIMORE LOSES ONE ACE AT MIDNIGHT AND ANNOUNCES HIS SUCCESSOR BY SUPPER — PERALTA, LAUREATE OF OCTOBER, TAKES ONE HUNDRED TWENTY-FIVE MILLIONS OVER FIVE YEARS, THE RICHEST PITCHING PAPER IN THE BIRDS' LONG LEDGER

The Orioles lost Trevor Rogers to the Cubs late Monday night; they had his successor signed and announced before Tuesday was out. The club made official a five-year contract with the right-hander Freddy Peralta — $125 million by a source's account, carrying a $10 million signing bonus and wages of $23 million a year — and the sum is the largest Baltimore has ever committed to a pitcher, third on the franchise's all-time bill behind only Chris Davis's seven years and $161 million of 2016 and Pete Alonso's five and $155 million of last December. The president of baseball operations Mike Elias called the man "a winning player who understands what it takes to compete and succeed on the biggest stage," and thanked the control owner David Rubenstein for the resources — not idly, for five of the eight largest contracts in the club's history have been signed since August of 2025, the checkbook having opened with the new ownership.6

The signature closes a courtship these columns began counting on Sunday, when The Athletic numbered seven clubs in pursuit — the Rays seriously engaged on the man they restored, with the White Sox, the Cubs, the Friars and the Jays besides, and two establishments that kept their names to themselves — and the reader will observe that Baltimore's name never appeared in print at all; whether the Birds were one of the two anonymous bidders or a late arrival, the wire does not say, and either way the mystery resolves in orange. What they bought is October's laureate: "Fastball Freddy," 30 years old, twice an All-Star, nine seasons in the majors and the most of them in Milwaukee, whose 2026 ran the whole dramatic register — a 4.99 figure across 22 starts in Queens, a deadline passage to Tampa Bay, a 3.25 across ten starts down the stretch, and then the Most Valuable Player's honors of the league championship series on one earned run in 12 innings against the Lake Erie men, the heater that averages 94.3 miles an hour in summer sitting 97 and touching 99 in the autumn chill. October was not spotless — the Brewers reached him for five runs in Game 3 of the World's Series — but by then the laurels were banked.6

He joins a rotation got up largely of men who once held his new distinction: Kyle Bradish's five years and $90 million of July and Shane Baz's five and $68 million of March were each, briefly, the richest pitching paper in Birdland, and both now pitch behind the record's newest holder, with the right-hander Brandon Young likely in company and the fifth post contested between the left-hander Povich and the prospect Gibson. The club, a spectator to the last two postseasons, is understood to want one more starter yet, ideally left-handed; the formal introduction comes Monday at Camden Yards.6

THE LABOR QUESTION: SIX MORNINGS REMAIN — THE LEAGUE WITHDRAWS ITS ESCROW CLAUSE AND PRONOUNCES EVERY GUARANTEED DOLLAR SAFE, THE UNION'S AUDIT FINDS THE SAME DOLLAR MERELY COLLECTED A YEAR LATER, AND THE CAP BENEATH THE GILT STANDS WHERE IT STOOD

The bargainers' Tuesday produced a concession from the league and an unimpressed ledger from the union, which has become the week's established ratio. Major League Baseball withdrew the escrow provision from its salary-cap proposal — the mechanism, borrowed from the other leagues, by which a slice of every wage is held back against the season's final accounting — and declared that under its cap-and-floor design every guaranteed contract, new or existing, remains guaranteed in full, with no player money withheld at all. "MLB took another step today by withdrawing our escrow proposal," said the spokesman Glen Caplin, "removing any doubt that every single guaranteed player contract will remain fully guaranteed in the new Salary Cap and Floor system" — the union having argued for months that escrow was the end of the guaranteed contract by another name.7

The union read the fine print aloud. Under the amended design, any aggregate overpayment to the players in one season is folded into the computation of the cap and floor in the seasons following, and after an overpayment the league may reckon those figures against revenues lagged as much as two years — which is, the interim executive director Bruce Meyer observed, not holding the money back this year but taking the same sum from players' pockets the next. "It's a different way of achieving the same objective of the salary cap — to reduce and suppress player salaries and freedom of movement," he said, calling the offer one more proposal that "pits player against player, past, present, and future." The Herald's ledger-keeping on this question is of long standing and unchanged: the frame beneath every gilding remains a fixed pot, and the agreement that governs the game has 6 mornings left to live, expiring at one minute before midnight on the first of December. The week's furious signing calendar, set down above and below, is the market's own commentary on that date.7

THE EXCHANGE DESK: WHAT REMAINS ON THE SHELVES — KING IS TIPPED TO SIGN INSIDE THE WEEK, SIX CLUBS BID FOR LOWE'S FIVE-AND-THIRTY HOME RUNS, THE CAPITAL NINE JOIN THE CHISHOLM QUEUE, AND NEITHER CHICAGO NOR QUEENS CALLS ITS SHOPPING FINISHED

With Rogers, Peralta and Taira all off the board inside a day's span, Michael King stands this morning as the best starting pitcher at liberty, and the wire does not expect him to stand long: the insider Jon Paul Morosi said Tuesday he believes "wholeheartedly" that King finds a home by the end of this week. The queue is familiar — the Cubs and the Mets both linked, the Friars reported eager to bring their old right-hander home, and the Jays interested, though whether the Taira purchase retires that pursuit the wire cannot say. Behind him the position market stirs. Brandon Lowe, late of Pittsburgh and his 35 home runs, has six clubs in some measure of pursuit by Morosi's count — the Yankees, the Birds, the Jays, the Rays, the Friars and the Phillies — with a draft pick owed the Corsairs when he signs elsewhere, the qualifying offer having been declined; and Jazz Chisholm Jr., who spoke with eleven clubs at the GM Meetings, adds the Nationals to a queue already holding the Jays and the Mets, the wire weighing a down year with the bat — a 97 OPS+ — against a plus glove, 41 stolen bases, and a 30-30 season two years back.8

The two spending clubs, for their part, decline to be finished. In Chicago, ESPN's Jesse Rogers reckons the Cubs "probably sign one more starter" and then mind their bullpen once the agreement expires — Clay Holmes and David Peterson, who each finished the season in Cubs flannels, both in play — while the door on a Shota Imanaga reunion is reckoned shut after conversations earlier this winter. And in Queens the Mets, their rotation crowned and their first base minded, still shop for arms — judiciously, The Athletic reports, the club discussing two-year terms with pitchers who ask three, with Mahle, Boyd and Imanaga among the earlier conversations and King among the present interests — and have shown at least some level of interest in Chisholm besides, though the second-base post nominally belongs to Marcus Semien for two years more.8

THE MOTOR CITY DESK: GLOVES FOR THE ARMS — KIM, A GOLD GLOVE MAN LATELY UNDONE BY ICE AND INFIRMARY, TAKES ONE YEAR AND FIVE MILLIONS TO TIGHTEN THE DETROIT INFIELD, AND MELTON'S SIX-YEAR FORTUNE IS SIGNED WITH THE SAND OF A SPOILED MAUI HOLIDAY STILL IN HIS SHOES

The Tigers' president of baseball operations Scott Harris hinted Tuesday morning that a move for the infield defense was in the works; the ink wanted barely two hours to appear. Detroit agreed with the veteran shortstop Ha-Seong Kim on one year and $5 million, with another $1 million in incentives, pending a physical and unconfirmed by the club. The file is a study in what injury does to a resume: Kim at his peak, with the 2022 and 2023 Padres, was worth 5.0 and then 5.4 wins above replacement and took a Gold Glove; what followed was a shoulder operation that swallowed the better part of a year, and then this past season's absurdist misfortune — a right middle finger lacerated in a slip upon the ice in his native South Korea, operated upon in the spring, inflamed again in July — and a .116 average over 51 games for Atlanta when upright. The Tigers buy the glove and the bounce-back at the bottom of the market: Kim takes shortstop in rotation with Kevin McGonigle, the league's reigning Rookie of the Year,3 whose defensive figures argue for more of his time at third base in any case.9

The same morning, at Comerica Park, the club made official the six-year, $46.5 million extension of the right-hander Troy Melton, recorded in Saturday's edition of these columns, and the ceremony supplied the anecdote the terms deserved: Melton was in Maui with his girlfriend when the talks turned serious, and conducted a fortune's negotiation from a holiday. "I kind of ruined a Maui vacation a little bit, ruined a sunset cruise and a dinner, but I think it was worth it," the man allowed. "So maybe we'll go back to Maui someday and not be on the phone so much." The instrument is the longest Detroit has given a pitcher since Verlander's seven-year extension commencing in 2013, and it climbs as the man is expected to: wages of $1 million in each of the first two years, rising by steps to $18 million in 2032, with a club option for 2033 at $23 million and escalators that could carry the late years higher. Melton, who turns 26 on the third of December, pitched to a 2.76 earned-run average this past season — a run of 14 starts at 1.49 after his May return from elbow inflammation among it — and Harris pronounced the thesis of the whole Detroit desk in two sentences: "We're going to continue to add arms. We also want to protect these arms."109

THE INK DESK, SMALLER TYPE: A CATCHER KEEPS HIS ONLY FLANNELS IN THE QUEEN CITY, CLEVELAND PAYS SEVENTEEN MILLIONS AND A HALF FOR ONE YEAR OF A MENDED LEFT ARM, TAYLOR CROSSES CHICAGO TO BALANCE THE PALE HOSE OUTFIELD, AND SANTANA, RISING ONE-AND-FORTY, SAILS BACK TO THE SOUND

The day's smaller signatures covered the map. In Cincinnati, Tyler Stephenson — seven seasons a Red, the club's first selection in the 2015 draft, and one of the few catchers of any standing on the open market — agreed to stay for three years and $30 million, an opt-out standing after the second year, pending a physical. The season that earned it was his sturdiest: a career-best 2.5 wins above replacement, 15 home runs, a bat the adjusted figures rate a hair above the league's common run, and blocking work the instruments rank in the 97th percentile — though the same instruments mark the rest of the glovework at nine runs below par, so the purchase is the bat, the blocks and the incumbency.11 In Cleveland, the Guardians paid a premium for a single year of Kris Bubic, $17.5 million, betting that the arm which made an All-Star of him in 2025 — a 2.55 earned-run average in 20 starts for Kansas City, rebuilt around a changeup hitters batted .119 against this past season — outlasts a 2026 spent four months on the shelf with elbow and shoulder complaints. He joins a company fronted by Gavin Williams, whose 248 strikeouts led the league, and the young Parker Messick, runner-up in the Rookie of the Year balloting and third in the Cy Young voting,3 on the only staff in the majors that ran four starters to 30 starts apiece.12

In Chicago, Tyrone Taylor changed sides of town without changing cities: two years and $17 million from the White Sox, whose outfield — left-handed and switch-hitting nearly to a man, Brenton Doyle excepted — wanted precisely a right-handed bat of his description. Taylor, 32, remade his swing this past season and hit .279 with a .502 slugging mark and a 128 OPS+ between the Mets and the Cubs, batting .351 after the deadline carried him to Wrigley and posting a .921 on-base-plus-slugging against left-handed pitching; he brings besides a plus glove at all three outfield posts, an arm the instruments place in the 85th percentile, and a sprint the years have not yet taxed.13

And in Seattle, sentiment signed a minor-league contract. Carlos Santana, who turns 41 in April, returns to the Mariners with an invitation to spring camp — his third tour in the organization, counting the ten days of December 2018 when he was traded in and flipped out again — to stand as insurance behind Josh Naylor at first base and as something less measurable in the clubhouse, where his 2022 vintage furnished the win-dance, the home-run helmet, and a three-run clout in Toronto that turned a Wild Card series. The bat is nearly spent — eight games and two hits for Arizona this past season — but the Puget Sound men are weighing what a presence of his standing offers a camp, and a minor-league promise costs nothing to find out.14

A Wednesday paper of emptied shelves: the Pacific courtships these columns have carried since the posting bells of early November both closed in a single day, Baltimore crowned its costliest arm by nightfall, and the bargainers traded an escrow clause for a colder ledger — the whole of it set down above. The forward ledger was fetched before a word was written, as the house custom commands, and reads as it has all week: the camps' reporting dates remain unposted, so the count runs to the first rung bearing a date — the spring exhibition openers of Friday, the 19th of February, 86 mornings from this one, with Opening Night to follow on Wednesday, the 24th of March, 119 mornings off.2 The nearer columns press: the collective agreement has 6 mornings left to live; the republic carves its Thanksgiving bird on the morrow, and the before-the-feast prophecy on Sato, carried in yesterday's columns, is proven above with room to spare; Cooperstown's committee of sixteen reports in 11; the Winter Meetings convene at San Diego with the Rule 5 drafting on December 9, 14 mornings from this one; and the writers' envelope waits for the 19th of January, 55 mornings off. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
