entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Twenty-Fourth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 87 days until the first spring-training game.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 139 · Tuesday, the Twenty-Fourth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

87 days until the first spring-training game (Friday, the 19th of February, 2027).

News Around the League

THE INK DESK: THE SPREE FINDS ITS THIRD SIGNATURE IN AS MANY MORNINGS — GOLDSCHMIDT, NINE-AND-THIRTY AND NEVER ONCE BELOW THE COMMON RUN, TAKES ONE YEAR AND EIGHT MILLIONS TO MIND FIRST BASE IN QUEENS, AND THE THREE-DAY BILL STANDS AT FIVE HUNDRED FIFTY-THREE MILLIONS

Less than a day after writing the richest pitching contract in the game's history, the Mets bought the cheapest Hall of Fame case on the market. By the account of a source, the club agreed Monday with Paul Goldschmidt on a contract of one year and $8 million — the club not yet confirming — and the position these columns have watched them shop all week has its tenant. The file on the man is the kind the Herald keeps in its permanent cabinet: a career on-base-plus-slugging of .876 with 390 home runs and 65.1 wins above replacement by Baseball-Reference's reckoning; the National League's Most Valuable Player of 2022 with St. Louis, the eighth consecutive season he finished among the top twenty in that balloting; seven All-Star summons, five Silver Sluggers, four Gold Gloves; and, by adjusted OPS, never once in his whole career a season below the league's average. He has, moreover, not spent a day on the injured list in 12 consecutive seasons — a durability that reads like a misprint in the present age.3

What remains of the great hitter at 39 is a specialist's weapon, and the fit is almost indecently neat. With the Yankees this past season Goldschmidt put up a .967 on-base-plus-slugging against left-handed pitching — a .299/.393/.573 line — beside a .765 overall with 18 home runs, good for a 111 OPS+, and his glove was worth 6 outs above average in 77 games at first base. The incumbent Jared Young swings left-handed and hit all nine of his home runs against right-handers, so the platoon assembles itself. The warnings are entered in the same ledger: a .590 figure against right-handed pitching, a third consecutive career low, and a hard-hit rate of 35.9 percent, his faintest since the tracking instruments were switched on in 2015. The Herald notes also the man's October habit — .262/.347/.533 with eight home runs across 33 playoff games — which a club of the Mets' present designs does not reckon incidental.3

The post he fills has been a sore since Pete Alonso signed in Baltimore last winter. Jorge Polanco, the handpicked successor, lost most of the season to an Achilles that wanted surgery and hit .148 when upright; Young proved a surprise but was concussed in September; Mark Vientos, tendered his contract but shopped all the same — the callers were already ringing on him, as these columns noted Sunday — now reads more expendable still, and Brett Baty is bound for regular work at second base. The president of baseball operations David Stearns had said first base was the only position beyond pitching he meant to prioritize, and the reader of the weekend's columns will note the pivot: the club had been eyeing Ty France, who seeks three years; it bought one year of Goldschmidt instead, and keeps its powder.3

The arithmetic of the spree wants its own line. Between Saturday morning and Monday night the Mets committed $553 million in guaranteed wages to three men — the young Ewing's eight years and $95 million, the great Skubal's nine and $450 million, and now Goldschmidt's one and $8 million, a rounding error riding in the caboose. The winter's quietest position purchase may prove its shrewdest; it is in any case its best-decorated.3

THE FLOODGATES, AS FORETOLD: THE FINEST LEFT ARM REMAINING GOES TO THE NORTH SIDE — ROGERS SIGNS FOR FIVE YEARS AND SIX-SCORE MILLIONS, THE THIRD-RICHEST PITCHING PURCHASE IN THE CUBS' LONG LEDGER, AND AN EMPTIED ROTATION HAS ITS FIRST NEW TENANT

The forecast these columns carried only yesterday — the top of the free-agent class signed inside the week, once the Skubal verdict loosed the escrow — required one day to begin proving itself. On Monday night the Cubs reached agreement with the left-hander Trevor Rogers on a multiyear contract, pending a physical; the pact runs five years at $120 million by multiple reports, with MLB Network's Jon Morosi first to the news. It is the third-richest free-agent engagement ever given a pitcher on the North Side, behind Jon Lester's six years and $155 million and Yu Darvish's six and $126 million, and it answers a need these columns have inventoried all week: the entire season-ending rotation — Boyd, Imanaga, Holmes, Gausman and Peterson, all five — walked to the open market at the season's close. The bill runs past the treasury, too: Rogers having rejected Baltimore's qualifying offer of $23.15 million, the Cubs, a luxury-tax payor, surrender their second- and fifth-highest selections in the 2027 draft and $1 million from the international bonus pool for the privilege.4

The man was the finest left arm at liberty once the great one signed in Queens, and his file reads like a serial with a late redemption. Rogers, 29 as of the 13th of November, was an All-Star and the National League's Rookie of the Year runner-up for the 2021 Marlins before his lower half betrayed him — all but four games of his 2023 lost, a deadline sale to the Orioles in 2024 for Stowers and Norby — and then came the restoration: a 1.81 earned-run average across 18 games in 2025, and this past season, after a wretched 6.84 through ten outings, a 2.90 from June onward across 20 starts, the fielding-independent figure a near-identical 2.89, with 119 strikeouts against 21 walks in 121 innings. The season closed at 4.03 with 157 strikeouts; the career ledger reads 3.88 across 132 starts. The four-seamer sits a modest 93.8 miles an hour yet has held hitters to a .204 average since the start of 2025, delivered from a low, deceptive slot and dressed with a changeup, sweeper, sinker and cutter; and a career ground-ball rate of 42.7 percent now lands in front of an infield that took the team Gold Glove in 2026, with the Platinum Glove man Crow-Armstrong patrolling center. The Cubs mean to add more arms yet, the door left open even to their own departed; the first and hardest purchase is made.4

THE LABOR QUESTION: SEVEN MORNINGS REMAIN — THE LEAGUE GILDS ITS CAP WITH A MILLION-DOLLAR MINIMUM AND BONUSES AT EVERY STATION OF A CAREER, THE UNION COUNTS NOT ONE NEW DOLLAR IN THE PARCEL, AND OFFERS BESIDES TO DIVIDE THE LOCAL AIRWAVES THIRTY WAYS

Monday's bargaining, with the agreement's clock running out, produced sweeteners from the league and a cold audit from the union. Major League Baseball proposed raising the minimum wage from $780,000 to $1 million for 2027 — a $220,000 rise, the largest single increase in the game's history, the old record being $129,500 — with the minimum thereafter growing alongside the proposed cap and floor; a pre-arbitration man logging a full year of service, and less than half of it on the injured list, would bank at least $100,000 more from the bonus program, a raise of 41 percent in all. The league appended two new instruments besides: a centrally funded signing bonus of 5 percent for every arbitration-eligible player who settles without a hearing — some $33 million a year spread across roughly 175 men, by the league's estimate — and a $500,000 bonus each club may award one veteran of six years' service signing a one-year contract of $10 million or less. These ride atop the earlier concessions: the pre-arbitration pool fattened from $50 million toward $75 million, free agency at five years for men of 30 and older — subject to a club's right to hold such a man one further year at the average of the game's 125 highest wages — and the qualifying offer abolished outright. "MLB is trying to reach an agreement with the players by meeting their objectives," said the spokesman Glen Caplin.5

The union's answer was arithmetic, not gratitude. Every gilt edge is affixed to the same cap-and-floor frame — the figures as last proposed being a $258.2 million ceiling and a $180.2 million floor, commencing 2028 — and the interim executive director Bruce Meyer observed that the proposals "don't add a single dollar in overall player compensation," the purse being fixed and merely re-divided, a fact the league itself does not dispute. "Any supposed benefits to certain classes of players," he said, "are simply taken out of the pockets of other players." The union made its own motion at the same table: it formally agreed Monday to the equal division of local media moneys among the thirty clubs — the league's own concept, accepted outside any cap — which would end the territorial exclusivity of the regional networks and the blackouts with them, and it coupled the acceptance to a revenue-sharing design that would raise assistance to the low-revenue markets from roughly $700 million to better than $950 million next year, more than $1 billion over the agreement's life, with rewards of $20 million for a sharing club that reaches the postseason — or misses it with a better record than the worst club that got in — and $10 million for one that merely finishes above .500.6

The Herald's sympathies on matters of the purse are a matter of long record, and Monday asks little of them: one side proposes to pay the poor clubs more for winning and to split the airwaves evenly; the other proposes a fixed pot with prettier partitions, while the ink of Sunday's $450 million signature — the free market's own appraisal of the best pitcher alive — dries on the page beside it. The agreement expires at one minute before midnight on the first of December, 7 mornings from this one, and the expectation throughout the game is that a lockout follows the stroke; the last one ran 99 days.6

THE EXCHANGE DESK: WHAT THE LOSERS DO NEXT — TORONTO'S SECRET BID OF FOUR HUNDRED TWENTY MILLIONS COMES TO LIGHT AS THE MAPLE LEAF NINE TURN TO BATS, SAN DIEGO VOWS EVERYTHING POSSIBLE FOR KING, THE DODGERS CONFESS THEY NEVER BID AT ALL, AND A GRANDER WEBB DESIGN IS WHISPERED AT THE BAY

The Skubal file, closed yesterday, keeps disgorging footnotes. The Athletic's Mitch Bannon reveals that Toronto's losing bid ran to nine years and $420 million — $30 million shy of the verdict — and that the front office, having entered the winter meaning to spend chiefly on its batting, now simply resumes the original plan: the Maple Leaf nine scored the fewest runs in the majors this past season, and the wire links them to Suzuki, Arozarena, Sato, Lowe and Chisholm at liberty and to Arizona's Ketel Marte by trade, with multiple clubs inquiring after the utility man Clement should an infielder arrive. The rotation — Cease, Soriano, Yesavage, Ponce, Arrighetti — is the lesser worry, though the club still monitors Peralta, King and Taira; a fourth name on that watch list, Trevor Rogers, came off the shelf Monday night.7

San Diego's pivot has a vow attached. The new ownership of Kwanza Jones and José E. Feliciano pursued Skubal in earnest, but the rotation's glut of vacancies always argued against sinking the whole treasury in one arm; the club will now, by USA Today's Bob Nightengale, "do everything possible to bring back" Michael King, with a Pivetta reunion entertained besides — the $18 million club option was declined this month chiefly because exercising it would have handed the right-hander a $14 million player option for 2028 — and Peralta and Taira in the field of possibilities, a corner outfielder from among Sato, Suzuki and Boston's shoppable Duran not excluded. The Dodgers' audit, meanwhile, completes itself: ESPN's Alden Gonzalez reports the club wanted its rented champion back but never put an offer on paper at all, and The Athletic's Katie Woo finds them disinclined to move aggressively for pitching, the infield depth reckoned settled by the Lewis purchase these columns recorded Saturday and the left-field question — De Paula or Hernández — standing as examined Sunday.7

And at the Bay, the shop window these columns reported Sunday acquires a grander design. Nightengale relays the reckoning of several executives: the Giants' best chance of unloading one of their weightiest contracts — Adames, Chapman or Devers — may be a package that carries the ace Webb out the door beside it. A trade of that magnitude is doubtful before the agreement expires on the first of December, but the Bay men could line something up for the season beyond; The Athletic has them wanting a very strong return for the workhorse, with rival shops skeptical they will get their price.7

THE PACIFIC DESK: ANATOMY OF THE LION'S FASTBALL — TAIRA, FIVE FEET EIGHT AND NINE-AND-NINETY ON THE GUN, LOOSES THE BALL FROM A HEIGHT ONLY ONE BIG-LEAGUE STARTER GOES BENEATH, AND THE LABOR CLOCK FORECLOSES THE EASTERN MARKET A FORTNIGHT EARLY

The wire's David Adler puts the instruments to the arm these columns have courted all week, and the readings explain the crowded anterooms. Kaima Taira, 27, late of the Seibu Lions and posted at the beginning of November, carries a career 1.78 earned-run average in the Japanese league with 9.4 strikeouts per nine innings, and throws eight distinct pitches; but the engine is the four-seamer, which averaged 95.8 miles an hour this past season, touched past 99, and sat 96 or better in eight of his final ten starts. The marvel is the geometry. Standing 5-foot-8, Taira releases the ball 4.94 feet off the ground — level with Chris Sale for the second-lowest slot among regular big-league starters, only Joe Ryan beneath him — and 6.8 feet out in front of the rubber, more extension than the big-league average from a man shorter than nearly all of them; Sale and Wheeler were the only major-league starters last season to pair a release under five feet with velocity past 95. The flat approach makes the pitch seem to take off as it arrives, and it drew whiffs at 27 percent against a league norm of about 22; it is, moreover, his chief two-strike weapon against both sides of the plate. The suitors on the wire's list — the Mets, the Mission nine, the Maple Leaf nine, the Cubs and the White Sox — are the same establishments whose audiences these columns have carried since the posting.8

The clock beneath the courtship has tightened. Should no new labor agreement exist when the current one dies on the first of December, the league will neither freeze nor extend the 45-day posting windows — which makes that date the effective deadline for Taira, for Itoh, and for the slugger Sato alike, and forecloses the mid-December horizon these columns gave Itoh's clock on Sunday. On Sato the field narrows besides: industry sources, by the wire's Mark Feinsand, now rate the Yankees, the Philadelphias and the Maple Leaf nine the frontrunners — the five-club field of yesterday's columns shorn of the Mets and Cubs — and The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal hears the signature could come very well before Thanksgiving, which is two mornings from this one.7

THE BULLPEN COLUMN: SMALL STROKES FOR THE LATE INNINGS — SUTER MAKES A THIRD LEFT HAND IN THE BRONX, THIELBAR ON THE EVE OF FORTY TALKS HIS WAY HOME TO KANSAS CITY, AND THE DODGERS BUY A LOTTERY TICKET ON A THRICE-MENDED ARM

The day's smaller ink ran chiefly to relief. The Yankees agreed with the left-hander Brent Suter on one year and $4 million, pending a physical — the insider Jeff Passan reporting a club option for 2028 besides — and the profile wants no translation: 37 years old, a season split between the Angels and Atlanta at a 3.36 figure across 91 innings, ground balls at a rate in the 85th percentile and hard contact suppressed at the 94th. He joins Headrick and Hill as the third left hand in the room, and brings the Bronx bullpen bill to roughly $41.4 million this winter across Bednar's accepted qualifying offer, Hill, the returned Loáisiga — whose homecoming Saturday's columns recorded — and now Suter; the steward Cashman's shop, by the Post's Joel Sherman, still deliberates whether to crown the project with Morejon, the market's best reliever, or spread that money across the roster's other wants.910

In Kansas City the signing came with its own testimony. The Royals announced one year for Caleb Thielbar — ESPN setting the wage at $3.25 million — and the left-hander, who turns 40 on the 31st of January, allowed that he and his wife had been looking at moving to the city and he had hoped the club would call. The figures argue both ways: a 4.86 for the Cubs this past season, but a 2.28 on the road against a home ledger battered at windy Wrigley, and the man reckons his fastball plays in Kauffman's thicker summer air. He joins a bullpen that ranked 29th in the game at 5.07 and a staff makeover a week in motion, the Garcia freight having lately brought Miller, Evans and Ferrer to town, as these columns have recorded; the new man calls the club a dark horse that a tough 2026 has let the public forget.1112

And the Dodgers spent the price of a minor-league contract on a memory. Robert Stephenson, who signed three years and $33 million with the Angels before 2024 and has thrown 10 big-league innings since — a Tommy John reconstruction, a year of nerve irritation, then a second elbow operation amid thoracic-outlet symptoms that swallowed his 2026 entire — agreed to minor-league terms, by a source's account to the wire's Mark Feinsand. At his best, with the 2023 Rays, the right-hander ran a 2.35 across 42 appearances; he turns 34 in February, and behind Díaz and Scott a bullpen shorn of Phillips, now a Brave, and of Vesia to the open market has every reason to gamble small on the chance that the best of him survives the scars.13

A Tuesday paper of consequences: the Queens spree finds a third signature, the floodgates foretold in yesterday's columns open on the North Side, and the bargainers' Monday sitting yields gilt the union weighs and finds wanting — the whole of it set down above. The forward ledger was opened before a word was written, as the house custom commands, and reads as it has all week: the camps' reporting dates remain unposted, so the count runs to the first rung bearing a date — the spring exhibition openers of Friday, the 19th of February, 87 mornings from this one, with Opening Night to follow on Wednesday, the 24th of March, 120 mornings off.2 The nearer columns crowd closer by the day: the collective agreement has 7 mornings left to live; Cooperstown's committee of sixteen reports in 12; the Winter Meetings convene at San Diego with the Rule 5 drafting on December 9, 15 mornings from this one; and the writers' envelope waits for the 19th of January, 56 mornings off. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~

entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Twenty-Third of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 88 days until the first spring-training game.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 138 · Monday, the Twenty-Third of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

88 days until the first spring-training game (Friday, the 19th of February, 2027).

News Around the League

THE SKUBAL REGISTER, CLOSED: THE VERDICT IS FLUSHING — NINE YEARS AND FOUR HUNDRED FIFTY MILLIONS, A HALF-HUNDRED PER ANNUM, THE RICHEST CONTRACT EVER WRITTEN FOR A PITCHER, AND THE GREAT LEFT-HANDER IS A MET WITH EIGHT MORNINGS LEFT ON THE AGREEMENT'S LIFE

The register is closed. On Sunday, by the account of sources, Tarik Skubal agreed with the Mets on a contract of nine years and $450 million, running through 2035, with full no-trade protection and no opt-out anywhere in it — the club not yet confirming, a physical still to be passed. The ledger entries write themselves into the record book: the richest contract ever given a pitcher, past Yoshinobu Yamamoto's twelve years and $325 million of December 2023; an average wage of $50 million a year, the highest ever carried by a full-time pitcher, with only Shohei Ohtani, Kyle Tucker and Juan Soto drawing more per season in all the game. The reader of Saturday's register will note the arithmetic of the final hour: the reported offer then standing was nine years and very nearly $400 million, and the figure, when it hardened, had grown by some $50 million. The audited suitors — the Dodgers, the San Diegans, the Torontos, and at least one establishment that never gave its name — go home with their checkbooks intact, and the winter's grandest courtship is concluded with the collective agreement's clock still showing 8 mornings.3

The man the money bought turned 30 on Friday, and the file wants no embroidery. Two Cy Young Awards, 2024 and 2025 — the twelfth pitcher ever to take the honor in consecutive seasons — the first of them unanimous and fastened to the pitching Triple Crown, 18 wins beside a 2.39 earned-run average and 228 strikeouts; the second built on a league-best 2.21 with 241 strikeouts across 195 and a third innings. Over the four seasons since 2023 the figure reads 2.47, with very nearly seven strikeouts for every walk issued. None of it was promised him: a ninth-round selection out of Seattle University in 2018, he has three arm operations in his file — the first a Tommy John reconstruction that cost him the 2017 season, the most recent this past May's removal of loose bodies from the left elbow, a convalescence of barely six weeks. On the second of August, Detroit — hovering at the fringes of contention — sold him west to the Dodgers, and over his final 16 starts of the season, ten of them in Los Angeles, he pitched to a 2.36.3

What Flushing bought is a correction long overdue. The rotation's earned-run average has slid three seasons running — twelfth in the game at 3.91 in 2024, eighteenth at 4.13 in 2025, twenty-third at 4.47 this past year — and the president of baseball operations David Stearns allowed this month that only the young McLean and Scott held guaranteed posts. The club that paid Soto $765 million two Decembers ago has now written the pitching equivalent, and the wire observes that it makes Skubal the sixth Met to earn better than $19 million next season and the third above $42 million. The sobering page of the file is the last one: the final year, at $45 million, will be pitched entire at the age of 38, and only three regular starters that old took a big-league mound in 2026 — though the wager's defenders point to Sale, Wheeler, Scherzer and Verlander as proof that the elite arm ages better than most. Nor, the wire insists, is the shopping done: a first baseman and bullpen help remain on the Flushing list, and possibly another starter besides.34

THE MARKET AFTER THE VERDICT: ONE SIGNATURE UNLOCKS THE ESCROW — THE WIRE EXPECTS THE TOP OF THE CLASS SIGNED INSIDE THE WEEK, FIVE CLUBS CIRCLE SATO, AND THE JILTED SUITORS TAKE INVENTORY OF THEIR PURSES

These columns wrote Saturday that one signature held a dozen in escrow; the signature is now supplied, and the wire's Mark Feinsand reckons the consequence plainly: the bulk of the winter's top twenty or thirty free agents are expected to sign before the collective agreement expires on the first of December, the most of them in the final 72 to 96 hours — a rush driven, he notes, less by the Skubal verdict than by the calendar itself. Five years ago, six men signed nine-figure contracts in the days before the last agreement lapsed; the wire does not expect quite so rich a stampede this time, but the shape is the same. The next tier of arms — Michael King, Freddy Peralta, Clay Holmes, Trevor Rogers, Nick Martinez — offers no one of the Skubal class, so there is no logical consolation purchase; there is merely a healthy market, for the clubs needing pitching outnumber the pitchers. The slugger Teruaki Sato, the eastern market's grandest bat, is expected by industry sources to sign with one of five clubs — the Yankees, the Quakers, the Blue Jays, the Mets or the Cubs, the first three reckoned the favorites — and the posted men of the Pacific shelf, Taira and Itoh and Korea's Si-Hwan Roh, face in effect the same first-of-December date, else they must wait upon another year.5

The jilted suitors, meanwhile, take their inventory. The Dodgers, who rented the great man for a pennant drive and could not keep him, are read by the wire as having preferred a shorter engagement at a steeper yearly wage — the decade-long term is a vow that establishment has made only to Ohtani, Betts and Yamamoto, and nine years for a pitcher of 30 proved its breaking point — and they count seven starters on the premises without reckoning Ohtani among them, which made the pursuit a luxury rather than a necessity. Their winter turns now to a right-handed-hitting infielder, the at-liberty Mauricio Dubón suggested, and to the left-field question these columns examined only yesterday — whether young De Paula's September earns him the post, possibly at the price of a Teoscar Hernández trade. San Diego and the Cubs each need multiple starters and must shop the tier below. And in Philadelphia the wire reads no panic — Dombrowski is not expected to swerve from his plans — though the columnist Will Leitch counsels the Quakers to worry all the same, an aging roster built to win now having just watched the rival in Queens grow considerably better in the near term.54

THE INK DESK: THE CLUB THAT COULD NOT KEEP ITS OWN GREAT LEFT-HANDER BUYS A MENDED ONE — GIL, ROOKIE OF THE YEAR TWO AUTUMNS GONE, COMES TO DETROIT FOR A SINGLE YEAR, FRIDAY'S WASTE-BASKET PROVING SUNDAY'S BARGAIN COUNTER

Luis Gil spent precisely one weekend at liberty. Non-tendered by the Yankees at Friday's stroke of five — the headline casualty of the deadline, as these columns recorded Saturday — the right-hander agreed Sunday with the Tigers on a contract of one year and $2.3 million, with performance bonuses that could add $2 million more, the deal pending a physical and the club not yet confirming; MLB.com's Mark Feinsand first reported the terms. The résumé needs no restatement beyond its headline: Rookie of the Year in the American League in 2024, on a line of 15 wins against 7 losses with a 3.50 earned-run average across 29 starts, the first Yankee pitcher to take the honor since Righetti in 1981. What followed is the reason the price is $2.3 million and not ten times it — a lat strain that swallowed the first four months of 2025, shoulder inflammation that took three months of 2026, nine appearances all year and a final outing in September of four walks in two innings.67

Detroit's logic was stated on the record by its president of baseball operations, Scott Harris: "We need to add innings. I'm not going to run from that" — and, of the market at large, "everything's on the table for us right now." The Bengals' rotation company reads Valdez, Anderson, Jobe, Ryan and the newly extended Melton — whose six-year engagement these columns set down Saturday — with Olson mending from shoulder surgery behind them, and the pitching coach Chris Fetter is handed the winter's classic restoration: a fastball and a slider that have both lost their bite since 2024, and a frame the medical men must keep upright. The Herald cannot resist the weekend's symmetry: in the same hours the club that would not meet its own great left-hander's price watched him sign for $450 million in Queens, it spent $2.3 million on a gamble that a Rookie of the Year still lives in a mended shoulder. And the man arrives in familiar livery, for Gil winters even now with the Tigres del Licey, as Saturday's columns had him — he need not so much as change the cat upon his cap.67

THE FRONT OFFICE WIRE: A CATCHER OF THE OLD GUARD COMES HOME TO THE MILE HIGH NINE — SERVAIS, NINE SEASONS THE MARINERS' SKIPPER, TAKES A SENIOR DESK IN THE DENVER REBUILDING

The Rockies' busy winter added a name of standing on Sunday: Scott Servais returns to the organization where his front-office life began, as senior director of baseball operations, with official announcement of the club's new hires expected shortly. The man is 59 and his card runs the whole breadth of the trade — eleven big-league seasons a catcher, 820 games for the Astros, Cubs, Giants and Rockies, 33 of them in Colorado colors; special-projects work in the Denver shop at his playing days' end under Jerry Dipoto; the Rangers' player-development chair from 2004 to 2010; an assistant general managership with the Angels; and nine seasons managing Seattle, 2016 through 2024, at 680 wins against 642, five winning years and the breaking, in 2022, of a postseason drought twenty seasons old. He spent 2025 an assistant development coach with the Padres, and he keeps a home at Steamboat Springs — "looking forward," he said Sunday, "to helping the Rox any way possible."8

The appointment reads as a piece with the month. The DePodesta-Byrnes administration has bought two starting pitchers from Chicago in a single stroke — the Castillo and Martin freight these columns recorded Friday — added the sidearming aerospace man Lee on Saturday's page, and installed Ethan Katz at pitching coach; Servais arrives as one of several hires across player development, research and the performance sciences, his own expertise lying in the development line. A franchise that lately owned the game's highest earned-run average is assembling grown-ups at every desk, and the Herald, which has watched many a Denver winter produce nothing but altitude, notes that this one at least produces transactions.8

THE ALMANAC: FIVE HUNDRED BY THE LONG WAY ROUND — SCHWARBER, HIS FIVE-AND-FORTY CIRCUIT CLOUTS OF THE SUMMER FRESHLY BANKED, STANDS 115 FROM THE PANTHEON'S DOOR

The wire's Thomas Harrigan opens a file the Herald is pleased to keep beside its own almanac: Kyle Schwarber's march on 500 home runs, which would be among the strangest ever made. The Philadelphia slugger, 33, signed in that city through 2030, holds 385 for his career — 115 shy of the mark — and the oddity is all in the ledger's first half. Through his age-28 season Schwarber had struck 153, fewer at that age than all but two men who ever reached the five hundred: David Ortiz, who stood at 130 and finished at 541, and Rafael Palmeiro, at 132 on his way to 569. Since signing in Philadelphia in March 2022 he has hit 232 — about 46 a season — which is the second-most any man has hit in his first five years with one club, behind only Ruth's 235 in Yankee flannels from 1920 to 1924, and past the old Philadelphia five-year marks of Howard (229) and Schmidt (199). Only ten hitters in the game's history have put up a five-year span of 232 or better, and the company — Ruth, Sosa, Bonds, Rodriguez, McGwire chief among them — explains the raised eyebrow.910

The arithmetic forward is gentler than the arithmetic behind. The season just closed gave him 45 home runs, an .857 on-base-plus-slugging and a second Silver Slugger; to reach 500 inside the contract's four remaining years wants about 29 a season — a figure the summer just banked cleared with sixteen to spare — and Harrigan rates the errand a near-certainty if health allows. The Herald will keep the count in this column as it climbs, and observes only that the game's roll of late bloomers — Ortiz foremost, 58 home runs through age 26 and a plaque in Cooperstown now — has always read like an argument for patience.9

A Monday paper that retires its longest-running ledger: the Skubal Register, opened when the courtship began, closes above at nine years and $450 million, and the market it held in escrow now runs free — the full accounting, with the weekend's other ink, is set down in the columns. The forward ledger was consulted before the first word above was written, as the house custom commands, and reads as it has all week: the camps' reporting dates remain unposted, so the count runs to the first rung bearing a date — the spring exhibition openers of Friday, the 19th of February, 88 mornings from this one, with Opening Night to follow on Wednesday, the 24th of March, 121 mornings off.2 The nearer columns crowd closer than ever: the collective agreement has 8 mornings left to live, and the bargainers sit again this very morning;11 Cooperstown's committee of sixteen reports in 13; the Winter Meetings convene at San Diego with the Rule 5 drafting on December 9, 16 mornings from this one; and the writers' envelope waits for the 19th of January, 57 mornings off. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Twenty-Second of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 89 days until the first spring-training game.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 137 · Sunday, the Twenty-Second of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

89 days until the first spring-training game (Friday, the 19th of February, 2027).

News Around the League

THE INK DESK: QUEENS SIGNS ITS SUNRISE — YOUNG EWING, BUT TWO-AND-TWENTY, TAKES EIGHT YEARS AND FIVE-AND-NINETY MILLIONS, THE GRANDEST WAGER THE METS HAVE EVER LAID ON A MAN NOT YET ENTITLED TO ARGUE HIS WAGE

The quietest Saturday of the winter produced its loudest signature in Queens. By the account of a source, the Mets agreed yesterday with the center fielder A.J. Ewing on an extension of eight years and $95 million, with a club option for a ninth year, 2035, at $25 million — the club not yet confirming. It is the largest contract the franchise has ever written for a man still shy of arbitration, surpassing the six years and $55 million David Wright signed in 2006, and it binds to the organization, through at least 2034, a player who one year ago had yet to take a big-league at-bat.3

The season that earned it was no masterpiece, which is rather the point. Ewing, 22, an Ohio boy taken in the fourth round of the 2023 draft, came up in May, prospered, then fell into a midsummer slump deep enough to swallow a lesser temperament; he climbed out to the tune of an .879 on-base-plus-slugging over his final 25 games, and the club's evaluators marked the adjustment more admiringly than they would have marked an unbroken ascent. The full ledger reads .252/.324/.376 with 11 home runs and 25 stolen bases — a club rookie record — beside center-field work good enough to stand among the season's best arguments for him, and a ninth-place finish in the league's Rookie of the Year balloting on a club that placed three men among the vote-getters, his closest friend Carson Benge the runner-up. One official allowed that "all the arrows pointed in the right direction," and called the young man "the type of person you want to invest in"; the player, for his part, is said to have expressed a sincere wish to live and play his years in New York.3

The instrument itself deserves a paragraph, for it is the small-market club's tool in the big-market club's hand. The pre-arbitration extension — the Rays' and Brewers' habitual economy, the method by which Atlanta bound its whole core a decade ago — trades ceiling for certainty in both directions: the club buys a possible star's twenties at a discount, and the man guarantees his fortune, about $11.9 million a year, against every cruelty the game can inflict. The Mets have rarely bothered, Wright and Reyes in the mid-2000s and Niese and Lagares in the decade following being nearly the whole of the file; that they bothered now says what they think of Ewing. The outfield of Ewing, Benge and Juan Soto stands under club control through 2031 at the least, Ewing and Soto far longer, and the wire already wonders whether Benge, Nolan McLean or Christian Scott is handed the next pen.34

THE EXCHANGE DESK: THE BAY MEN WILL LISTEN ON THEIR WORKHORSE — WEBB, THIRTY AS OF WEDNESDAY, IS PLACED IN THE SHOP WINDOW ONE DAY AFTER THESE COLUMNS HAD SAN FRANCISCO SHOPPING FOR ARMS TO STAND BEHIND HIM, AND THE AMERICANS TAKE CALLS ON TWO YOUNG OUTFIELDERS

The reader of yesterday's columns met the Giants hunting rotation help behind Logan Webb and Landen Roupp, their only two certainties. This morning one of the certainties is in the window. By the account of FanSided's Robert Murray, San Francisco is now "open to listening" to trade offers for Webb — a reversal from the summer, when the club would entertain no such conversation at the deadline. The right-hander turned 30 this past Wednesday and is midway through a five-year, $90 million extension that runs to 2028; what a buyer would be buying is the steadiest freight-horse in the business, no man in the game having thrown more innings these past five seasons — 980 and two-thirds of them — at a 3.40 earned-run average with three top-six finishes in the Cy Young balloting, the runner-up's place of 2023 among them. The past season was the lightest of his prime — knee bursitis and a blistered finger held him to a 4.31 figure over 160 and two-thirds innings — but the signature virtues held, the walks still scarce and the ground balls still better than half of all contact for a seventh consecutive year. He is, moreover, the home product entire, a Northern California boy drafted by the club in the fourth round of 2014, which is precisely the kind of man a fan base does not forgive a front office for selling.4

In the Bronx the telephone rings on the young rather than the old. The steward Brian Cashman, by way of The Athletic, allows that rival clubs "are asking a lot about" the outfielder Spencer Jones, with inquiries on Jasson Domínguez besides — whether the Americans are merely listening or actively selling, the wire cannot say. Jones, 25, is penciled toward the center-field post after a rookie year that closed at .254/.312/.459 with nine home runs over his final 55 games, the ball leaving his bat with an authority — a 52.6 percent hard-hit rate, a barrel rate of 19.8 — that the league's instruments rank among the elite. Domínguez, 23, is the harder case: a shoulder-marred season spent largely in the minors, a .225 average in 57 big-league games, and no evident path past Jones, Bellinger and Judge. But the Herald's island correspondence supplies the counter-argument, for the switch-hitter is at this hour batting .348/.439/.609 through 57 plate appearances for the Águilas Cibaeñas — the selfsame Eagles whose command Francisco Cervelli assumed on Thursday, as these columns recorded Friday — and a man restoring his value under a new manager's eye is exactly the sort the callers keep calling about.4

THE ANGELENO QUESTION: A PHENOM OF ONE-AND-TWENTY PRESSES AT THE GARDEN GATE — DE PAULA'S SEPTEMBER HAS LOS ANGELES WEIGHING WHETHER HERNÁNDEZ'S LAST GUARANTEED YEAR IS BETTER SPENT IN SOMEBODY ELSE'S OUTFIELD

The Dodgers' winter has an examination beneath its grand pursuit, and the wire's Los Angeles desk set it out Saturday: what to do with left field. Under the standing arrangement Teoscar Hernández keeps the post through the final guaranteed season of his three-year, $66 million contract — $14.5 million for 2027, with a $15 million club option or a $6.5 million buyout to follow — but Josue De Paula, reckoned by MLB Pipeline the fourth-best prospect in the game, spent September making the arrangement look less than settled. Called up directly from Double-A Tulsa at 21 to stand in for an ailing Shohei Ohtani, the young man went 10 for 31 and reached base in half his plate appearances across 11 games, hardly blinking at the altitude; the bat, the club is persuaded, plays now. The glove is the open question — he logged all of six big-league innings in left, and the front office wants another winter's progress from it.5

The arguments stack neatly on either side. For a sale: the open market is thin on right-handed-hitting outfielders, Hernández closed the season batting .343 with a .980 on-base-plus-slugging over his final 27 games, and a club that means to play its young men — the general manager Brandon Gomes professing himself uncompelled but adding, "as far as due diligence, we'll always listen" — cannot also pay $14.5 million for the post the young man wants. Against it: the lineup leans left-handed without him, the glove behind De Paula is unproven, and the clubhouse has already lost Miguel Rojas to retirement — his utility post filled only Friday by the Lewis purchase, as yesterday's columns recorded — and Kiké Hernández to the open market, which makes a veteran of Teoscar's standing worth more than his slash line. The Herald files the question where the wire leaves it: open, and worth watching through the Winter Meetings.5

THE SKUBAL REGISTER: THE QUEUE BEHIND THE GREAT LEFT-HANDER GROWS RESTLESS — SEVEN CLUBS PRESS UPON PERALTA, WHO MAY NOT WAIT FOR THE VERDICT AFTER ALL, WHILE THE METS ARE RUNG ON VIENTOS AND THE FRANCE INTEREST ACQUIRES A TERM

The register these columns keep on the winter's grandest courtship stands this morning where yesterday's edition left it — the Mets' reported offer of nine years and very nearly $400 million still the only hard figure in the file — but the wire allows that the biggest free-agent story of the offseason "could soon have a resolution," and it is the queue behind the great man that supplies the Sunday news. The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal and Will Sammon count seven clubs now pursuing Freddy Peralta — the Rays, who "remain seriously engaged" on the man they remade, with the Pale Hose, the Cubs, the Friars, the Canadians and two mystery establishments besides — and report that Peralta may sign before Skubal decides at all, which would upend the orderly procession the insider Jon Paul Morosi has described, with Peralta and Michael King waiting politely upon the verdict. The right-hander's 2026 explains the crowd: a 5.01 figure across 21 starts in a Mets uniform, a midsummer trade to Tampa Bay, then an 0.79 over his final six starts of the regular season and the Most Valuable Player's honors of the league championship series — as thorough a restoration as the year produced.4

The Metropolitans' periphery, meanwhile, keeps its own column moving. The club tendered Mark Vientos his contract Friday, but Sammon reports rival clubs have been calling on the first baseman all the same, his 81 OPS+ across 87 games having dimmed his claim on the post; and the Ty France interest these columns carried yesterday now has a term attached, The Athletic reporting that France — a 139 OPS+ this past season, and one of the finest gloves at the position — seeks a contract of three years. A club that extended its center fielder Saturday, covets the market's best pitcher, and shops for a first baseman besides is a club conducting its winter at full orchestra, and the register stays open.4

THE PACIFIC DESK: THE SAWAMURA MAN CALLS ON THE SECOND CITY — ITOH, LATELY OF THE NIPPON-HAM FIGHTERS, IS SEEN IN CHICAGO WITH HIS POSTING CLOCK RUNNING, AND BOTH LOCAL ESTABLISHMENTS HAVE REASON TO HAVE SET THE KETTLE ON

The eastern shelf these columns have watched all week gains a destination city. Hiromi Itoh, the right-hander posted by the Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters on the first of November, paid a visit to Chicago on Friday, by the account of ESPN's Jesse Rogers and Jorge Castillo — and the town offers two plausible hosts, though the wire cannot say whether the man sat with the Cubs, the White Sox, or the pair of them. The reporter Francys Romero has lately placed the South Siders' interest on the record, and their motive is written in these columns' own file: a rotation remade by the May signing and then thinned again by the Castillo sale, with the steward Getz promising continued pursuit. The North Side's motive is no fainter, the club's winter list of departed arms — Imanaga, Boyd, Gausman and the rest — having been set down in Friday's edition.4

The credentials travel well. Itoh, 29, pitched to a 3.18 earned-run average with 159 strikeouts across 172 and two-thirds innings this past season, one year after taking the Sawamura Award, the Japanese game's highest honor for a pitcher. The clock is the story's spring: a posted player has 45 days from his posting date to come to terms, so the window wound on the first of November runs only into mid-December, and every audience now is an audience under the glass. The Herald notes for the completist that this makes two arms of the Japanese leagues under active courtship in these pages — the Seibu right-hander Taira, his planned Mets video audience and his South Side admirers alike, having been recorded Friday — and the stove wants only a signature from either to open the market entire.4

THE HERALD LOWERS ITS COLORS: LANCE BROADWAY, FIRST-ROUND MAN OF 2005 WHO TRADED THE MOUND FOR THE PICTURES, IS DEAD AT THREE-AND-FORTY

The wire from Dallas brings the paper's saddest item. Lance Broadway, right-handed pitcher of the White Sox and the Mets, died Tuesday in that city at the age of 43; the county medical examiner's report, posted Thursday, gave no immediate cause. Broadway pitched his college ball at Dallas Baptist and at TCU, was taken by the White Sox in the first round of the 2005 draft, and appeared in 27 big-league games between 2007 and 2009 — and when the game was done with him, he declined to be done with performing, making his picture debut in Olympus Has Fallen in 2013 and appearing in several television series besides.6

Most men are allotted one improbable career; Broadway built himself two, and gave his name's marquee promise an honest second act. The Herald dips its masthead to a man who understood that the show goes on, and sends its sympathies to all who loved him.

A Sunday paper of signatures and shop windows: a Met of 22 signed into the next decade, the steadiest Giant listed for inquiry, and a posting clock ticking in two Chicago anterooms — the whole of it set down above. The forward ledger was opened before a word was written, per the house custom, and reads as it read yesterday: the camps' reporting dates remain unposted, so the count runs to the first rung bearing a date — the spring exhibition openers of Friday, the 19th of February, 89 mornings from this one, with Opening Night to follow on Wednesday, the 24th of March, 122 mornings off.2 The nearer columns allow no dozing: the collective agreement has 9 mornings left to live, and the bargainers return to the table on the morrow, Monday, their first sitting since Friday's rare day of motion;7 Cooperstown's committee of sixteen reports in 14; the Winter Meetings convene at San Diego with the Rule 5 drafting on December 9, 17 mornings from this one; and the writers' envelope waits for the 19th of January, 58 mornings off. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 90 days until the first spring-training game.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 136 · Saturday, the Twenty-First of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

90 days until the first spring-training game (Friday, the 19th of February, 2027).

News Around the League

THE FIVE O'CLOCK RECKONING: FOUR-AND-FORTY MEN ARE LOOSED UPON THE MARKET IN A SINGLE AFTERNOON — A ROOKIE OF THE YEAR AMONG THEM, MINNESOTA CUTS THREE AT A STROKE, AND SIX CLUBS KEEP EVERY HAND THEY HOLD

Five o'clock came and went on Friday, and when the hour had passed, 44 men who woke that morning under club control went to bed free agents, their employers having declined to tender them contracts for 2027. Six clubs — the Angels, the Athletics, the Brewers, the Marlins, the Orioles and the White Sox — kept every hand they held; the other twenty-four did their cutting, and the headline casualty wore pinstripes. Luis Gil, Rookie of the Year in the American League only two autumns ago — 15-7 with a 3.50 figure and 171 strikeouts across 29 starts in 2024, the first Yankee pitcher to take the honor since Dave Righetti in 1981 — was let go along with the reliever Fernando Cruz, the body having lately kept none of the promises the arm once made. A lat strain cost Gil the first four months of 2025, shoulder trouble better than three months of this past season, and his nine appearances of 2026 produced a 4.61 figure in 27 and a third innings; the steward Brian Cashman pointed to the depth of his pitching staff, and three seasons of club control went into the waste-basket with the man. The reader of these columns' island correspondence will relish the address on his winter mail: Gil is pitching even now for the Tigres del Licey, the same establishment that holds Vladimir Guerrero Jr.'s rights and the Águilas' new manager in its headlights. Cruz, for his part, goes to market with a partially torn elbow ligament he means to mend without the knife, and a splitter that struck out 139 men in 102 and two-thirds innings over his two Bronx seasons.345

The heaviest single stroke fell in Minnesota, where the front office that spent Wednesday buying Sonny Gray spent Friday subtracting: Bailey Ober, Trevor Larnach and Matt Wallner, all cut loose at once, on the same afternoon the club traded Royce Lewis — of which more in the column below. Ober is the name that answers Thursday's arithmetic, when these pages counted nine rotation names for five posts and reckoned a sale the likeliest relief; the ledger chose the simpler instrument. The big right-hander pitched to a 3.66 figure across 68 starts from 2022 to 2024 but has been below the league's average since, and with Gray returned and both Pablo López and Mick Abel expected back from elbow surgery, his seat was wanted.5 Wallner carries elite raw power — a barrel rate of 16.2 percent across 2023 to 2025 and a ball struck at 116.8 miles an hour — and four years of control, yet never held a steady post; Larnach has hit .255/.341/.431 against right-handed pitching since 2021 and .583 by on-base-plus-slugging against the left-handed kind, a split that finally told.5

The rest of the roll rewards the browser. Seattle cut Luke Raley, whose bat lost its room when the Garcia purchase of Thursday's lead remade the roster, and whose season ended under the surgeon's flexor-tendon repair after an on-base-plus-slugging of .929 through his first 53 games gave way to a .157 batting average thereafter.5 Kansas City let go Kyle Isbel and his 51 outs above average in center field since 2022 — third among all outfielders in that span, behind only Pete Crow-Armstrong and Daulton Varsho. Cleveland parted with the utility man David Fry; Washington with Josiah Gray, an All-Star of 2023 who underwent the Tommy John operation in 2024 and has made five appearances these past three years; Detroit with Matt Vierling and Trey Sweeney; St. Louis with Nolan Gorman, whose 41 home runs and 111 OPS+ across 2022 and 2023 have shrunk to a 66 OPS+ in 85 games this past season; and Toronto with Davis Schneider, who hit a leadoff home run in the fifth game of the 2025 World's Series and posted a 1.008 on-base-plus-slugging as a rookie he never matched again.35 And in Boston the formality was completed: Connor Wong, unseated Wednesday when the Fortes purchase crowded him off the roster — as these columns recorded Thursday — was by five o'clock cut loose altogether.3

THE EXCHANGE DESK: THE FIRST NAME CALLED IN THE DRAFT OF 2017 CHANGES HANDS — ROYCE LEWIS GOES WEST TO THE DODGERS FOR BOBBY MILLER AND A CATCHER OF NINETEEN, AND THE UTILITY POST LATELY VACATED BY ROJAS HAS ITS NEW TENANT

The day's one trade of consequence was struck in the hours before the tender deadline: the Dodgers acquired the infielder Royce Lewis from Minnesota, sending back the right-hander Bobby Miller and the 19-year-old catcher Francisco Espinoza. Lewis, 27, was the first name called in the draft of 2017, a schoolboy out of JSerra Catholic in San Juan Capistrano whose professional life has been a running quarrel with his own lower half — twice only in five seasons has he reached 100 games. The past season was, by that grim standard, his healthiest: a career-high 125 games, a lean .227/.287/.380 at the plate, and work at three stations — third base chiefly, with 82 games at first and 16 at second.6

The fit is plain enough. Los Angeles wanted a right-handed-hitting utility infielder from the day Miguel Rojas retired at the season's close, and Lewis — in his second winter of arbitration, under club control through 2028 — answers the description at every point: second-base work to free Tommy Edman for his roving commission, and rest days bought for Max Muncy and Freddie Freeman when a left-hander has the ball.6

Minnesota's side of the ledger is a wager on pedigree. Miller, also 27, went 11-4 with a 3.76 figure as a rookie of 2023 and was for a season the celebrated heir of the Los Angeles pitching line; injury and erosion have limited him to five big-league appearances since the start of 2025, and he arrives as a reclamation. Espinoza, of the Dodgers' international class of 2024, batted .296 with a .713 on-base-plus-slugging in 32 games of Single-A ball.6 Set the trade beside the afternoon's three non-tenders and the Minnesota roster turned over six names between breakfast and dark — four men out, two in, and a front office whose chairman promised a spending winter, as these pages have recorded, revealed to be pruning with the other hand.

THE LABOR QUESTION: TEN MORNINGS LEFT ON THE AGREEMENT'S LIFE — THE LEAGUE WITHDRAWS ITS DESIGNS ON THE SCHOOLBOY DRAFT, THE UNION ANSWERS WITH A CHARTER FOR THE INTERNATIONAL AMATEUR, AND THE TABLE IS SET AGAIN FOR MONDAY

Friday's bargaining session concerned not the veteran's wage but the amateur's door, and produced the rarest article in the current negotiation: a concession. Major League Baseball withdrew its proposal to strip high-school players of their eligibility for the domestic draft, proposing instead to keep the present entry rules for domestic amateurs — this in recognition, said the league spokesman Glen Caplin, of the union's feedback. On the international side no such comity: the Players Association formally rejected the league's international draft proposal from earlier this year and countered with a charter of its own for the amateur entry process abroad. "The enhanced transparency of the International Draft that we have proposed best addresses the root causes of corruption in the current system," Caplin maintained for the league's part.7

The union's counter-proposal is a document of parts. It would raise the clubs' signing-bonus pools and permit teams to exceed them; lift the bonus-pool exemption from $10,000 to $75,000, fattening the envelopes at the low end of the scale; introduce new bonuses for players as they climb the minor-league ladder; establish clear penalties for club conduct the agreement forbids; and eliminate the pre-agreement arrangements — the handshakes made with boys years before they may lawfully sign — that the union holds to be the system's true corruption. For the smaller markets it offers inducements besides: added pool money within the agreement's term, bonuses for reaching the postseason funded by the taxes of pool-exceeding clubs, and strengthened rewards for clubs that lose free agents. "We are committed to negotiating a system that preserves opportunities for future generations of players, protects young prospects from exploitation, and provides flexibility without further burdening international players with new artificial restrictions like a draft," said the interim executive director Bruce Meyer.7

The Herald, whose sympathies on matters of the purse are a matter of long record, notes simply that one side spent Friday proposing to pay young men more and the other withdrew a restriction it had proposed to impose — a day, on balance, of motion in the right direction. The cap and the floor over which the commissioner and the union exchanged broadsides in Thursday's columns went unaddressed in Friday's accounts, and the clock concedes nothing to the amateurs' progress: the agreement dies at one minute before midnight on the first of December, ten mornings from this one, and the two sides are expected back at the table Monday.7

THE SKUBAL REGISTER: THE FIGURE IS NAMED AT LAST — NINE YEARS AND NEAR FOUR HUNDRED MILLIONS REPORTED FROM THE FLUSHING TREASURY, A FIFTH SUITOR TAKES ITS AUDIENCE BY VIDEO, AND THE WHOLE PITCHING MARKET WAITS ON ONE MAN'S PEN

The register these columns keep on the winter's grandest courtship records its first hard number. By the account of MLB Network Radio's Jim Duquette, the Mets have laid before Tarik Skubal an offer of nine years and very nearly $400 million — terms that would carry the highest average yearly wage ever given a free-agent starting pitcher — and it remains unclear, the wire allows, whether any rival establishment has yet put a figure on paper at all. The audiences, meanwhile, multiply: to the four suitors who have sat with the man in person — the Mets, Toronto, San Diego, and the Dodgers, his employers of this past season, who took him from Detroit at the 2025 deadline — the insider Jon Heyman adds a fifth, unnamed, that held its audience by video on Wednesday — one of the two mystery establishments these columns have carried all week, an in-person sitting possibly to follow. The expectation of a choice by the first of December stands — the very day the collective agreement dies.89

Beneath the register, the whole pitching market stands in queue. Jon Paul Morosi reckons that Michael King and Freddy Peralta — the finest arms at liberty after the great left-hander — will both wait upon the Skubal decision before signing anywhere, and Jim Bowden counts better than six clubs in pursuit of Peralta, both Chicago establishments, the Padres and the Rays among them. One signature, in short, holds a dozen in escrow, and the register stays open.9

THE INK DESK: THE CLUB THAT LOST SKUBAL LOCKS UP ITS NEW ACE — MELTON SIGNS IN DETROIT FOR SIX YEARS AND SIX-AND-FORTY MILLIONS AND A HALF, SAN DIEGO KEEPS ITS 'HO-LY SHEETS' MAN, AND TWO BULLPEN PRODIGALS COME HOME TO THE BRONX AND THE BAY

The day's largest signature belongs to Detroit, and the moral writes itself. The Tigers agreed with the right-hander Troy Melton on an extension of six years and $46.5 million guaranteed, with a club option for 2033 and as much as $98 million obtainable through options and incentives, the deal pending a physical — the longest engagement any Detroit pitcher has been offered since Justin Verlander's seven years and $180 million beginning in 2013. Melton, who turns 26 in about two weeks, was a fourth-round selection of 2022 out of San Diego State; his 2026 opened two months late for elbow inflammation and then announced him entirely, a 7-1 record with a 1.49 figure across his first 14 starts and a closing ledger of 8-5 with a 2.76, the final week spent resting an arm whose tests showed no structural harm. With barely a year of service to his name, the contract buys out every arbitration winter and up to two free-agent years besides.10

The resonance is what elevates the item. This is the organization that could not come to terms with Skubal — two Cy Young Awards notwithstanding — and traded him to Los Angeles at the 2025 deadline; it is an organization that has flinched from long pitching contracts since the Zimmermann affair of the previous decade. That it now binds itself to Melton for six years is as plain a statement as a front office can make about which lesson it drew.10

In San Diego the ink ran warmer. The Padres announced a three-year contract for Gavin Sheets worth $11 million, with player options of $4 million apiece after 2027 and 2028 — the lefty slugger had been entering his final arbitration winter, and chose certainty with escape hatches. The figures since he arrived on a minor-league wage two springs ago: a .736 on-base-plus-slugging and 36 home runs, this past season's .212 earned the hard way, the second half played on a torn plantar plate in the left foot that he will rehabilitate rather than have repaired, by the steward A.J. Preller's account. The man's October requires no footnote at Petco Park, where his pinch-hit two-run homer clinched the Wild Card series against the Cubs and the "Ho-ly Sheets" chants have not altogether died down since.11

And two bullpen prodigals found their way home. Jonathan Loáisiga returns to the Yankees — two years at roughly $18 million with a club option for 2029, pending a physical — after a single Arizona season taken on a minor-league deal: a 2.42 figure across 67 innings and a career-high 67 appearances, a sinker at 98 miles an hour, and ground balls at a rate in the game's 95th percentile. He spent his first eight seasons in the Bronx, and his signing advances the bullpen restoration the steward Cashman called his November priority, Bednar's tender and the submariner Hill's return beside it.12 In San Francisco, Camilo Doval signed for one year and $6.3 million to avoid arbitration — the 2023 All-Star whose 39 saves tied for the league's best, whose road since ran through demotion, a deadline sale to the Yankees, and a 4.30 season split with Pittsburgh, until the club that made him claimed him off waivers in September. The Orange and Black will attempt the restoration where the legend was first built.13

THE EXCHANGE DESK, CONTINUED: SMALL STROKES AND LARGER DESIGNS — ARIZONA BUYS A MENDED ARM OFF BOSTON, THE CUBS GATHER A CATCHER FROM THE WAIVER WIRE, DENVER ADDS AN AEROSPACE ENGINEER WHO THROWS SIDEARM, AND THE METS SHOP FOR A FIRST BASEMAN WHILE ATLANTA HUNTS A SHORTSTOP

The smaller strokes of the day filled a ledger page of their own. Arizona bought the right-hander Johan Oviedo from Boston, sending back the 22-year-old left-hander Luke Dotson with a player to be named or cash; Oviedo, 28, made 32 starts with a 4.31 figure for Pittsburgh in 2023 before the Tommy John operation took his 2024 entire and an elbow sprain most of his 2026, and he arrives as insurance for a Sonoran rotation thinned by the departures of Gallen and Soroka to the open market — Burnes, Kelly, Nelson, Rodriguez and Pfaadt stand as the five.14 The Cubs claimed the catcher Joey Bart off the waiver wire from the White Sox and signed him for 2027 — the 29-year-old hit .214 across three clubs and a broken hand this past season, and pairs with Amaya now that Carson Kelly is at liberty — and fetched the reliever Braxton Roxby from Washington for cash, 60 strikeouts in 40 Triple-A outings recommending him; the steward Carter Hawkins allowed that his club must "take risks" to reach its goals.15

Denver kept buying — its second strike in two days, after yesterday's columns recorded the Castillo-Martin freight arriving from Chicago — taking the reliever Chase Lee from Toronto for cash considerations, and the Herald submits Lee's card as the day's finest reading: a walk-on at Alabama who took his degree in aerospace engineering, then taught himself into a sixth-round pick, now delivering sliders and sweepers from a sidearm angle, 5-1 with a 4.60 figure in 40 big-league games. The veteran Jimmy Herget was designated for assignment to make the room, and by five o'clock cut loose altogether.163 The Giants, for their part, sent the infielder Christian Koss to the Rays for Cole Stokes, 21, a twelfth-round selection of the summer's draft out of Florida State who has yet to throw a professional pitch.13

The speculative shelf restocked briskly besides. The insider Heyman reports the Mets — Bauers having gone off the board to Boston, as these columns have recorded — turning their eye to Ty France, 32, who hit .295/.363/.502 with 21 home runs in 133 games for San Diego and whose glove at first base has been worth 14 fielding runs over the past two seasons, tied for second at the position. The incumbent arithmetic argues the case: the Flushing first-base company of Young, Vientos and Baty combined for 18 home runs, an 85 wRC+ and the worst WAR figure in the game at the station, while Jorge Polanco, signed to be Alonso's successor, played two games at first and hit .148 in 37 games in all.9

And in Atlanta the shortstop question has aged into a crisis openly admitted. Since Dansby Swanson's leaving after 2022, Atlanta shortstops rank last in the game by wRC+ and by FanGraphs' wins alike; Ha-Seong Kim hit .116 in 51 games and is at liberty, as is Mauricio Dubón, who started 62 games at the post. With J.P. Crawford the best of a thin free-agent shelf, the steward Alex Anthopoulos allowed on a podcast that his club has discussed trades, and Heyman supplies the names worth the discussing: Corey Seager of Texas, Zach Neto of the Angels, and Jacob Wilson of the Athletics. The Giants, meanwhile, hunt rotation help behind Webb and Roupp, their only two certainties — Morosi has them on Matthew Boyd, 35, an All-Star of 2025 and lately of the Cubs' at-liberty class as yesterday's columns noted, and on Nick Pivetta, 33, whose career-best 2.87 of 2025 gave way to eight elbow-shortened starts this past season.9

Forty-four men put to the street at the stroke of five, the first name of the 2017 draft traded west by sundown, and a bargaining table that for one Friday moved instead of merely glaring — the Saturday columns hold the whole of it above. The forward ledger was opened before a word was written, per the house custom, and tells its patient story: the camps' reporting dates remain unposted, so the count runs to the first rung bearing a date — the spring exhibition openers of Friday, the 19th of February, 90 mornings from this one, with Opening Night to follow on Wednesday, the 24th of March, 123 mornings off.2 The nearer columns press close: the collective agreement has 10 mornings left to live, with the bargainers back at the table Monday;7 Cooperstown's committee of sixteen reports in 15; the Winter Meetings convene at San Diego with the Rule 5 drafting on December 9, 18 mornings from this one; and the writers' envelope waits for the 19th of January, 59 mornings off. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
