entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Twentieth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 91 days until the first spring-training game.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 135 · Friday, the Twentieth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

91 days until the first spring-training game (Friday, the 19th of February, 2027).

News Around the League

THE HIT KING PARDONED: FROM THE PRESIDENTIAL AEROPLANE, A 'COMPLETE AND TOTAL' CLEMENCY FOR PETE ROSE, SEVEN-AND-THIRTY YEARS AFTER THE BAN AND TWO YEARS BEYOND THE GRAVE — THE TAX CASE IS STRUCK FROM THE FEDERAL LEDGER, BUT COOPERSTOWN KEEPS ITS OWN BOOKS

The winter's business paused Thursday for a dispatch from an altitude the wire rarely files from. President Trump, flying home from Asia aboard Air Force One, announced upon his social channels that he had granted a posthumous pardon to Pete Rose, the game's all-time leader in base hits, better than two years after the man's death. "I have just given a Complete and Total Pardon to the Late, Great Pete Rose, a true Baseball SUPERSTAR & LEGEND," the President wrote. The gesture was first promised in March of 2025, to be signed "over the next few weeks"; the pen took roughly twenty months to find the paper. What precisely the pardon covers was not specified — asked for particulars, a White House official pointed to the tax charges.3

Those charges are the one entry a president's pen can reach. On April 20, 1990, Rose pleaded guilty to two counts of filing false income-tax returns, admitting he had failed to report $354,968 across four years; that July, Judge S. Arthur Spiegel of Cincinnati sentenced him to five months in federal prison, a $50,000 fine and 1,000 hours of community service. Rose repaid the revenue men $366,042, reported to a minimum-security facility in Illinois in August of 1990, and was released the following January. That is the case now wiped from the books.3

The game's own sentence was never the President's to commute. Rose accepted a permanent banishment in August 1989, after the investigator John M. Dowd concluded he had bet numerous times on his own Cincinnati club while playing for and managing it from 1985 to 1987 — and that ledger was already settled by a different hand: Commissioner Manfred ruled in May 2025 that permanent ineligibility ends at death, a stroke that restored seventeen men, Rose and Shoeless Joe Jackson the most notable of the company. The road to bronze thus runs on Cooperstown's clock alone, and the earliest either man could be inducted is 2028. The Herald observes only this: it has spent the week in a Brooklyn gallery where the game's ancient quarrel with the wagering man is still being litigated at public expense, and the reader may weigh the week's two gambling dispatches in whatever order he pleases.3

THE EXCHANGE DESK: THE ROTATION PRINTED WEDNESDAY IS CROSSED OUT BY THURSDAY NIGHT — CHICAGO SENDS CASTILLO AND MARTIN TO THE MOUNTAIN MEN FOR TWO PROSPECTS, DENVER ASSUMES THE WHOLE OF THE VETERAN'S WAGE, AND GETZ PROMISES MORE BUSINESS IN THE COMING WEEKS

When these columns set down the South Side rotation account on Wednesday — Burke, Martin, Castillo, the young Schultz, Taylor — the ink was scarcely dry before the ledger crossed two names out. On Thursday the White Sox introduced their new man Dustin May at a press conference, the steward Chris Getz spoke of getting back on the telephone the moment it ended, and by nightfall he had: Luis Castillo and Davis Martin, both right-handers, were traded to Colorado for the left-hander Sean Sullivan and Douglas Veliz, a 17-year-old catcher out of the Dominican Summer League.54

What the Mountain men have bought is experience, at full freight. Castillo, who turns 34 next month, is a three-time All-Star — twice for the Reds, once for Seattle — with a career ledger of 88-95 and a 3.75 earned-run average across 272 games and ten seasons, an above-average figure in his rookie year of 2017 and every season from 2019 through 2025 before a rough spell followed his deadline trade to Chicago; Colorado takes on the whole of his $24.15 million wage for 2027. Martin, 30 in January, went 9-8 with a 3.95 this past season after opening it 8-1 with a 2.00 through 11 starts, remains under club control through 2030, and is reunited with the new Rockies pitching coach Ethan Katz, who held the same post in Chicago. The need could hardly be plainer: starting pitching is Denver's declared first priority, the staff having lately owned the game's highest earned-run average both in sum (5.59) and from its rotation (6.28), and with Freeland, Sugano and Quintana all exploring free agency, Ryan Feltner had stood as the most experienced starter on the premises. It is the second time the DePodesta-Byrnes front office has bought pitching from this same shop, after the summer's Doyle trade.4

Chicago's side of the ledger is the future and the purse. Sullivan, 24, a second-round selection out of Wake Forest in 2023, made his debut in June and took his lumps — 0-3 with an 8.87 in six starts before shoulder and elbow trouble ended his summer — then steadied himself in the Fall League at 2-1 with a 3.07; the move is a homecoming of sorts, the big lefty having begun his collegiate career at Northwestern. Veliz, signed out of Venezuela for $50,000, batted .300 in 29 games on the island circuit. The savings on Castillo's wage, the club allows, will be reinvested in another arm, and Getz put the winter's intent plainly: "We're going to look for opportunities in the coming weeks. We're going to continue the pursuit." The parting note belongs to Martin, who leaves as the longest-tenured White Sox man by service time — proof, if November needed any, that the hot stove honors no seniority.54

THE SKUBAL REGISTER: THE FOURTH AUDIENCE IS HELD AND A DARK HORSE DECLARES ITSELF — SAN DIEGO SITS WITH THE PRIZE ARM AND IS STYLED 'ULTRA-AGGRESSIVE' WITH NEW MONEY BEHIND PRELLER, WHILE THE WIRE'S SOURCES STILL MAKE QUEENS THE FAVORITE

The register these columns keep on the winter's grandest courtship duly records its fourth audience: the Mission nine sat with Tarik Skubal on Wednesday, completing the round these pages forecast — the Mets on Monday, the Dodgers and the Maple Leaf nine on Tuesday, San Diego to follow — with two of the six sittings booked still belonging to hosts unnamed. The insider Jon Heyman supplies the morning's color: the club's new ownership will be "uber-committed" behind the general manager A.J. Preller, the wire styles the pursuit "ultra-aggressive," and while Heyman stops short of calling San Diego a frontrunner, he allows the club "a shot to upset" the Mets, Toronto and the Dodgers. The complication is arithmetical — the Mission nine must rebuild very nearly an entire rotation besides, and keep an interest in the bat of Seiya Suzuki into the bargain.76

The handicapping, for all that, holds its shape. ESPN's sources continue to reckon the Mets the favorite as the pursuit quickens, and the counsel on timing stands as yesterday's columns had it: no decision is imminent, and the weekend may well pass without one. The figures under discussion remain historic — the largest guarantee ever written for a pitcher is reckoned to be in danger — and so the register stays open, with the collective agreement's clock ticking audibly beneath every sitting.86

THE INK DESK: THE METROPOLITANS SHOP IN JAPAN FOR LEFT-HANDED HELP — DARWINZON HERNANDEZ, LATELY OF THE SOFTBANK HAWKS, COMES BACK ACROSS THE PACIFIC ON A THREE-YEAR WAGER OF TWELVE MILLIONS

The Metropolitans made the day's quietest purchase and perhaps its shrewdest. By the account of a source, the Mets have agreed with the left-handed reliever Darwinzon Hernández on a contract of three years and $12 million — the club not yet confirming — to bring the Venezuelan back across the Pacific. Hernández, who turns 30 in December, has spent the last four seasons with the Fukuoka SoftBank Hawks of Japan, pitching to a 2.46 earned-run average across 131 and two-thirds innings, this past year a 1.48 with 52 strikeouts in 42 and two-thirds. His last major-league work came for Boston in 2022, the close of a four-season Fenway tenure that read 5.06 with 133 strikeouts against 73 walks in 85 and a third innings — power stuff forever at war with the strike zone, and whether the Japanese seasons have ended that war is the question the wager turns on.9

The reasoning was stated on the record weeks ago. "We're at a point in the industry where we've got to be able to get left-handed hitters out," said the president of baseball operations David Stearns at the Las Vegas meetings — and the arithmetic backs him, left-handed batters having taken 49 percent of all big-league plate appearances last season, the highest share since at least 1961. The Flushing bullpen, meanwhile, was stripped of its left hands at the summer deadline, Minter sent to Minnesota and Raley to Philadelphia; Hernández arrives as the likeliest southpaw in the 2027 relief corps, and he and the closer Devin Williams now stand as the only Mets relievers on guaranteed money. Nor is the eastern shopping done: a video audience is planned with Kaima Taira, the Seibu right-hander posted off a league-best 1.36 — the same Taira the White Sox eye, as Wednesday's columns noted.96

THE EXCHANGE DESK, CONTINUED: HALF A DOZEN CLUBS AND MORE RING ON LOWE WHILE BOTH OLD EMPLOYERS KEEP THE DOOR AJAR, BUBIC'S MENDED ARM DRAWS A CROWD, THE NORTH SIDERS SCOUT SATO AND DURAN, AND SEATTLE GOES SHOPPING FOR ITS GARDEN

The market around Brandon Lowe has filled quickly. Three days after the second baseman declined his $23.15 million tender — with a fresh silver bat under his arm, as these columns recorded Wednesday — the insider Jon Paul Morosi reports "very strong interest" from more than half a dozen clubs in a man coming off a .260 season of 35 home runs and 96 driven in. Both former employers linger at the door: the Pittsburgh steward Ben Cherington says his club remains in touch and open to a reunion, and the Tampa men, who sold Lowe to the Smoky City only last winter, are reckoned open to taking him back. Toronto is linked in multiple reports, the Yankees have checked in, and whoever signs him pays the draft-pick toll, Pittsburgh collecting a premium selection for its trouble.6

The left-hander Kris Bubic draws a comparable crowd from the pitching aisle. The surgeon's catalogue is lengthy — the Tommy John operation in 2023, a rotator-cuff strain in 2025, elbow soreness this past season — but so is the ledger beside it: a 2.90 earned-run average across the last three years, an All-Star turn as a Kansas City starter in 2025, and October work from the Dodgers' bullpen after a deadline trade. The Athletic reports interest from contenders and non-contenders alike; Morosi expects him signed as a starter and names the Royals, Tigers, Cubs, Birds, Toronto and the Cardinals as sensible shorter-term fits, with Baltimore's want sharpened by Rogers' free agency and the Capital nine making their own inquiries.6

On the North Side the winter's shopping list runs long — Imanaga, Boyd, Gausman, Holmes, Peterson and Rea are all at liberty from the rotation, and neither Happ nor Suzuki is reckoned likely to return to the garden. The Athletic's Patrick Mooney reports the Cubs have "extensively scouted" the Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato — the same Sato that Toronto covets, as Thursday's columns noted — and the club has evaluated Boston's Jarren Duran as a change-of-scenery addition besides, a possibility these pages mapped Wednesday that grows likelier now that the Bauers purchase has crowded the Fenway outfield.6

And in Seattle, the rotation shop having been declared shut in yesterday's lead, the buying turns to the grass. The club seeks a corner outfielder, bullpen help and a versatile infielder, the steward Dipoto calling another right-handed bat "ideal"; the linked names include Happ — four consecutive Gold Gloves in left, and old ties to the new Seattle manager Jason Kanzler, lately the Cubs' farm director — and Suzuki, with Donovan reckoned for left field now that Arozarena has gone to market, and face-to-face sittings with several free-agent relievers already held.6

THE WINTER ISLANDS: THE SPRING'S ITALIAN SENSATION TAKES THE EAGLES' HELM — CERVELLI IS NAMED MANAGER OF THE AGUILAS CIBAEÑAS, HOURS AFTER A WALK-OFF LOSS TO THE SELFSAME LICEY THAT COURTS GUERRERO

The island chapter gains a new character. The Águilas Cibaeñas of Santiago announced Thursday morning the hiring of Francisco Cervelli as manager, the former big-league catcher replacing the veteran skipper Luis "Pipe" Urueta — and the timing told the whole story, the announcement coming hours after a walk-off loss to the Tigres del Licey at the Quisqueya, a two-run drive over the wall by the Arizona farmhand Ángel Ortiz, that left the Eagles last in the league at 9 and 16. It is Cervelli's first command in winter-league play, and his brief is nothing less than the island's proudest rivalry: the Águilas hold 22 championships since the league's founding in 1951, second only to Licey's 24, and have not raised a banner since the winter of 2020-21.10

The man arrives with the year's best managing story already in his pocket. Cervelli caught thirteen big-league seasons — a ring with the 2009 Yankees, then the Pirates, Braves and Marlins — served as catching instructor on the 2022 Padres club that reached the league championship series, and took the Italian national post fourteen months before this spring's World Classic, honoring the country of his father while the land of his own birth, Venezuela, went on to take the trophy. His Azzurri went 5 and 1 — a sweep of their Houston pool with upsets of the United States and Mexico, a quarterfinal win over Puerto Rico, and a semifinal exit against the eventual champions. The roster he inherits is no winter hobby outfit, counting the Yankees' Jasson Domínguez, the San Diego right-hander Randy Vásquez and the Arizona reliever Justin Martínez among its hands. And the reader of Thursday's columns will note the standings' finest subplot: the club Cervelli must now chase is the same Licey whose blue Vladimir Guerrero Jr. waits on Toronto's blessing to wear.10

A presidential pen scratching at a 36-year-old tax case, a rotation unmade the day after this paper printed it, and a new skipper for the winter islands — the Friday columns range farther afield than November usually permits, and every mile of it is set down above. The forward ledger was opened before a word was written, per the house custom, and tells its patient story: the camps' reporting dates remain unposted, so the count runs to the first rung bearing a date — the spring exhibition openers of Friday, the 19th of February, 91 mornings from this one, the ledger already printing the matchups themselves, the remade Rockies at the Desert nine among them — with Opening Night to follow on Wednesday, the 24th of March, 124 mornings off.2 The nearer columns hold their stations: the collective agreement has 11 mornings left to live, Cooperstown's committee of sixteen reports in 16, the Winter Meetings convene at San Diego with the Rule 5 drafting on December 9, 19 mornings from this one, and the writers' envelope waits for the 19th of January, 60 mornings off. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Nineteenth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 92 days until the first spring-training game.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 134 · Thursday, the Nineteenth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

92 days until the first spring-training game (Friday, the 19th of February, 2027).

News Around the League

THE WINTER'S FIRST BLOCKBUSTER: SIX MEN CHANGE FLAGS IN ONE GREAT WEDNESDAY SWAP — GARCIA OF THE GOLD GLOVE GOES TO THE PUGET SOUND MEN FOR MILLER AND TWO ARMS BESIDE, AND DIPOTO DECLARES HIS ROTATION CLOSED FOR BUSINESS

The trade market, which had spent the month clearing its throat, found its full voice Wednesday morning. Kansas City and Seattle struck the biggest blow of the winter's business so far: a six-player affair that sends the third baseman Maikel Garcia — Gold Glove winner and first-time All-Star in 2025, and signed through the decade's end — to the Puget Sound men along with the right-hander James McArthur and the pitching prospect L.P. Langevin, while the Missourians carry off the starters Bryce Miller and Logan Evans and the left-handed reliever José A. Ferrer. The seed was planted when the Kansas City steward J.J. Picollo allowed early this offseason that Garcia could be had if Seattle would open its rotation; the talks took root at the Las Vegas meetings and, in the words of the Seattle president Jerry Dipoto, "picked up steam very, very quickly."3

What Seattle has bought is order at a station that had none. Ten different men started at third base for the club last season, Brendan Donovan's 36 turns the most of them; Garcia, 26, arrives as the settled answer, and on terms a bookkeeper would frame — the five-year, $57.5 million extension he signed only last December pays him $7 million in 2027, rising by steps to $19 million in 2030, with a club option for 2031. The 2025 season states his case: .286/.351/.449 with a career-high 16 home runs and 5.6 wins by FanGraphs' reckoning, second among all third basemen to José Ramírez's 6.3, though strains of the hand and hamstring cut his 2026 to 82 games and a leaner .268/.334/.381. The glove needs no advocate — since taking the position full-time in 2023 he stands second among third basemen in Statcast's fielding runs and in outs above average alike. "He's got range like a shortstop, but playing at third base," said Dipoto, penciling him into an infield of Emerson, Young and Naylor, with Donovan freed for the outfield grass.3

The reader will recall from Monday's columns that the wire's thirty-club exercise nominated George Kirby as the Seattle man likeliest to move, Dipoto having allowed that his rotation ran eight deep. The ledger answered otherwise: Miller, who battled bone spurs in 2025 and ailments of the oblique and lat in 2026, and Evans, who missed the whole of the past season after an internal-brace operation, are the arms that go, and Kirby stays — the depth now reads six, Gilbert, Woo, Kirby, Hancock and the rookie Kade Anderson among them, and Dipoto pronounced the shop shut: "the likelihood of us trading a starter just went from very high to zero." Kansas City, for its part, buys low on Miller's pedigree and takes two more arms besides, having — by ESPN's account — floated Garcia to rival clubs before the strike was made. One almanac note hangs over all of it: Seattle's roster now stands at 38 with less than two weeks to run on the collective agreement, and every front office in the land is working against that same clock.34

THE EXCHANGE DESK, CONTINUED: THE FENWAY MEN FETCH A CATCHER FROM THE PENNANT-WINNERS, THE SERAPHS BUY JUNG FOR CASH, AND THE HOUSTON NINE WEIGH SELLING WALKER TO BUY AN ARM

The day's other business ran brisk. Boston bolstered the position behind the plate, fetching Nick Fortes from the Sunshine nine — a division rival fresh off the pennant — for the 17-year-old minor-league right-hander Angel Roa; Fortes, 30, a strong defender who played 109 games for Tampa Bay this past season with a .258 average and the second-lowest strikeout rate of any regular American League catcher, will carry the backup's mitt behind Adley Rutschman, and the veteran Connor Wong was designated for assignment to make the room.5 The Seraphs, meanwhile, took the infielder Jace Jung off Detroit's hands for cash considerations — a first-round selection of 2022, handed a fresh start out west.6

The speculative shelf restocked besides. The insider Jon Paul Morosi reports the Houston nine gauging the market for Christian Walker, the four-time Gold Glove first baseman entering his final season before free agency at a wage of $20 million — moving him would shift Isaac Paredes across the diamond, hand third base to Carlos Correa, and free the purse for a rotation that ranked 27th in the game with a 4.81 earned-run average; Morosi reckons the club "could afford a Rogers or a Clay Holmes" if the deal is done. ESPN's Jeff Passan adds the Frisco nine to the sellers' column, naming the breakout utility man Casey Schmitt — 21 home runs in 98 games before a torn meniscus ended his season — as a possible chip in a search for pitching the correspondent calls desperate, and The Athletic counts multiple clubs interested in the Phillies' reliever Orion Kerkering, high-octane stuff and a rough 4.97 season notwithstanding.4

THE LABOR QUESTION: THE COMMISSIONER DRAWS HIS LINE — 'CAN'T IMAGINE' THE OWNERS RATIFYING A DEAL WITHOUT A CAP AND FLOOR, THE UNION ANSWERS IN KIND, AND A FRANCHISE MEANWHILE CHANGES HANDS AT FOUR THOUSAND MILLIONS

With 12 mornings left on the collective agreement's life, the commissioner put away the diplomatic phrasing. "The owners want a deal with a salary cap and floor," Rob Manfred said following the owners' meetings, declaring the thirty clubs "100% unanimous in support of the proposals that have been made" and adding that he "can't imagine the owners ratifying a deal that does not include a cap and floor." The league's latest proposal sets the cap at $258.2 million and the floor at $180.2 million, to take effect in 2028; by this season's closing payrolls, twelve clubs would be obliged to raise their wages by a combined $636 million to reach the floor, and eight to shed a combined $528 million to duck under the cap. The commissioner's case is that the system serves the players — a guaranteed half-share of revenue, a dramatic raise to the minimum wage, free agency opened early for men of 30 with five years' service — and that the fans demand it: "We are not prepared to tell 70% of our fans that they're wrong on this issue."7

The union's answer came within the hour, and gave no ground. "There can be no clearer example of the league's lack of seriousness," said the interim executive director Bruce Meyer, "than their insistence that they will not negotiate over the economics outside of a radical change to the system" — one that would, by his accounting, suppress pay across every class of player and strip the guaranteed contract itself. "They want to make more money in profits and franchise values by artificially suppressing player salaries," Meyer said.7 On the question of franchise values, the morning's own wire filed a supporting document: the league expects the sale of the Angels to Kroenke Sports and Entertainment, at a valuation of $4 billion, to close in January.8 The Herald, whose sympathies on matters of the purse are a matter of long record, merely sets the two dispatches side by side and invites the reader to read them in either order.

As for the balance the cap is said to cure, the commissioner met the obvious exhibit head-on — the season just ended crowned the small-market Brewers over the small-market Rays — by observing that Milwaukee is the first small-market champion since the 2015 Royals, and that such a thing "should not be a once-in-a-decade phenomenon." He professed his overriding object to be an agreement and an uninterrupted season of 162 games, while noting that the last negotiation came "within inches of losing games" with no cap on the table at all. The clock, in any case, is indifferent to the rhetoric: the agreement dies at one minute before midnight on the first of December, and nearly everything else in this morning's paper — the trade market's hurry, the Rule 5 drafting's fine print, the timetable of the winter's grandest courtship — is being conducted in its shadow.7

THE INK DESK: SONNY COMES HOME TO THE TWIN CITIES — GRAY SIGNS FOR TWO YEARS AND FIVE-AND-FIFTY MILLIONS, THE RICHEST PITCHER'S WAGE IN THE FRANCHISE'S BOOKS, AND THE NORTH COUNTRY ROTATION NOW RUNS NINE DEEP

Minnesota made the largest free-agent investment it has made in years on Wednesday, agreeing with the right-hander Sonny Gray on a contract of two years through 2028 — expected to be worth $55 million by the account of the insider Jon Heyman, with ESPN's Jeff Passan reporting an opt-out after the first season. The figure, which the club has not confirmed, would make Gray the highest-paid pitcher in the franchise's history, and the guarantee the third-largest it has ever extended, behind only two separate engagements of Carlos Correa. Taken together with the catcher Jeffers' acceptance of the qualifying tender — yesterday's lead in these columns — the week reads as the chairman Tom Pohlad promised the winter would: the Twin Cities nine are spending again.910

The man returns to a familiar address. Gray, 37, pitched two seasons in Minnesota in 2022 and 2023, a 2.90 earned-run average across 56 starts and a Cy Young runner-up finish to Gerrit Cole in the latter year; he comes back off a season in Boston that read 18-5 with a 2.72 figure over 169 innings — the most wins of any pitcher in the game, the best winning percentage in the American League, and a fifth-place Cy Young finish — having declined his half of a $30 million mutual option and taken the Fenway men's $10 million buyout to go to market. Among active pitchers he ranks fourth in both starts and wins, and sixth in innings, earned-run average and strikeouts.9

The arithmetic of the thing all but guarantees further business. The rotation account now holds six established veterans — López, Ryan, Bradley, Ober, Kremer and Gray — with the young arms Prielipp, Matthews and Abel behind them, nine names for five posts; López, Ryan, Ober and Kremer can all reach free agency after 2027, the lineup still wants a bat, and the simplest way to buy one may be to sell a starter. The wire expects multiple moves before the camps open, and the Herald will keep the account current.9

THE SKUBAL REGISTER: FOUR COURTS HELD AND TWO IN SHADOW — THE DODGERS AND THE TORONTOS TAKE THEIR AUDIENCES, THE FRIARS FOLLOW, AND THE WIRE EXPECTS A SIGNATURE BEFORE THE AGREEMENT DIES

The register these columns have kept on the winter's prize arm gains three entries in two days. After the Mets' Monday audience in Orange County, ESPN's Jeff Passan reports that the Dodgers and the Torontos each held court with Tarik Skubal on Tuesday, and the Friars were scheduled for Wednesday, per the insider Jon Heyman — four known suitors of the six clubs booked, with two mystery establishments still unnamed. The timetable sharpens too: Heyman's expectation is that the two-time Cy Young laureate signs before the collective agreement expires at one minute to midnight on December 1, though his colleague Jon Paul Morosi counsels that no decision is imminent and the weekend may pass without one.114

The handicapping, meanwhile, has narrowed to two. Passan writes that the Mets left their meeting impressed, "reinforcing their status as favorites," while ESPN's Buster Olney reports the expectation among those inside the negotiations that the matter comes down to the Flushing establishment versus Toronto — a club Passan describes as "flush with cash and prepared to spend it," and for whom, this offseason, "nothing is off-limits." The Canadian shopping list runs well past the great left-hander: Brandon Lowe is reckoned a possibility at second base, with Chisholm on the radar should Lowe sign elsewhere, the incoming Japanese bat Teruaki Sato and the outfielder Suzuki are both linked, and Ketel Marte remains the trade-market alternative. The Dodgers, for their part, would prefer the shorter engagement the man himself does not want, and the Friars may elect to spread their money over several additions rather than one grand one. The register stays open, but the candle is burning at both ends.411

THE LAW COURTS: 'SEND SOME OF THAT' — THE PROSECUTION PRODUCES THE CLOSER'S OWN WORDS IN BROOKLYN, A BETTOR'S TEN THOUSAND ON A FIRST PITCH AND A REQUEST THAT A SHARE GO HOME

The federal trial of Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz, whose testimony this paper has followed through the week — the cooperating bettors first, the house of FanDuel after — turned Tuesday to the defendant's own correspondence. Prosecutors introduced evidence that Clase, upon learning an associate had won nearly $10,000 wagering on the closer's first pitch the previous night, asked the man to "send some of that to the [Dominican Republic]."12 Both pitchers, as these columns have recorded, have pleaded not guilty to the conspiracy charges against them, and the Herald will keep its seat in the gallery as the government's case proceeds.

THE WINTER ISLANDS: THE DREAM PUTS ON THE UNIFORM — GUERRERO TAKES HIS SWINGS IN LICEY BLUE AT THE QUISQUEYA, WHERE HIS FATHER TOOK HIS LAST AT-BATS, AND WAITS ONLY ON TORONTO'S BLESSING

Yesterday's columns reported the curiosity — Vladimir Guerrero Jr. traded, within the winter league, to the Tigres del Licey — and left open whether the man would ever appear for them. The answer took one day. On Wednesday Guerrero climbed the dugout steps at the Estadio Quisqueya Juan Marichal in Licey gear, took batting practice in a shade of blue uncannily near his Toronto colors, and sat before the Dominican press beside the Tigres' general manager. "It means a lot to me. Since I was a kid, I always admired this team and always dreamed about being here," he said in Spanish. "And today, one of my dreams is coming true." One formality stands between the man and the batter's box: "We're working on getting the approval," he said of his employers in Toronto. "They're the ones who will ultimately say yes or no."13

The appeal of the work is not hard to read. Guerrero is coming off the season he would soonest bury — a .688 on-base-plus-slugging and nine home runs, a year after his October heroics — and live pitching with something at stake is the cheapest medicine on sale; the romance, meanwhile, writes itself, his father having taken the final at-bats of a Hall of Fame career in the same Tigres colors in the winter of 2012-13. The roster he would join runs from Jesús Made, the 19-year-old reckoned the finest prospect in the game, to the old Blue Jay Emilio Bonifácio, still going at 41; the club holds Juan Soto's island rights besides, and it was Soto, the record should show, who texted Guerrero first when the trade was made. The island season runs to December 22, and the Herald's ear stays to the water.13

Six men swapped in a morning, the richest pitcher's wage in Minnesota's books by evening, and the commissioner and the union exchanging broadsides over it all — the stove is no longer merely lit but roaring, and the whole blaze is set down above. The forward ledger was opened before a word was written, per the house custom, and tells its unchanged story: the camps' reporting dates remain unposted, so the count runs to the first rung bearing a date — the spring exhibition openers of Friday, the 19th of February, 92 mornings from this one, with Opening Night to follow on Wednesday, the 24th of March, 125 mornings off.2 The nearer columns crowd close: the collective agreement has 12 mornings left to live, Cooperstown's committee of sixteen reports in 17, the Winter Meetings convene at San Diego with the Rule 5 drafting on December 9, 20 mornings from this one, and the writers' envelope waits for the 19th of January, 61 mornings off. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~

entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Eighteenth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 93 days until the first spring-training game.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 133 · Wednesday, the Eighteenth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

93 days until the first spring-training game (Friday, the 19th of February, 2027).

News Around the League

THE DAY OF ANSWERS RENDERS ITS VERDICTS: TWO YESES AND FIVE NOES AT THREE-AND-TWENTY MILLIONS THE QUESTION — BEDNAR STAYS A YANKEE AND JEFFERS A TWIN, WHILE AROZARENA, LOWE, SUZUKI, ROGERS AND MOREJON TAKE THEIR CHANCES WITH THE TOLL

The seven answers owed by four o'clock arrived on schedule, and the ledger closed by evening: two yeses, five noes. David Bednar remains a Yankee and Ryan Jeffers a Twin, each taking the certain $23.15 million for 2027; Randy Arozarena, Brandon Lowe, Seiya Suzuki, Trevor Rogers and Adrian Morejon declined, and go to market carrying the draft-pick toll — joining Jake Bauers, who answered early and in Boston's ink, and whose old employers in Milwaukee duly collect a selection between the first round's end and the compensation round for their trouble.9 History held nearly to form: of the 157 men tendered qualifying offers before this winter, just 18 had ever accepted, roughly 11 in a hundred, and this year's eight produced two.2

The Bronx's yes was the closer's. Bednar, 32, whom the general manager Brian Cashman calls "a cool customer," stays installed in the ninth inning of the bullpen that was the club's difference-maker this past season — and it is the second winter running that a Yankee has taken the tender, the outfielder Trent Grisham having done so a year ago. The books justify the keeping: since his arrival from Pittsburgh in July 2025 the man has pitched to a 2.39 earned-run average with 45 saves across 86 appearances, and this past season he saved 35 games — the most by any Yankee since Chapman's 37 in 2019 — with a 2.47 figure over a career-high 69 and a third innings, surrendering no run in 37 of his final 43 outings. With the submariner Hill already re-inked, as Monday's columns recorded, the winter's declared first priority is being answered largely from within.3

Minnesota's yes came with a flourish of loyalty. "I didn't want to close the chapter on the Minnesota Twins," said Jeffers, the best catcher on the market, whose reported suitors included both New York establishments; he returns instead to the only organization he has known, off a .256/.353/.461 season in 369 plate appearances around a broken hamate bone, and the rulebook holds a quiet sweetener besides — a man may be tendered but once in his career, so his next trip to market carries no toll at all.4 The ripples spread at once: Carson Kelly and Tyler Stephenson become the best catchers at liberty, and Morejon stands alone as the prize of the relief shelf — a man who means to stay in relief work, with a San Diego reunion reckoned strong and the Yankees, Mets, Cubs and Giants in the mix besides.2

THE SILVER BATS FIND THIRTEEN NEW HANDS, THE MOST IN TWENTY YEARS — TWO ROOKIES TAKE SILVER TOGETHER FOR ONLY THE THIRD TIME SINCE THE AWARD WAS STRUCK, THE ASTROS AND CUBS CLAIM THE TEAM PRIZES, AND THE TENTH BAT ELUDES TROUT ANOTHER YEAR

The silverware promised for Tuesday evening arrived on the hour, and the engraver met more new names than he has in twenty years: thirteen of the twenty silver bats went to first-time winners, and two of those to rookies — Kevin McGonigle of Detroit at the utility station and Chase DeLauter of Cleveland in the garden — only the third time since the award was struck in 1980 that two freshmen have taken silver in one year, the prior company being Ichiro and Pujols in 2001 and Nokes and Santiago in 1987. McGonigle collected his beside the Rookie of the Year laurel he already owns, and the Bengals claimed three bats in all, the catcher Dillon Dingler and the outfielder Riley Greene joining him.5

The American roll besides: Pete Alonso, whose 43 home runs led the league, takes a second bat in his first Baltimore year; Chase Meidroth becomes the first White Sox second baseman ever to win one; Junior Caminero, 23, adds silver to a pennant; Bobby Witt Jr. takes a third at shortstop at all of 26; Arozarena, Greene and DeLauter hold the outfield; and Yordan Alvarez — lately laureled the league's Most Valuable, as these columns have recorded — takes the designated hitter's prize off a season that led every qualified bat in the game in average, on-base and slugging alike.5 In the National: Gabriel Moreno of Arizona, whose .311 made him the fifth catcher ever to win a batting title and the first since Buster Posey in 2012 — the same Posey whose name went to the writers only Monday, as yesterday's lead recorded; Matt Olson and his 41 home runs; Lowe, the first Pirate so honored since McCutchen in 2015; Elly De La Cruz, a 30-30 man at last and owner of the best on-base-plus-slugging of any qualified shortstop; Alex Bregman, in his first North Side year; the outfield of Pete Crow-Armstrong — the unanimous Most Valuable, seventh member of the 40-40 fraternity, league-best .943 on-base-plus-slugging — with James Wood and the 22-year-old champion Jackson Chourio beside him; Kyle Schwarber and his 45 home runs at designated hitter; and Bauers, the utility man, adding a silver bat to his October laurels. The team prizes went to the Astros, whose 226 home runs led their league, and the Cubs, whose 850 runs led the whole of the Majors.5

The pursuit this paper carried through the week ended a rung short: Mike Trout, a finalist in the American outfield for what would have been a tenth silver bat — a shelf where only Piazza, with ten, and Bonds, with twelve, keep house — watched the three outfield prizes go to Arozarena, Greene and DeLauter, and the old master must wait another winter.65 The day's finest crossing of ledgers, though, belongs to the almanac: Arozarena and Lowe each took silver within hours of declining a certain $23.15 million — two men betting on themselves with fresh hardware under the arm — and the reader may judge the spirit of the wager by the lead column above.

THE INK DESK: THE WINTER'S FIRST STARTING ARM LANDS ON THE SOUTH SIDE — MAY SIGNS WITH THE PALE HOSE FOR THREE YEARS AND FIFTY-TWO MILLIONS AND A HALF, AND DETROIT MAKES ITS PAGÁN PURCHASE OFFICIAL AT ELEVEN AND A HALF

The starters' market has its first signature. Dustin May — an arm these columns lately called the most democratically courted of the winter after Skubal himself — has agreed with the White Sox on a contract of three years and $52.5 million, by the account of a source, the club not yet confirming; it is the first starting-pitching strike of consequence this offseason.79 The buyers know what they are purchasing: a right-hander of 29 whose career has run from celebrated Dodger prospect and champion of 2020 through the surgeon's whole catalogue — the Tommy John operation, an esophageal tear, a lost 2024 — to two healthy seasons since, the latest a career-high 145 and two-thirds innings split between St. Louis and Milwaukee, where he was fetched at the deadline and served the eventual champions in October as starter and reliever alike.7

The fit is a club on the rise and short of arms. The South Siders won 84 games this past season, entered the playoffs as the sixth seed, swept the Astros in the Wild Card round and won the first two games of the Division Series — with Sean Burke employed as very nearly the lone starter — before Cleveland took three straight; depth was the plainest need on the premises. May joins a rotation picture of Burke, Davis Martin, Luis Castillo, the young Noah Schultz and Grant Taylor, the last moving from the closer's post to starting work in 2027, and the steward Chris Getz is not finished: Freddy Peralta, Clay Holmes and Patrick Sandoval are among the free agents of interest, and the club eyes Kaima Taira, the 27-year-old posted from Japan off a 1.36 earned-run average that led his league.7

Detroit, meanwhile, put its ink to paper. The Tigers made official a contract of one year and $11.5 million, with another million obtainable in bonuses, for the veteran closer Emilio Pagán — who declined his $10 million Cincinnati option on Halloween, whereupon the club president Scott Harris, by his own telling, "picked up the phone and called his agent immediately." The second half of Pagán's season recommends him: back from a hamstring strain in July, he converted all 19 of his save chances with a 1.88 earned-run average and 34 strikeouts against 5 walks, and he inherits the ninth-inning post lately held by Kenley Jansen. The Bengals may count themselves doubly fortunate this morning, for one of the market's few proven closers took himself off it at four o'clock, as the lead column attests.8

THE EXCHANGE DESK: TRADE WINDS BLOW STRAIGHT THROUGH THE LABOR CLOUDS — TEXAS LISTENS ON GORE, THE DURAN MARKET DRAWS ITS MAP, THE YANKEES RING AROZARENA'S PEOPLE, AND THE MEGILL DRUM BEATS A THIRD MORNING RUNNING

The industry's operating theory this winter holds that men with a single year of control left will be hard to move, the 2027 season being clouded by the collective agreement's uncertainty — and the telephones ring regardless. The Athletic reports Texas fielding interest from multiple clubs on the left-hander MacKenzie Gore, acquired from Washington only last offseason at a price of five prospects and now entering his final year of arbitration; the costly veterans Seager, deGrom and Eovaldi are discussed as well, though their wages make heavier freight. Logan Gilbert of Seattle, Nick Lodolo of Cincinnati and the Cream City pair of William Contreras and Trevor Megill draw inquiries besides — the Megill drum having now beaten in these columns three mornings running — while Rasmussen, Ryan and Alcantara sit in the same expiring class but behind doors their clubs have signaled shut.9

In Boston the Duran question has advanced from whether to where. The Bauers purchase filled the last seat in the Fenway garden — Anthony, Rafaela and Abreu hold the outfield, with Bauers and Willson Contreras to rotate between first base and the hitter's chair — and Jarren Duran, 30, coming off a lean .627 season but worth 13.5 wins by FanGraphs' ledger across 2023 to 2025, grows dearer with each arbitration winter. The map of suitors, as MassLive draws it: Houston has shown the heaviest past interest, though a new steward there muddies the reading; San Diego, long an admirer, is doing its background work again; Seattle and Philadelphia make their diligence; and Arizona and the Angels are named as sensible fits. The reader will recall the wire's thirty-club exercise naming Duran for Boston only Monday — the timetable, evidently, advances.9

And the Yankees, their closer question answered, have checked in on Arozarena, the insider Jon Heyman counting them among the clubs to sit with the newly silvered outfielder's camp at last week's meetings. The appeal is arithmetical: only Cleveland and Washington gave more plate appearances to left-handed swingers this past season, and with Judge held to 66 games, the club's right-handed hitters produced a .709 on-base-plus-slugging in sum — while Arozarena, off a 148 OPS+ season of 26 home runs and 26 steals, answers the description exactly. The Orioles and Phillies keep their own interest. As for the winter's grandest courtship, the register merely thickens: at least six clubs are scheduled to sit with Skubal — the Mets, whose Monday audience was reported to have gone very well, with the Padres, Jays and Dodgers also on the list and two mystery establishments besides.9

THE PROSPECT FIELDS: THE FORTY-MAN DOORS SWING SHUT ON RULE 5 EVE — FIFTY-THREE RANKED PROSPECTS IN A HUNDRED AND THIRTY-ONE ARE TUCKED SAFELY ONTO ROSTERS, ALL EIGHT OF THE TOP HUNDRED AMONG THEM, AND THE DECEMBER DRAFTING WAITS ON THE LABOR WEATHER

Tuesday evening brought the quieter of the day's deadlines: by six o'clock every club had set its 40-man roster, and every eligible man left outside the door became fair game for the Rule 5 drafting, appointed for December 9 at the Winter Meetings in San Diego. The almanac notes with a raised eyebrow that the drafting is scheduled for the week after the collective agreement expires, and the wire allows the event could be disturbed if no new accord is reached by then — even the minor calendar, it seems, now consults the labor forecast. The mechanics are unchanged: $100,000 buys a selection, the man must keep a big-league seat the whole season through, and $50,000 offers him back if he cannot.10

The count ran true to recent form: of 131 ranked prospects requiring a decision, 53 were protected, roughly two in five, and all eight eligibles from the game's Top 100 were gathered in without exception — Christian Zazueta of the Dodgers the highest-ranked at No. 33, Washington protecting both Travis Sykora and Jarlin Susana, the Mets adding Jefferson Rojas, and Demetrio Crisantes, Josue Briceño, Nolan Perry and Bryan Rincon tucked away besides — extending a perfect record now twelve years long in which no Top-100 man has ever been left exposed. The Herald notes two names with recent business in these pages: Carter Graham, whose cry of "Best team in the nation, baby!" rang over the Fall League final in Sunday's columns, got his roster spot from Cincinnati, and the champions of Milwaukee found room for the young infielder Jett Williams.10

THE WINTER ISLANDS: VLADDY IS TRADED — COMPOSE YOURSELF, TORONTO, IT IS ONLY THE WINTER LEAGUE — GUERRERO GOES FROM THE TOROS TO LICEY, WHERE HIS FATHER TOOK THE LAST AT-BATS OF A HALL OF FAME CAREER

A headline to stop the Canadian heart crossed the wire Tuesday night: Vladimir Guerrero Jr., traded. The particulars restore the pulse — it is the Dominican Winter League, where the Toros del Este have sent the first baseman's rights to the Tigres del Licey for the relievers Misael Tamárez and Cam Robinson, and the Blue Jays are touched not at all. The island clubs hold a big leaguer's winter rights whether he suits up or no, and Guerrero has not played a LIDOM inning since the winter of 2020-21, when he took the field partly to press his old case for third base; his rights have traveled without him since, once fetching no less a personage than José Ramírez in a 2023 exchange.11

Whether the man himself appears for Licey is unsettled, but the romance of the thing writes itself: his father took the final at-bats of a Hall of Fame career in the Tigres' colors in the winter of 2012-13, at the Estadio Quisqueya in Santo Domingo, and the son now holds the option of batting where the father bowed out. The island season runs through December 22, and the Herald will keep an ear to the water.11

For once the almanac's promises were kept to the hour — answers at four o'clock, silverware by evening — and both accountings stand rendered in the columns above, with the forty-man doors shut and a winter-island curiosity besides. The forward ledger was consulted before a word was written, per the house custom, and tells the story it has told all week: the camps' reporting dates remain unposted, so the count runs to the first rung bearing a date — the spring exhibition openers of Friday, the 19th of February, 93 mornings from this one, with Opening Night to follow on Wednesday, the 24th of March, 126 mornings off.1 Nearer at hand the book thickens rather than thins: the collective agreement has 13 mornings left to live, Cooperstown's committee of sixteen reports in 18, the Winter Meetings convene at San Diego with the Rule 5 drafting on December 9, 21 mornings from this one, and the writers' envelope waits for January 19, 62 mornings off. The stove, in short, is fully lit. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 94 days until the first spring-training game.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 132 · Tuesday, the Seventeenth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

94 days until the first spring-training game (Friday, the 19th of February, 2027).

News Around the League

THE COOPERSTOWN DESK: SEVEN-AND-TWENTY NAMES GO TO THE WRITERS — POSEY AND LESTER HEAD FOURTEEN NEWCOMERS ON THE BALLOT FOR 2027, UTLEY LEADS THE RETURNING CLASS FROM JUST SHY OF SIXTY PERCENT, AND THE ENVELOPE IS APPOINTED FOR THE NINETEENTH OF JANUARY

The writers have been handed their examination paper. The Baseball Writers' Association unveiled its Hall of Fame ballot for 2027 on Monday — 27 names in all, 14 of them standing before the electorate for the first time — and Cooperstown thus has both of its winter questions on the table at once, for the reader will recall from Sunday's columns that a committee of sixteen already weighs eight managers and executives toward a December 6 verdict. The writers' timetable is longer: ballots must be cast by December 31, three-quarters of them spell election, and the results are to be announced on January 19 at 6 o'clock in the evening, with induction at Cooperstown next July 25 — a date the almanac at Baseball-Reference already carries.231

The newcomers are headed by a catcher with little left to prove. Buster Posey of the Giants was Rookie of the Year in 2010, Most Valuable in 2012 — when his .336 average made him the first National League catcher to win a batting title in 70 years — and a champion three times over, in 2010, 2012 and 2014; he batted .302 across twelve seasons with a 129 OPS+ that ties Mickey Cochrane for fourth among catchers of at least a thousand games, and he walked away in 2021 fresh from a .304 season for a Bay nine that won 107 games, retiring at the very top of his powers. Beside him stands Jon Lester, who beat lymphoma in 2007 and threw a no-hitter the following May, and who closed his books at 200 wins, 2,488 strikeouts and three rings — in the Modern Era, only Spahn, Johnson, Glavine and Kershaw among left-handers have matched that ledger of wins, innings and strikeouts at his quality. The supporting bill runs from Brett Gardner, whose 274 stolen bases as a Yankee trail only Jeter and Henderson in that club's books, to Ryan Zimmerman, Mr. National himself and author of 11 walk-off home runs, to Kyle Seager, a Mariner his whole career and nicknamed, with fraternal cruelty, "Corey's Brother."23

Among the holdovers the arithmetic favors Chase Utley, the only returning man above fifty percent: his support leapt 19.3 points last cycle to 59.1, and another such leap elects him. Andy Pettitte stands at 48.5 in his ninth year of ten; Félix Hernández more than doubled his backing in year two, to 46.1; Alex Rodriguez holds at 40; and Omar Vizquel, at 18.4, faces his tenth and final ballot. The Herald will keep the ledger open through the winter.3

THE SKUBAL REGISTER: THE METROPOLITANS COME CALLING IN PERSON — THE FLUSHING NINE HOLD THEIR FIRST AUDIENCE WITH THE WINTER'S PRIZE ARM IN CALIFORNIA, THE WIRE ALREADY CALLS QUEENS HIS EXPECTED DESTINATION, AND THE ASKING TERMS MAY RUN TO TEN YEARS

The courtship of Tarik Skubal has moved from the telephone to the parlor. On Monday the Mets made their first pitch to the two-time Cy Young laureate in person, sitting down with him in Orange County, California — so reports the insider Jon Heyman in the New York Post, by way of the wire's running register on the man.4 The development surprises no one who has read these columns since Las Vegas: the widespread expectation coming out of the general managers' meetings, as the wire's Mark Feinsand reported it, is that Skubal ends up in Queens, one National League executive putting it baldly — "I don't know who else is really even in the conversation."4

The conversation nonetheless has other voices. The Angelenos, who paid three prospects to rent the left-hander at the summer's trade deadline, remain in it, with the Jays and the Mission nine besides — the reader will recall from Sunday's columns that San Diego has a sitting of its own booked. But the shape of the asking favors the deepest purse and the longest patience: Skubal, 29, seeks a long engagement, the figure mentioned running to somewhere between seven and ten years, and both records on the pitchers' ledger — Yamamoto's twelve-year, $325 million guarantee, and the $43.33 million annual wage shared by Scherzer and Verlander — are reckoned to be in danger. The Herald files the Monday meeting under opening formalities, and keeps its register open.4

THE LAW COURTS: THE HOUSE ITSELF TAKES THE STAND IN BROOKLYN — FANDUEL'S MAN TESTIFIES THAT ACCOUNTS IN CLASE'S ORBIT WAGERED ON ORTIZ'S PITCHES TOO, ONE OF THEM COLLECTING TWELVE THOUSAND ON A SINGLE BALL THROWN WIDE

The federal trial of Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz, whose opening testimony this paper's earlier dispatches from the Brooklyn courtroom set down, produced on Monday a witness from the counting-house side of the business. Joshua Mehta, director of legal and regulatory affairs for the house of FanDuel, testified that accounts registered to men linked to Clase during the trial placed heavy wagers on first pitches in two Cleveland games of June 2025 — on the 15th against Seattle and on the 27th against the Cardinals — and that Ortiz was the starting pitcher in both. The bettors risked thousands on the result of a specific pitch without knowing the batter, nor whether the starter would even still be on the hill.5

The particulars have a bookmaker's precision. Against Seattle, the house took a handful of wagers that the first pitch of the bottom of the third inning would be a ball or a hit batsman; several came from an account registered to Enoc Pena — the close associate of Clase's whom earlier testimony placed at the center of the scheme — and when Ortiz threw the pitch outside the strike zone, Pena's wagers collected approximately $12,000. Some of the same accounts bet big on Cleveland's first pitch of the third inning against the Cardinals twelve days later; that one, too, arrived wide. Mehta said at least five of the accounts were suspended in June 2025, the use of inside information being a violation of the house's terms — and the calendar duly records that Ortiz was placed on leave by the league on July 3, with Clase following roughly four weeks after.5

Earlier Monday the cooperating witness Jenner Olivo testified that he won bets on selected Clase pitches across the 2023, 2024 and 2025 seasons on information received from Pena; the government alleges the bettors took at least $400,000 on the result and speed of at least 18 Clase pitches. Both pitchers have pleaded not guilty to conspiracy charges touching wire fraud, sports bribery, honest services and money laundering. And the day closed on a stranger footnote: a FanDuel account registered to Clase himself, opened in May 2023, whose only recorded bets were on basketball — which, the record should note, no rule of the game forbids.5

THE EXCHANGE DESK: BOHM SITS DOWN WITH BOTH NEW YORKS, THE BIRDS DRAW A SHOPPING LIST WITH AROZARENA'S NAME AT ITS HEAD, AND THE WALKER PURCHASE SETS THE WIRE TO ASKING WHETHER MEGILL'S MILWAUKEE DAYS ARE NUMBERED

The corner infielder Alec Bohm has taken meetings with both New York establishments. The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal and Will Sammon report that the Yankees and the Metropolitans each sat with the former Philadelphia man at last week's meetings — and his season explains the double appeal. Bohm's season read a modest .698 in sum, but it concealed an .821 from August 4 onward, after the Quakers moved him across the diamond to first base; the Bronx men could platoon him at third with the left-handed McMahon, while the Mets, whose first basemen produced a .667 mark this past season, third-worst in the majors, might simply hand him the new position outright.6

In Baltimore the shopping list has grown long enough to publish. The Baltimore Banner's Andy Kostka reports the Birds interested in Randy Arozarena, the right-handed outfield bat their lefty-heavy order wants — though the man carries a qualifying offer, and signing him would cost a draft pick's toll to Seattle. Luis Robert Jr., whose $20 million option the club declined after his three-game, hamstring-shortened Baltimore tenure, remains a candidate to return at a friendlier wage; the club is operating with the intent of adding a left-handed starter, with Kris Bubic and Matthew Boyd of interest and a reunion with Trevor Rogers open — the same Rogers expected to decline his tender by this afternoon's deadline in search of a longer engagement. Calls have come in besides on the third baseman Jordan Westburg, and the Marte dialogue these columns recorded Sunday grinds on with no deal near.6

And in Milwaukee, Sunday's reclamation purchase is already casting its shadow. The wire asks plainly whether the acquisition of Ryan Walker — a man with ninth-inning experience and three years of control — makes Trevor Megill, entering his final year before free agency with 81 saves across the last three seasons, the more expendable; the Milwaukees have sold exactly this way before, sending Devin Williams to the Yankees ahead of his own walk year. The reader will note the wire's survey named Megill the club's likeliest man to go only yesterday in these columns; the drumbeat quickens. The left-hander A.J. Minter, meanwhile, has become one of the market's most pursued relievers, the insider Jon Paul Morosi counting the Jays, the Capital nine, the Phillies, the Rangers and the Royals among his suitors after a 2.56 season split between Queens and Minnesota; the Mets, who employed him last, have checked in as well.6

THE INK DESK: THE SPIDER-MAN OF THE CAPITAL GETS HIS FIGURES SET DOWN — YOUNG'S FOUR-YEAR ENGAGEMENT IS FINALIZED AT THREE-AND-TWENTY MILLIONS, AND IN THE DESERT, LAWLAR'S MENDED ELBOW IS EXPECTED BACK FOR THE SEASON'S OPENING

The quiet signature these columns recorded from Las Vegas on the twelfth now has its figures attached. The Nationals have finalized the four-year extension of their center fielder Jacob Young: $23 million guaranteed beginning in 2027, covering three of his arbitration years, with a club option at $8 million for 2031. It is the second extension of the young Toboni administration, following the four years and $47 million settled on the right-hander Cade Cavalli in September — brick by brick, the Capital nine are buying out the questions around their young core of Abrams, Wood, Crews and Lile.7

What the club has secured is the best wall-climber in the business. Young, 27, led all outfielders with 20 outs above average in 2024 and has followed with 14 and 11 in the two seasons since; the clubhouse calls him "Spider-Man," and the nickname earned its keep on August 23, when he covered 93 feet, scaled the wall at Miami, robbed Heriberto Hernández of a home run and threw back to the infield to finish a double play. The bat, long the asterisk on the profile, improved this past season to a .252 average with 10 home runs — doubling his career total at a stroke — a career-best 50 driven in, and 18 steals in 22 tries. A seventh-round selection paid like what he has become: a cornerstone of the game's third-highest-scoring offense.7

From the infirmary ward, one note out of the desert: Jordan Lawlar of the Desert nine underwent internal-brace surgery on his right elbow earlier this offseason, and the club expects the young man ready at or about the start of the regular season.8

THE ALMANAC: THE DAY OF ANSWERS IS AT HAND — SEVEN MEN MUST SPEAK FOR THREE-AND-TWENTY MILLIONS APIECE BY FOUR O'CLOCK THIS AFTERNOON, AND THE SILVER BATS ARE HANDED ROUND THIS EVENING

The day these columns have spent a week pointing toward has arrived. By 4 o'clock this afternoon, Eastern time, every man tendered the qualifying offer must answer: take the certain $23.15 million for 2027, or decline it and carry a draft pick's toll to any new employer. Eight were tendered; Jake Bauers answered early and in Boston's ink, as Saturday's lead recorded; seven answers remain outstanding. The roll deserves printing whole: Arozarena of Seattle, whose 148 OPS+ was the finest full-season figure of his career; Brandon Lowe of Pittsburgh, he of the 35 home runs and the remade glove; Seiya Suzuki of the Cubs, well above the league with the bat across his five American seasons; Rogers of the Birds, whose year away from one rough stretch read a 2.76; Morejon of the Mission nine, the first setup man ever so tendered; the catcher Jeffers of the Twins, quietly sixth among the position's regulars in OPS+ these past four seasons; and Bednar of the Bronx men, 35 saves in 39 chances. History counsels patience with predictions — since the system was instituted in 2012, just 18 men have ever accepted.9

The same evening brings the silver bats, whose finalists yesterday's columns arranged: Trout in pursuit of a tenth, a shelf only Piazza at ten and Bonds at twelve have reached.10 Answers and ornaments together, then — and the Herald will have the whole accounting, tenders and trophies alike, polished and arranged in tomorrow's columns.

A Tuesday that will answer more questions by nightfall than most Novembers answer in a week: seven tenders due by four o'clock, silver bats by evening, and a fresh Cooperstown ballot already circulating among the electors, as the lead column attests. The forward ledger was consulted before the first word, as the house requires, and shows what it showed: the camps' reporting dates await posting, so the count runs to the first rung bearing a date — the spring exhibition openers of Friday, the 19th of February, 94 mornings from this one, with Opening Night to follow on Wednesday, the 24th of March, 127 mornings off.1 The nearer columns of the almanac fill regardless: the collective agreement has 14 mornings left to live, the committee of sixteen reports from Cooperstown in 19, and the writers' envelope is opened in 63, on the 19th of January. The game plays nothing; the docket, meanwhile, has rarely been fuller. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~

entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Sixteenth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 95 days until the first spring-training game.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 131 · Monday, the Sixteenth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

95 days until the first spring-training game (Friday, the 19th of February, 2027).

News Around the League

THE INK DESK: THE LINE FOR LEFT-HANDED RELIEF NEVER SHORTENS — SO THE BRONX DECLINES TO STAND IN IT, KEEPING HILL THE SUBMARINER FOR A YEAR AT TWO MILLIONS AND A QUARTER, THE FIRST BRICK LAID IN A BULLPEN ITS STEWARD CALLS THE WINTER'S MAIN PRIORITY

The Yankees' winter of relief work has begun at home. Tim Hill — the left-hander who delivers from down under, whose name stood in three clubs' notebooks when yesterday's columns surveyed the southpaw market, his admirers numbering the Dodgers, the Mets and his own employers — will stand in no line at all: man and club are agreed on a contract of one year and $2.25 million, with a club option at $2.5 million for 2028, the terms allowed by a source Sunday though the club had not yet confirmed them.2 It is the first move upon the bullpen whose rebuilding Brian Cashman declared, in the quote these columns carried Saturday, "It's our main priority, to be honest" — and the Herald observes that a paper which wrote only yesterday that the line for left-handed relief never shortens has been answered within the day: the simplest way to beat the queue is to own the merchandise already.

What the Pinstripes are keeping is the game's foremost dealer in groundballs. Hill, who turns 37 in January, pitched to a 4.60 earned-run average over 67 appearances and 58 and two-thirds innings this past season — an ordinary figure concealing an extraordinary trade, for his 68.9 percent ground-ball rate led every reliever in the Majors, he stranded 33 of the 35 runners he inherited, and the 5.7 percent of inherited men who came home against him was the stingiest figure in the game. Since New York claimed him in 2024, after a journeyman's road through Kansas City, San Diego and the South Side, he has given the club a 3.34 earned-run average across 172 appearances; the wage is modest, the angle is singular, and the fit is proven.2

The larger rebuilding remains. The Yankee bullpen's 3.13 earned-run average stood second-best in the Majors this past season, and much of it is now at liberty: David Bednar weighs the $23.15 million qualifying tender whose answer falls due tomorrow, with Paul Blackburn, Ryan Yarbrough, John Schreiber and Michael Fulmer free besides, and the club has rung the representatives of Adrian Morejon and of Jonathan Loáisiga — the same Loáisiga yesterday's columns reported nearing a verdict with five clubs bidding.2 The consolation of the market is its stock: the wire's survey of the winter's relievers calls the class at large a lean one but the relief shelf its deepest, with Morejon at the head of it — so the shoppers, in the Bronx and everywhere else, will find the store open all winter.3

THE CHAMPIONS' LEDGER: THE WORLD'S CHAMPIONS SEND TWO ARMS WEST FOR ONE THAT LOST ITS WAY — WALKER, ONCE AMONG THE LEAGUE'S BEST FIREMEN AND LATELY OF THE GIANTS' CELLAR, IS BOOKED INTO THE SAME ESTABLISHMENT THAT MADE MEGILL, WHILE THE WIRE NAMES MEGILL HIMSELF THE WINTER'S LIKELIEST MAN TO GO

Milwaukee has taken in another reclamation. By Sunday's business the champions acquired the right-hander Ryan Walker from the Giants for two minor-league arms — Blake Holub, 28, who pitched to a 2.10 earned-run average with five saves across 50 games at Nashville, and Gavin Perry, 23, an 11th-round selection of the summer's draft who has yet to throw a professional pitch — and the manager made no secret of the method. Pat Murphy likens his pitching laboratory to the "H&H Car Wash," the initials belonging to the coaches Chris Hook and Jim Henderson, who take in arms that have lost their shine and return them gleaming; the establishment's famous customer is Trevor Megill, fetched from obscurity in a minor trade of 2023 after indifferent service with the Cubs and the Twins, and lately the man who recorded the final six outs of the World's Series.4

Walker arrives wanting exactly that treatment. In 2024 he was among the best relief pitchers alive — a 1.91 earned-run average over 76 appearances, ten wins to lead all National League relievers, ten saves, a 0.85 walks-and-hits figure — and in 2026 he was among the most lost, a 7.16 earned-run average in 33 appearances before San Francisco sent him down in May to shuttle between the Bay and the minors. He turns 31 ten mornings hence, on November 26, carries three years of club control, and cost two arms the champions could spare: a wager on the car wash, at the car wash's usual price.4 The bullpen book he joins holds Megill in his final year of arbitration alongside Abner Uribe, Aaron Ashby, DL Hall and Chad Patrick, with Antonio Senzatela and JoJo Romero at liberty — and the reader should mark that the wire's man, surveying trade candidates for all thirty clubs this morning, names Megill himself the champion likeliest to be moved, three mornings after the front office serenaded him in these columns from a Metallica concert at the Sphere.5 The telephone in Milwaukee, as this paper has observed of the catcher Contreras, does not distinguish between the men it rings for.

The rotation behind them poses the winter's quieter question: which Kyle Harrison reports to the spring. Through 11 starts the young left-hander owned a 1.57 earned-run average with 73 strikeouts in 57 and a third innings — second in the game in strikeouts per nine — before a forearm complaint and an August return that found the fastball dimmed; from August onward he pitched to a 7.31 figure over 32 innings and finished the season in the bullpen, unused through October. The ailment was reckoned mild, the underlying numbers kinder than the surface ones, and the house arithmetic is plain: the April version makes a front three with Misiorowski and Logan Henderson, while Woodruff and May sit among the free agents.6

THE PINSTRIPE VACANCY: CHISHOLM GOES TO MARKET UNTENDERED AND SECOND BASE STANDS OPEN IN THE BRONX — THE WIRE NOMINATES LOWE OF THE SMOKY CITY, WHOSE FIVE-AND-THIRTY HOME RUNS WERE DRAWN, NEARLY EVERY ONE, TOWARD A PORCH LIKE THE ONE AT THE STADIUM

The same Bronx front office keeping its left-hander has a vacancy up the middle. Jazz Chisholm Jr. has gone to the open market after two seasons and more in pinstripes, and the club declined to attach a qualifying offer to him — a quiet verdict of its own, for the tender it did extend went to the closer Bednar. Chisholm's season explains the hesitation: 19 home runs with a .399 slugging mark, the underlying measurements grading his contact at a .366 expected slug, down in the 24th percentile of the league, though his glovework at second — 15 outs above average, the best of his career — will be missed by a defense that can ill spare it. The internal answers are familiar: Anthony Volpe, who moved to second when young George Lombard Jr. took shortstop, with the utility men José Caballero and Luis García Jr. behind him.7

The wire's suggestion is Brandon Lowe, the left-handed second baseman who struck 35 home runs with an .824 on-base-plus-slugging for Pittsburgh this past season — a Ray for seven and a half years before the Smoky City nine acquired him in mid-2025.8 The case is a matter of architecture. Of his 35 home runs, 32 went to right field, pulled in the air at a career-high rate — and he compiled them in the yard the statisticians rank 27th of 30 for the long ball, while Yankee Stadium, with its short right porch, ranks among the friendliest; by Statcast's reckoning the same batted balls at the Stadium would have numbered 39. Nor is the glove the liability it was: from ten runs below average in 2025 he swung to twelve above in 2026, third-best at the position and a finalist for the National League's Gold Glove, tied for the largest year-over-year turnaround the measurers have recorded. For a lineup that hit 223 home runs, second-most in the game, yet batted ten percent below league average while Judge convalesced from the first of June to the seventh of September — only the Angels fared worse in that stretch — the appeal writes itself. The club enters its 18th year without a championship, tied for the longest such passage since Ruth came over in 1919; the winter's shopping list, bullpen first and second base close behind, is drawn up accordingly.7

THE EXCHANGE DESK: ONE NAME PINNED TO EVERY CLUBHOUSE DOOR — THE WIRE'S MAN NOMINATES A TRADE CANDIDATE FOR ALL THIRTY CLUBS, AND THE HERALD FINDS HALF ITS WINTER'S STORYLINES ALREADY ON THE LIST

The wire's senior correspondent has performed the winter's great parlor exercise — one plausible trade candidate named for every club in the land — and the Herald, reading down the list, keeps meeting its own back pages.5 Jarren Duran stands for Boston, the outfielder an evaluator called "clearly available" in Saturday's columns, his outfield crowded further by the Bauers purchase. Shane McClanahan stands for the Tampa men, confirming the sorting these pages recorded Saturday of the pennant-winners' rotation into the kept and the biddable. Ketel Marte stands for the Snakes — the twice-silvered second baseman whose dialogue with Baltimore filled yesterday's columns, his ten-and-five veto noted in the same breath — and for the Baltimores themselves the nominee is Jackson Holliday, the young infielder whose September wrist surgery helped open the very vacancy Marte would fill: the buyer's own candidate, in other words, is the price the seller may ask. George Kirby stands for the mariners of the Sound, one of the two names these columns reckoned likeliest to be had when Dipoto allowed on Friday that his rotation was eight deep and his lineup listing.5

The fresher entries concern the coasts. For the Dodgers the nominee is Teoscar Hernández, whose departure would clear a garden spot for the prospect Josue De Paula; for the Yankees it is Jasson Domínguez, the once-celebrated young outfielder still without a settled station, squeezed now by the arrival of Spencer Jones. Add the champions' Megill, treated in the column above, and the exercise reads less like speculation than like a timetable: the names the winter has been circling, now written down in one place.5

THE ALMANAC: THE SEVENTEENTH ARRIVES ON THE MORROW BEARING ANSWERS AND SILVERWARE TOGETHER — QUALIFYING VERDICTS FALL DUE AT LAST, AND THE SILVER BATS ARE HANDED ROUND WITH TROUT IN PURSUIT OF A TENTH, COMPANY ONLY PIAZZA AND BONDS HAVE KEPT

The appointment this paper's calendar has carried for a week arrives tomorrow, and it is a double one. The qualifying offers meet their deadline: Bednar of the Yankees and Morejon of the Padres are among the men still dragging the $23.15 million tender behind them, and by evening each must take the certain money or the open market — the reader will recall that Bauers answered his tender early, in Boston's ink, and that the compensation machinery has already begun to grind in Milwaukee.2

The same evening brings the silver bats. The Silver Slugger awards, whose finalists were posted on the fifth of the month, are to be revealed tomorrow, and the ornament of the slate is Mike Trout: the old master seeks his tenth silver bat, a shelf only Mike Piazza, with ten, and Barry Bonds, with twelve, have ever reached, and his case is honest — an .803 on-base-plus-slugging across 142 games, his best figure in ten years. Elsewhere among the finalists stand the newly laureled Alvarez, who led the game in each leg of the batting line; Alonso of the Baltimores and his league-best 43 home runs; and Bauers again, nominated at first base and in the utility class alike — while the team prize for the best offense in each league pits the Astros, Tampa men, Twins and White Sox in the American against the champions, the Cubs, the Boys in Blue and the Nationals in the National.9 The Herald will have the verdicts in Wednesday's columns, polished and arranged.

A Monday on which the winter kept its shops open through the weekend: a left-hander retained in the Bronx, a reclamation project carted into Milwaukee, and the morrow's docket already posted, as the almanac column attests — qualifying answers and silver bats together on the seventeenth. The forward ledger was ruled open before a word was written, per the house custom, and stands unchanged: the camps' reporting dates are still to be posted, so the paper counts to the first rung bearing a date — the spring exhibition openers of Friday, the 19th of February, 95 mornings from this one — with Opening Night to follow on Wednesday, the 24th of March, 128 mornings off.1 Nearer at hand, the collective agreement has 15 mornings left to live, and Cooperstown's sixteen electors report their verdict on December 6, 20 mornings from this one. The game plays nothing and decides everything, which is November's whole constitution. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
