Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 96 days until the first spring-training game.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 130 · Sunday, the Fifteenth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

96 days until the first spring-training game (Friday, the 19th of February, 2027).

News Around the League

THE PROSPECT FIELDS: PEORIA TAKES THE DESERT'S LAST PRIZE — THE JAVELINAS BREAK SURPRISE 8-3 FOR AN EIGHTH FALL LEAGUE CROWN, THE MOST IN THE CIRCUIT'S BOOKS AND THEIR FIRST SINCE 2018, BEHIND FIVE SCORELESS INNINGS FROM HOLMAN OF THE QUEEN CITY CHAIN

The desert kept its appointment. The Fall League championship that Saturday's columns commended to every restless scorecard hand was decided at the Peoria Sports Complex on Saturday night, and it was the home club's evening throughout: the Peoria Javelinas 8, the Surprise Saguaros 3, and the title — an eighth for Peoria, the most any club has gathered in the circuit's history and its first since 2018 — was denied to the defending champions, finalists now seven autumns running. The occasion extended one of the minor calendar's quieter marvels besides: one of these two clubs has appeared in the title game in each of the last 17 seasons, the last final without either being played in 2008. Carter Graham of Cincinnati's chain supplied the victors' epigraph, shouting to anyone in earshot, "Best team in the nation, baby!"2

Luke Holman, whom Saturday's columns sent to the hill trailing a 0.69 earned-run average, pitched precisely to the billing: five scoreless innings, six strikeouts, 16 swings-and-misses drawn across three offerings — a fastball at 92 to 94 mph, a splitter, a curve — and the game's honors as its best player. The evening's loudest contact belonged to his systemmate Yerlin Confidan, the Fall Stars Game's Most Valuable man, who ripped a single at 116.7 mph and a double at 110.3 in a 3-for-4 night, while Graham added two singles and a walk. Justin DeCriscio of the San Diego chain lined an RBI double, Brandon Eike of the Seattle chain another; Ike Irish, the young Baltimore outfielder whose sacrifice fly had won the semifinal, went hitless yet scored twice, drove in a run and stole a bag; Kannon Kemp threw the 13 hardest pitches of the night across two scoreless innings of relief; and Francis Peña ran his heater to 97.5 mph in the ninth to lock the trophy away.2

The champions' ledger reads like a period of its own: 219 runs scored, the most of any club across the six-week term, and 112 stolen bases in 28 games — 16 clear of the next-nearest club, the circuit having experimented this autumn with a single disengagement per plate appearance. The whole enterprise answered to Danny Worth, a man of parts of six big-league seasons who had never managed at any level before this fall, and who, dripping with the remains of the water cooler, allowed that he might simply retire on top: "We're gonna be watching all these guys on TV for a long time." And the autumn's individual laurel went where these columns said it belonged — Welbyn Francisca of the Lake Erie chain, whose .427 average led the league, was named winner of the Joe Black Award as its Most Valuable player, a consolation carried home in Surprise's otherwise empty luggage.2

THE EXCHANGE DESK: THE FRIARS, SHORT SEVEN STARTERS, GO COURTING EVERY ARM AT LIBERTY — A SITTING WITH SKUBAL IS BOOKED, OLD FRIENDS KING AND PIVETTA ARE EYED FOR REUNION, AND THE DODGERS JOIN A FIVE-CLUB QUEUE FOR LOÁISIGA

San Diego's winter brief is written in a single line of its general manager's: "you can never have too much" starting pitching — and A.J. Preller, who is losing seven starting pitchers to free agency at a stroke, is conducting himself accordingly. The Friars stand among the most active clubs in the starters' market and are leaving no door unknocked: a meeting is booked with Tarik Skubal himself, adding San Diego's name formally to the suitors' register these columns have kept all week; reunions are eyed with Michael King and Nick Pivetta, former men of the Mission both; and the club has expressed interest in Freddy Peralta — the right-hander who rediscovered his best self after the midseason trade to Tampa Bay and carried the honors of the league championship series in October — as well as Nick Martinez, whose career-best year read 31 starts, a first All-Star nod and the Game 1 assignment of the World Series, and who pitched to a 3.45 earned-run average in San Diego colors in 2022 and 2023. The register runs on: Matthew Boyd, Shota Imanaga and Dustin May — the last of whom yesterday's columns called the most democratically courted arm of the winter after Skubal — have all had their doors knocked as well.3

The relief market, meanwhile, nears its first verdict. Jonathan Loáisiga is reported "getting closer" to his next contract, with five clubs in the bidding — the Dodgers, Phillies, Mets, Yankees and Jays — for a right arm that rebounded from two injury-ruined seasons to a 2.42 earned-run average over 67 appearances in Arizona's employ. The Dodgers are also named among the pursuers of Tim Hill, the submarining left-hander lately of the Bronx, whose admirers include the Mets and his former Yankee employers besides — for in this winter's market, as in every winter's, the line for left-handed relief never shortens.3

THE SONORAN QUESTION, A SECOND WINTER RUNNING: THE BIRDS COME CALLING FOR MARTE — BALTIMORE AND ARIZONA ARE IN DIALOGUE ON THE TWICE-SILVERED SECOND BASEMAN, NO DEAL NEAR, AND THE MAN HIMSELF HOLDS THE VETO

The Marte question, which these columns found reopened at Las Vegas on Thursday, has produced its first named suitor. The Orioles have dialogued with the Diamondbacks regarding Ketel Marte — so a source allowed on Saturday evening — though no deal was imminent and neither club would confirm the discussions; the Jays, shopping for hitters generally, are reported among the interested as well. Arizona's steward Mike Hazen has supplied the winter's framing himself: "I just think I need to be open to making adjustments to what the roster looks like."43

The fit at Baltimore is at once obvious and awkward. Obvious, because the Birds drew a collective .628 on-base-plus-slugging from second base this past season, the fourth-worst figure in the majors, while Jackson Holliday, 22, long cast as the second baseman of the future, fought injuries culminating in September wrist surgery. Awkward, because the infield house is already crowded — so crowded that Mike Elias allows the club has spoken with some infielders about taking outfield work this spring. Yet Baltimore has shown exactly this appetite before: a year ago it wanted no first baseman and signed Pete Alonso to five years and $155 million anyway, a purchase that has aged handsomely.4

As for the man, the ledger states the case plainly. Marte is 33, a three-time All-Star and twice a Silver Slugger, a .277 hitter across 1,371 games with 193 home runs and an .815 on-base-plus-slugging; this past season he batted .249 with 22 home runs and a .748 mark in 141 games, around a brief August stay on the restricted list after failing to appear for a game at Fenway Park — an absence of some two weeks, closed with an apology to his manager and his teammates and a quiet, blameless remainder of the season. Four guaranteed years remain on his $116.5 million extension, with a player option for 2031 behind them, and his ten years of service — the last five in one uniform — give him the veto over any destination proposed. The desert may open the question; only Marte can close it.4

THE TRADE WINDS BLOW THROUGH SHORTSTOP COUNTRY — CALLERS RING THE WHITE ELEPHANTS ON WILSON, THE LONE STAR NINE LISTEN ON SEAGER, AND THE FISH FIELD OFFERS ON THREE YOUNG REGULARS AT ONCE

The winter's trade talk has found the game's middle infield. Bob Nightengale of USA TODAY reports that clubs have called the Athletics to inquire after Jacob Wilson — a name that would have seemed untouchable a year ago, when the shortstop batted .311 as a rookie, became the first rookie shortstop ever elected by the fans to start an All-Star Game for the American League, and finished second in the Rookie of the Year balloting to his own teammate Nick Kurtz. The Elephants extended him for seven years and $70 million before the 2026 season, control running through at least 2032; the season that followed is the reason the callers think it worth dialing — a .266 average over just 80 games, three separate trips to the injured list, and a nagging left shoulder that ended his year in mid-August. He turns 25 in March. Elsewhere in the shortstop country, the Lone Star nine are reportedly listening on Corey Seager, while Washington's CJ Abrams is held unlikely to move.3

And in Miami, Barry Jackson of the Miami Herald reports the Fish fielding offers on three young regulars at once: the middle infielders Otto Lopez and Xavier Edwards — for whom the club "would want a ton to even consider moving" either — and the first baseman and outfielder Kyle Stowers. The asking prices have their reasons. Lopez, 28, was a first-time All-Star who led the majors with 191 hits, stole 34 bases and saved 14 outs above average at shortstop; Edwards, 27, batted .280 with a .360 on-base mark and 21 steals, worth three wins above replacement in each of the past two seasons; Stowers, 28, struck 21 home runs with a .790 on-base-plus-slugging through hamstring strains in each leg, a year after 25 and .912. All three are under club control through 2029 — which is precisely why the offers keep arriving, and precisely why Miami need accept none of them.3

THE COOPERSTOWN DESK: EIGHT NAMES GO BEFORE THE SIXTEEN — BOCHY OF THE FOUR TITLES AND MADDON OF THE BROKEN CURSE HEAD THE CONTEMPORARY ERA BALLOT, WITH BAKER, PINIELLA, ALDERSON, SABEAN, TURNER AND WHITE BESIDE THEM, THE VERDICT DUE THE SIXTH OF DECEMBER

The village on Otsego Lake has posted its winter docket. The Contemporary Baseball Era ballot — the committee's turn, this cycle, to weigh managers, executives and umpires — carries eight names: Sandy Alderson, Dusty Baker, Bruce Bochy, Joe Maddon, Lou Piniella, Brian Sabean, Ted Turner and Bill White. A 16-member panel of Hall of Fame players, executives, writers and historians will sit in judgment, twelve votes of the sixteen being required for election, and the results for the Class of 2027 are to be announced on December 6 — 21 mornings from this one.56

Two managers head the bill. Bochy's credentials scarcely require the committee's reading glasses: 2,252 wins, sixth on the all-time roll, with the five men above him — Mack, La Russa, McGraw, Cox and Torre — already enshrined; four World Series titles, making him the sixth manager to win so many and the first to do it for two clubs, the fourth ring fetched from retirement in his first Texas summer. "It's unthinkable for something like this to happen," says the man, 71, with a catcher's modesty. Maddon's case is the romantic's: 1,382 wins across parts of 19 seasons in Tampa Bay, Chicago and Anaheim — one of 35 managers to reach 1,300, and one of only 16 of those to win at a .532 clip or better — three Manager of the Year awards, two pennants, and the 2016 championship that ended the North Siders' 108-year wait, delivered by a man who governed with mantras ("9=8," "Try Not to Suck") and wore No. 70 on his back. His partisans have already minted the campaign slogan: Respect 70.5

The Herald notes, for the completeness of the record, that the remaining six names span the game's whole administration — Baker and Piniella from the dugout, Alderson and Sabean from the front office, Turner from the owner's box and White from the league presidency — and that a committee's arithmetic is harder than a season's. Eight worthies, sixteen electors, and three weeks to the envelope.5

A Sunday of consequence for the almanac: with the desert's trophy handed over, as the lead column records, the last diamond in the land occupied by big-league organizations has gone dark,2 and the American game is now, until the camps open, a matter of ledgers, telephones and ballots. The forward ledger was ruled open before a word was written, per the house custom, and stands unchanged: the camps' reporting dates are still to be posted, so the paper counts to the first rung bearing a date — the spring exhibition openers of Friday, the 19th of February, 96 mornings from this one — with Opening Night to follow on Wednesday, the 24th of March, 129 mornings off.1 The nearer appointments crowd the book regardless: Tuesday the 17th brings the qualifying answers and the silver bats together, as this paper's calendar has long carried; the collective agreement has 16 mornings left to live; and Cooperstown's sixteen electors report their verdict on December 6. The game has stopped playing, but it has by no means stopped keeping score. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~

entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 97 days until the first spring-training game.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 129 · Saturday, the Fourteenth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

97 days until the first spring-training game (Friday, the 19th of February, 2027).

News Around the League

THE INK DESK: THE ANSWER ARRIVES FOUR DAYS EARLY — BAUERS, HERO OF THE LATE OCTOBER, TAKES EIGHT-AND-FIFTY MILLIONS OVER FOUR YEARS FROM THE CRIMSON HOSE, AND THE CHAMPIONS, WHO KNOW THIS RITUAL BY HEART, STAND TO POCKET A PREMIUM PICK FOR THEIR TROUBLE

The answer was not due until Tuesday. The qualifying offer that Milwaukee tendered its first baseman carried a deadline of the 17th — an appointment this paper's ledger has kept all week — and Jake Bauers answered it four days early, in another club's ink. The Red Sox and the hero of the late October have agreed on a contract of four years and $58 million, pending a physical, the figures confirmed to MLB.com's Mark Feinsand after ESPN's Jeff Passan first carried the report: the largest signature of the young offseason, and the first of the winter's dominoes to fall with an audible report.23 The purchase is Boston doctrine made flesh. Craig Breslow, the president of baseball operations, had lately observed that a club without obvious holes must be "open-minded, flexible and opportunistic" in its improving, and an attack that finished 26th in home runs and 20th in slugging has now bought itself the most patient bat on the open market.2

What the Fenway men are buying is a career year with the receipts to argue it no accident. Bauers, 30, batted .266 with a .389 on-base mark and a .484 slug across 578 plate appearances, struck a team-high 26 home runs and drove in 86; he walked at a 16.3 percent rate that stood in the 98th percentile of the league, and by the Statcast ledger he hit the ball harder than ever in his life — an average exit speed of 92.1 mph, a hard-hit rate of 51.9 percent, a barrel rate of 14 percent, every one of them above the 90th percentile — though the whiffs remain plentiful, his 27 percent strikeout rate being the price of the patience.2 October wants no retelling in these columns, but shall have a little anyway: the 12-pitch walk that set up the second game's victory in the league championship set, the go-ahead clout off Blake Snell at the end of an 11-pitch audience in the third, the series' Most Valuable honor as the Suds men swept the two-time defending titleholders of Los Angeles — and a quiet Fall Classic that mattered not at all, his club winning it in five. Nor should the romance beneath the figures go unrecorded: after the 2024 season, when he batted .199, Bauers was minded to give the game up entirely, until his wife, Lauren, revealed she was expecting, and the man reconsidered. Two years from that crossroads he is a champion with $58 million in promised wages.2 The fit at Boston is a winter's puzzle happily deferred — Willson Contreras keeps first base, the designated place is shared with Masataka Yoshida in the final year of his engagement — but the Monster's wall stands 310 feet from the plate, and Bauers' habit of taking his singles and doubles the other way will find it a friendly neighbor.2

And in Milwaukee, the ritual plays out precisely as the house has rehearsed it. Because the Cream City men extended their qualifying offer and the man signed elsewhere for more than $50 million, they stand to receive a compensation pick between the end of the first round and the start of Competitive Balance Round A in next summer's draft — the same toll collected when Willy Adames took the Giants' $182 million two winters ago, a toll that became the 32nd pick and the prep shortstop Brady Ebel, today the fourth-ranked prospect in their system.4 The succession at first base is already sketched: Andrew Vaughn, the right-handed half of the late platoon, enters his final year of arbitration, and the minors offer Blake Burke, 23, a left-handed hitter who struck 34 home runs between Biloxi and Nashville this past season.4 The method — the contract-year man exchanged for tomorrow, which yesterday's columns rehearsed in the catcher's context — has thus claimed its newest entry, and the question those columns weighed concerning William Contreras acquires a sharper edge this morning: Milwaukee has now lost the first baseman who handed its manager the final-out ball, and the telephone about the catcher has not stopped ringing.

THE EXCHANGE DESK: THE WRIGLEY MEN GO SHOPPING FOR A ROTATION ENTIRE AND KNOCK ON FIVE DOORS AT ONCE, BOSTON'S NEW PURCHASE CROWDS ITS OWN HOUSE, THE GULF COAST CLUB KEEPS ITS ACE AND LEAVES TWO OTHERS ON THE SHELF IN VIEW, AND MORE THAN HALF THE LEAGUE COMES CALLING FOR ONE LEFT ARM

The Cubs' predicament, which these columns set out yesterday — a unanimous laureate in center field and not one incumbent starting pitcher — now has a shopping list attached. To the five free agents of the late rotation add the swingman Colin Rea, also at liberty, and Jameson Taillon, moved along in August: seven arms that made 121 starts for Chicago this past season, all gone, with Javier Assad the lone returning starter coming off a healthy year.5 The register of targets runs wide: Michael King, a pairing the MLB Network's man calls long forecasted; Kaima Taira, the Japanese right-hander who led his league with a 1.36 earned-run average over 146 innings, in whom Chicago's interest is reported strong; Freddy Peralta, whom Craig Counsell managed for years in Milwaukee and whom the Athletic's correspondent calls an obvious fit; Trevor Rogers; and Dustin May. The club is also said to want Clay Holmes and David Peterson back from its own departed shelf.5

May, as it happens, is the winter's most democratically courted arm — the pitcher drawing the most interest at the meetings after Skubal himself, with the Cubs, White Sox, Padres, Astros and Marlins all in the circle. His 4.70 earned-run average across 145 and two-thirds innings for St. Louis and Milwaukee is no ornament, but the velocity has climbed back toward its early-career marks, his strikeout-minus-walk figure was a five-year best, and at 29 he is among the youngest starters at liberty.5 At Boston, meanwhile, the morning's lead item casts its shadow sideways: with Bauers installed and Contreras at first, the house is crowded, and the trade talk now turns on Jarren Duran — "clearly available," one National League evaluator says of the oft-rumored outfielder, though his cratered season and climbing wage complicate the return — and on the squeezed first baseman Triston Casas, whose accustomed stations are now doubly occupied.5 And on the Gulf Coast, the pennant-winners have sorted their rotation into the kept and the biddable: Erik Neander professes "every intention" of holding his ace Drew Rasmussen, whose $20 million option — the largest single-season wage in the franchise's books — was exercised last month, while the trade reports a deal involving Shane McClanahan or Ryan Pepiot a live possibility, both men lately acquainted with the surgeon and each a year or two from the open market.5

The relief market, where the only actual ink of the meetings was spilled — Phillips, Pagán and Weiss, all chronicled in these columns this week — still holds its marquee names: David Bednar and Adrian Morejon, each dragging a qualifying offer behind him, with Raisel Iglesias and Kenley Jansen at liberty besides. In the Bronx the matter is declared urgent. "It's our main priority, to be honest," Brian Cashman says of his bullpen, two of whose three late-innings keepers — Bednar, tendered at $23.15 million, and Paul Blackburn — are free agents: "I am casting a wide net. We are asking around, and we need to find some stuff so we can feel good and sleep at night."6 The Yankees would have Morejon should Bednar walk, and would keep their left-hander Tim Hill — the same Hill the Mets are sniffing at, that club being linked to nearly every southpaw at liberty: Hill, Brooks Raley, A.J. Minter and Alex Vesia, the last of whom is reported to interest more than half the clubs in the league. One left arm, and a queue at the door sixteen clubs long at the least: the winter's arithmetic in miniature.5

THE DUGOUT DESK: AUSMUS TAKES THE HOUSTON CHAIR WITH BAGWELL AND BIGGIO IN THE FRONT ROW — A FOUR-HOUR LUNCH AT SAN DIEGO SEALED THE MATCH, AND THE NEW MAN DECLINES ALL TALK OF GLORY DAYS

The homecoming this paper recorded on Thursday was made ceremonial on Friday. Brad Ausmus was introduced as manager of the Astros at Daikin Park, with Jeff Bagwell and Craig Biggio, his old teammates, seated in the front row — and the story behind the hiring, told at last, turns out to have begun with a disappointment. Ausmus left the park on October 29 after interviewing for the general manager's position and told his wife, Liz, he did not expect to get it; he was right, Randy Flores being hired a day later. But Flores telephoned within days, offered to travel to San Diego, and the two men clicked over a four-hour lunch — Flores having first done his diligence through, among others, Aaron Boone, his college teammate and lately Ausmus's employer in the Yankee coaching rooms.7

The introduction had its vaudeville — Flores, a pitcher in his playing days, asked from the dais whether Ausmus had owned him at the plate, and got back "I was 0-for-1 with a walk, and that's the truth" — but the new manager kept the sentiment on a short leash. "Looking back on my career, if I picture myself, it's wearing an Astros uniform," he said. "That being said, I'm not here to talk about the glory days. I'm here to talk about the Astros today, and the Astros going into 2027, which is now my main focus, and certainly the goal is to win the World Series." The work is considerable: a coaching staff to assemble, a bench coach first among the vacancies, and a roster that, for all the pleasure of writing the newly laureled Alvarez into the middle of its order, was swept from October's opening round and wants improving in several departments. Berkman and Oswalt have already rung with congratulations; the Herald suspects the congratulatory period will be brief.7

THE FAR PACIFIC DESK: THE EASTBOUND TRAFFIC THICKENS — KOO, MOST VALUABLE OF THE KOREAN SERIES, ENGAGES AN AGENT TO TRY THE AMERICAN MARKET AT FOUR-AND-THIRTY

The procession across the Pacific, which brought Teruaki Sato's name to these columns on Tuesday and Kaima Taira's to the exchange desk above, now adds a Korean chapter. Ja-Wook Koo, the 33-year-old corner outfielder of the Samsung Lions — he turns 34 in February — has engaged Jaron Long of the Mako Corporation to explore a move to the Majors.8 The credentials are a batting champion's: a .371 average this past season, the best in his league, with a .458 on-base mark, 15 home runs and 102 driven in across 114 games, his 1.039 OPS standing third among the circuit's qualified hitters; and when the Lions reached the Korean Series he batted .500 over the five-game set and was named its Most Valuable man. A left-handed hitter twelve seasons in the same uniform, he brings a career line of .322, which is the sort of number that travels well in any language. Where the younger Sato commands projections running toward nine figures, Koo's age makes him the value proposition of the eastbound register — and the Herald, which has watched this winter's market grow more international by the morning, adds his name to the watch list with pleasure.8

THE PROSPECT FIELDS: THE DESERT CROWNS ITS CHAMPION THIS EVENING — SURPRISE, SEVEN TIMES RUNNING A FINALIST, MEETS PEORIA FOR THE FALL LEAGUE TITLE BEHIND A SEMIFINAL IN WHICH ONE MAN DROVE HOME SEVEN

The prospect calendar of 2026 closes this very evening. The Arizona Fall League, finishing school of the rising class, stages its championship game tonight at the Peoria Sports Complex, 8 o'clock Eastern on the MLB Network: the Surprise Saguaros, in the final for a seventh consecutive autumn, against the Peoria Javelinas, whom they beat for last year's title — the two clubs having posted the circuit's two best records besides.9 The semifinals supplied their own theater. Cole Mathis, a first baseman in the Mets' chain, drove in seven runs — a Fall League playoff record — in Surprise's 10-4 dispatch of Glendale, while Peoria edged Salt River 6-5 on a decisive sacrifice fly from Ike Irish, the Orioles' young outfielder.9

The pitching assignment alone recommends the broadcast: Peoria sends Luke Holman of Cincinnati's system, who returned from elbow surgery to lead the league in earned-run average at 0.69 and hold the desert's hitters to a .114 average, against Justin Lamkin of the Kansas City chain. And whatever this evening decides, the autumn's breakout belongs already to Welbyn Francisca of Cleveland's system, who led the circuit in hitting at .427, in slugging, in OPS, in hits, in total bases and in runs driven in — a $1.375 million signing out of the Dominican Republic making a loud case for larger stages. The Herald commends the fixture to any reader whose scorecard hand has grown restless these sixteen gameless mornings.9

A Saturday on which the winter found its voice. The silver season adjourned Thursday night; by Friday afternoon the market had produced its first great signature, as the lead column attests, and the desk observes that the sport allowed itself scarcely a night's repose between the last trophy and the first fortune. The forward ledger was ruled open before a word was written, per the house custom, and it stands as it stood: the camps' reporting dates are still to be posted, so the paper counts to the first rung with a date on it — the spring exhibition slate of Friday, the 19th of February, 97 mornings from this one, with Opening Night to follow 130 mornings off, on Wednesday, the 24th of March.1 Nearer at hand, the desert plays its Fall League championship this very evening, as the prospect column records, and the 17th keeps its appointment three mornings hence — qualifying answers and silver bats together — though one answer, as the reader now knows, has already come back early and addressed to Boston. The collective agreement has 17 mornings left to live, and the week's dealings suggest the clubs intend to spend them busily. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
